item.title: Coding agents
item.description:
Running an agent

An agent runs where you start it, so you start it in the VM’s shell, not on this machine. On this machine, devvm opens the VM’s shell, and the VM’s prompt starts with (devvm):

~/some-project $ devvm
(devvm) ~/some-project $ claude

In the VM the agent sees only your project folder, and your agents’ settings from devvm’s agent store, which it gets read-only. Whatever it runs, such as a script a package installs, runs in the VM too. You don’t install any agent on this machine, because devvm installs each one in the VMs that have it.

The guide in every VM

Every VM has a guide to devvm for the agents in it, at /usr/share/doc/devvm/README.md, and devvm-help in the VM prints it. It tells an agent what a devvm VM is, how its network tiers and secrets work, where its installs go, and which commands to ask you to run on this machine, such as devvm network allow for a blocked host or devvm agent login for a login. The guide is the same in every VM, so it says nothing about the VM’s own tier, ports or layers. Each launch installs it again whenever it differs from devvm’s, and it belongs to root and is read-only, so nothing that the VM’s user runs without sudo can change what the agents read, and a change made with sudo lasts only until the next launch. Ask your agent to read it, or to run devvm-help, when it doesn’t know where it’s running. devvm adds nothing about it to the agents’ instruction files.

Supported agents

A new VM gets an agent when you choose it as you customize the VM, or when you name it with --agents. A VM that exists gets one from devvm tools, which shows the same list with the VM’s agents already chosen, or from devvm tools add:

devvm # a new VM: customize it, then choose its agents in the list
devvm --agents claude,codex # a new VM with Claude Code and Codex, without the list
devvm tools # the VM that exists: choose its agents in the list
devvm tools add opencode # the VM that exists: add opencode without the list

In the VM, you run each agent by its name in the table, such as claude.

Name Agent What devvm adds Allowlist, on the allowlist and none tiers
claude Claude Code the newest release, with its auto-update off, since the shared copy is read-only, and its telemetry off Anthropic’s API, Claude’s login and Claude Code’s downloads: api.anthropic.com, claude.ai, downloads.claude.ai, platform.claude.com and mcp-proxy.anthropic.com
codex Codex the newest release, with its analytics and metrics off unless your config sets them the OpenAI API and the ChatGPT login: api.openai.com, chatgpt.com and auth.openai.com
opencode opencode the newest 2.x release, because opencode marks its 1.x releases as its latest on GitHub opencode’s own service and its model catalog: opencode.ai and models.opencode.ai
pi pi the newest release, with its check for a newer pi and its install report off, and fd, which pi finds files with, in base pi’s model catalog: pi.dev

Claude Code’s telemetry hosts aren’t on its allowlist, because blocking them costs nothing. opencode and pi talk to the model provider you choose, so on the allowlist tier you allow that provider’s API host yourself, such as devvm network allow api.anthropic.com (changing rules), unless devvm keeps the agent’s login or API key for that provider, because the VM’s proxy then allows its host. Every VM sets OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATE=1, as it sets DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1 for Claude Code, because the agents are read-only shared tools that can’t update themselves, and devvm keeps their versions. For the same reason every VM sets PI_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1, so pi doesn’t ask you to run pi update, and PI_TELEMETRY=0, which turns off pi’s report of its install and the attribution headers it adds to some providers’ requests. Claude Code’s telemetry and error reports are off with DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 and DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING=1. devvm writes every agent’s variables into each VM at every launch, whichever agents the VM has, and every shell in the VM gets them, login or not, so an agent that an editor’s terminal or ssh runs gets them too. pi would download fd and rg into ~/.pi/agent/bin whenever they’re missing, so base has both, from Ubuntu’s or the container image’s own packages, and pi finds Ubuntu’s and Debian’s fd by its name there, fdfind.

pi’s releases are built for glibc alone, so a VM made --from an Alpine-based container image can’t have pi, and devvm refuses it there (shared tools and glibc). Every other agent runs on Alpine too.

Agents are shared tools, like the toolchains, so you can combine them with any layers and with each other, as in devvm --tools node --agents claude,codex. devvm follows each agent’s newest release, because agents release several times a week, and devvm update or devvm tools update moves a VM to newer versions (adding and removing tools).

Setup’s default agents

devvm setup chooses the agents that the list checks for every new VM, and that a new VM gets without a terminal. devvm asks for them on its first run in a terminal and again in devvm setup’s questions, and devvm setup --agents claude,codex or devvm setup --agents none sets them without asking. They’re a setting for new VMs only, so a VM that exists keeps its agents (devvm setup).

devvm’s agent store

devvm keeps the agents’ settings and logins on this machine in a store of its own, and every VM with an agent gets that agent’s settings and logins from there. devvm never reads the agents’ own files in your home folder for a VM, such as ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.config/opencode, ~/.local/share/opencode or ~/.pi/agent, so a VM gets the same settings and logins whether or not this machine has the agent. The one command that reads those files is devvm agent import, which copies them into the store when you run it, and devvm agent save copies the settings you changed in a VM into the store.

The store has two folders for each agent, and each one holds the agent’s files at the same paths below it as the agent keeps them in a home folder:

  • Settings go in ~/.config/devvm/agents/<agent>/, such as ~/.config/devvm/agents/claude/.claude/settings.json and ~/.config/devvm/agents/claude/.claude/skills. You can edit these files and make or delete these folders yourself, and a VM gets the change on its next launch, as mounts and copies describe.
  • Logins go in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/<agent>/, such as ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/codex/.codex/auth.json and ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/claude/.claude.json, and so does a login that you make inside a VM, such as Codex’s (Codex and opencode logins) or Claude Code’s in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/claude/.claude/.credentials.json (Claude Code login). Only you can read them, because devvm makes each agent’s logins folder yours alone (mode 700) and each login file mode 600. On macOS, devvm keeps each agent’s logins folder out of Time Machine’s backups.

Each VM gets its agents’ settings and logins from the store, but never your history. Transcripts, sessions and databases aren’t in the store, and each VM’s own stay in that VM. Before you leave an agent running unattended, read staying safe and rogue agents.

flowchart TD
home["the agents' files<br>in your home folder"]
subgraph store["devvm's agent store"]
folders["settings folders:<br>skills, plugins…"]
files["settings files<br>and logins"]
end
subgraph guest["The VM"]
links["linked into ~"]
copies["copies in ~"]
own["its own history"]
end
home -- "devvm agent import,<br>never your history" --> store
folders -- "mounted<br>read-only" --> links
files -- "copied on every<br>launch, without<br>your secrets" --> copies
copies -- "devvm agent save,<br>after a diff and a yes" --> store
own -- "devvm history export,<br>devvm rm" --> export["a .tar.gz<br>on this machine"]
export -. "devvm history import,<br>or yes when a new VM<br>offers it" .-> own

Each row lists the agent’s paths in the VM’s home, and the store keeps each one at the same path below the agent’s settings or logins folder:

Mounted read-only, linked into ~ Copied in on every launch
claude ~/.claude/{skills,agents,commands,output-styles,plugins} ~/.claude/settings.json, ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, and from the logins ~/.claude.json (merged, only its settings, account state and MCP servers)
codex ~/.codex/{prompts,skills} ~/.codex/{config.toml,AGENTS.md}, and from the logins ~/.codex/auth.json
opencode the subfolders of ~/.config/opencode (not node_modules) the files in ~/.config/opencode (not lock files), and from the logins ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json
pi ~/.pi/agent/{extensions,skills,prompts,themes} ~/.pi/agent/{settings.json,keybindings.json,models.json,mcp.json,AGENTS.md,SYSTEM.md,APPEND_SYSTEM.md}, and from the logins ~/.pi/agent/auth.json

Importing from this machine

When you already use an agent on this machine, devvm agent import copies its settings and logins from your home folder into the store, so your VMs get them. With no argument it imports every agent that your home folder has files of, and devvm agent import claude codex imports only the agents you name:

devvm agent import # copy every agent's settings and logins into the store
devvm agent import codex # copy only Codex's
devvm agent import --force # replace what the store has without asking

The import copies only the paths in the table above, from ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.config/opencode, ~/.local/share/opencode and ~/.pi/agent, so it never copies your history, such as ~/.claude/projects, ~/.codex’s sessions or ~/.pi/agent/sessions, and never ~/.claude/.credentials.json. From ~/.claude.json it keeps only the settings, account state and MCP servers, so your API key and your per-project entries stay out of the store. Claude Code’s plugin records name the plugins’ folders by their paths, so the store’s copies of the JSON files in ~/.claude/plugins name the plugins’ folders in the store, where the VMs mount them. devvm says which agents it imported and where, and an agent you named that your home folder has nothing of gets a warning.

devvm reads each agent’s settings inside the agent’s own folder, such as ~/.claude, and it never follows a link out of it. A link to a file inside the folder becomes a copy of that file, and a link that leads out of the folder, by a relative or an absolute path, or to a folder, is left out with a warning that names it. A login file that’s a link is left out with a warning too. So when your settings live elsewhere, such as in a dotfiles repo with links into ~/.claude, copy them into the store yourself.

When the store already has settings or a login of an agent you import, devvm asks in a terminal whether to replace them, with no as the default. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm refuses and names --force, which replaces them without asking. A replacement writes each file again and takes out what your home folder no longer has, but it keeps the store’s folders, so a running VM’s mounts still show them. An agent whose settings aren’t in your home folder keeps the store’s settings, and one without a login there keeps the store’s login.

On macOS, Claude Code keeps its own login in the Keychain, and devvm neither reads it nor copies it. You log Claude Code in from a VM instead, with devvm agent login claude, and every VM with Claude Code gets that login (Claude Code login).

opencode 2 keeps its logins in its own database rather than in ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json, so when this machine’s opencode is version 2 or later, devvm reads its logins with opencode auth export and saves them in the store in the format of auth.json, the file that devvm copies for opencode 1. It saves the API key of each provider, and your OpenAI login when you made it with one of opencode’s Codex logins, the browser or the headless one. Any other login is left out with a warning that names it, such as opencode’s Sign in with ChatGPT, whose tokens a VM can’t use, or another provider’s OAuth login, and you log in from a VM instead, with devvm agent login opencode (logging in with devvm agent login). When opencode auth export fails, the import fails too, and the store keeps the login it had.

Saving a VM’s settings

When you change an agent’s settings in a VM, for example by installing a plugin or writing a skill there, devvm agent save copies them into the store, so every VM with that agent gets them. With no argument it saves every agent that the folder’s VM has, and devvm agent save claude saves only the agents you name. devvm starts a stopped VM for it.

devvm agent save # show what changed in the VM's agents' settings, then save them
devvm agent save codex # save only Codex's

The save reads only the settings in the table above from the VM’s home, and never the logins, so it never reads your history, ~/.claude/.credentials.json, ~/.codex/auth.json, opencode’s auth.json or pi’s. From the VM’s ~/.claude.json it keeps only the settings, account state and MCP servers, as the import does, and the VM leaves out its per-project entries before it sends anything. devvm puts that part in the store’s logins folder, where the import keeps it too. A folder that the store already has is mounted read-only in the VM, so the agent there can’t change it, and the save leaves it as it is. A folder that the store doesn’t have yet is the VM’s own until you save it, and once the VM next starts with the store’s new folder mounted, its setup links that folder in place of its own (mounts).

Before it saves anything, devvm shows what would change. For each folder it lists the files it adds (A), changes (M) and removes (D), and then it shows a diff of each file it adds or changes against the store’s copy, with a line when a file’s mode changes. The diff shows the settings files and ~/.claude.json as a VM gets them, written out again with devvm-redacted in place of the values that look like secrets, so it never prints your secrets, and it says so when only those values or the file’s layout changed. Every character that a terminal wouldn’t show, such as a control character, a zero-width character or a character that reverses the text, appears in the diff as its code, such as \u{200b}, so a VM can’t hide a line from you. The diff names a binary file without showing it, and it shows a file of more than 1 MiB or 10,000 lines, and every line past the first 20,000 of the whole diff, only as a count. Then devvm says that every VM with these agents runs the hooks, the MCP servers’ commands and the plugins you save, and it asks whether to save them, with no as the default. Read the diff before you answer, because a hook or a plugin that a rogue agent added in one VM runs in every VM once you save it. devvm agent save always asks, and no flag answers for you, so without a terminal, or with --no-input, it shows what would change and then refuses.

devvm treats everything the VM sends as untrusted, because the agent in the VM could have changed any of it. It reads at most 128 MiB from the VM, in at most 20,000 files, folders and links, none of the files larger than 16 MiB, and when the VM sends more, or sends a path outside the agents’ settings or a name with a character that a terminal wouldn’t show, devvm saves nothing. Each file it saves is yours alone (mode 600), or mode 700 when it was executable in the VM, so it never keeps a set-user-ID or set-group-ID bit. A link in a settings folder that leads to a file in the same folder becomes a copy of that file. devvm leaves out any other link, any other kind of file, such as a socket, and a settings file that it can’t parse whole, such as a settings.json that isn’t JSON, and it warns you about each. When it leaves out a file in a folder, the store keeps its own copy of that file. A settings file that the VM doesn’t have stays in the store. A folder that the VM sends replaces the store’s folder whole, so devvm writes each of its files again and takes out the files that the VM’s folder doesn’t have, but it keeps the store’s folder itself, so a running VM’s mounts still show it.

The VM’s copies of the settings files and of ~/.claude.json hold placeholders, such as devvm-redacted, where the store has your secrets. devvm puts the store’s secret back in place of each placeholder, as long as the VM’s copy had that placeholder in that place and nothing around it changed, such as the URL of the MCP server that a header is for. When something around a placeholder changed, devvm leaves the whole file out and warns you, so a VM can’t send a secret it never saw to another host, and you can make that change in the store’s file yourself. devvm also leaves out any other file that holds a placeholder, such as a skill. No VM gets opencode’s files in ~/.config/opencode that are neither settings nor Markdown, such as a .env, so devvm leaves out the VM’s own file of that name and keeps the store’s.

Mounts

devvm mounts the store’s settings folders that exist when it creates the VM read-only, at the same path as in the store on this machine, and links them from the VM’s home. Absolute paths in them, such as Claude Code’s plugin paths, still work. This machine enforces read-only, so even root in the VM can’t write to them. devvm mounts each folder whole, whatever the VM’s network tier, so the VM reads every file in it, a .env or a key file in a plugin’s folder included, and the git config of a private plugin marketplace whose URL holds a password. devvm takes no secrets out of these folders, because they hold plugins, skills and their scripts that the agent runs as they are. So keep secrets out of these folders, as you keep them out of the project folder (why devvm mounts them whole). The VM follows a symlink in these folders among its own files, so a link to a file outside the folder, by a relative or an absolute path, doesn’t reach that file on this machine, on macOS’s virtiofs mounts and on Linux’s 9p mounts alike. devvm doesn’t mount a folder whose path has a comma, on any backend, and it warns you. Lima can’t mount such a path (Lima’s limits).

When you make or delete one of these folders in the store later, by hand or with devvm agent import, devvm notices on the VM’s next launch and names the folder. A VM’s mounts change only when it starts, so a stopped VM gets the new mounts as the launch starts it. For a running VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart it now, which stops anything running in it, in the one question that covers every change waiting for the VM’s next start, and because the mounts are among those changes, the default answer is yes (restarting). If you answer no, or there’s no terminal, or you pass --no-input, the mounts change when the VM next starts, for example with devvm restart.

Copies

devvm copies the store’s files into the VM’s home on every launch, over the VM’s own. On every network tier, the copies of the logins and settings files have your secrets taken out, and the VM’s proxy puts them into requests instead (agents’ logins and settings).

devvm merges the settings and MCP servers from the store’s .claude.json into the VM’s own ~/.claude.json, so servers added in the VM stay (MCP servers). Your API key, your answers about API keys and your per-project entries never reach the VM. devvm also replaces the secrets in the agents’ settings files with devvm-redacted, and names what it replaced. Those are the values under keys that look like secrets, every env value and header, and the secrets in URLs and in arguments. In other text, such as a hook’s command, devvm replaces the secrets in its URLs, the keys that start like a known key, such as sk- or ghp_, and the credential after Bearer or Basic, and keeps the words around them (keys in settings files). pi’s settings files that can hold a key are settings.json, models.json and mcp.json, so a provider’s apiKey in models.json reaches the VM as devvm-redacted, and pi’s keybindings.json and Markdown files reach it as they are. From the env of Claude Code’s settings.json, the VM gets only Claude Code’s own settings, such as ANTHROPIC_MODEL, the CLAUDE_CODE_*, DISABLE_* and MAX_* variables and those ending in _TIMEOUT_MS, but none whose name marks it as a credential, such as ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN. It also gets the values that only name where a secret is, base URLs without their passwords, true, false and short numbers. Every other env value, and every env value of an MCP server, becomes devvm-redacted. When devvm can’t parse a settings file to take its secrets out, the VM doesn’t get a copy of it, and neither does it get opencode’s files in ~/.config/opencode that are neither settings nor Markdown, such as a .env. devvm names each file it doesn’t copy, and when it can’t make the copy of a login, it says why.

Claude Code login

You log Claude Code in once, from inside any VM that has it, and devvm keeps the login on this machine for every VM with Claude Code, so this machine never needs Claude Code:

devvm agent login claude # log Claude Code in to your Claude subscription
devvm agent login claude --setup-token # get a long-lived Claude Code token with claude setup-token instead

devvm starts the folder’s VM first if it’s stopped, as devvm host does, and then runs Claude Code’s own login in the VM, on your terminal: claude auth login --claudeai, or claude setup-token with --setup-token. Claude Code shows an address, which you open in a browser on any machine. When you approve the login there, the browser shows a code, which you paste back at Claude Code’s prompt, so devvm forwards no port. The VM’s proxy saves the login as it reaches Claude’s token endpoint, and Claude Code in the VM gets only placeholders. devvm then sets the VM up again, so it uses the login at once, and every other VM with Claude Code gets it from its next launch. When the login ends without a new login in the store, devvm says so and fails.

devvm keeps one Claude Code login, either your subscription’s login or a Claude Code token, and the newest replaces the other, so every VM uses the account you logged in to last:

  • Your subscription’s login, from devvm agent login claude or a claude /login that you run in a VM yourself, goes in devvm’s agent store, in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/claude/.claude/.credentials.json, only yours to read. The VM’s ~/.claude/.credentials.json holds placeholders, with no refresh token and an expiry in 2099, so Claude Code in the VM never refreshes the login itself. The VM’s proxy puts the login into the VM’s requests to api.anthropic.com, and refreshes it on this machine when it’s due, through the company proxy when config.toml names one. devvm keeps only a login that can use Claude’s models and can’t make API keys, so a login to an Anthropic Console account, which Claude Code uses to make an API key, fails in a VM, and no API key reaches it. Only a VM that has Claude Code can log it in.
  • A Claude Code token, from devvm agent login claude --setup-token or a claude setup-token that you run in a VM yourself, goes with the other secrets. You can also save one with devvm secret set claude and paste the token that claude setup-token printed on another machine (sk-ant-oat01-…), not the code the browser shows. devvm neither saves nor sends a Claude Code token that isn’t a setup token. Every VM with Claude Code gets the token in its environment as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, holding a placeholder of its own, and its proxy puts the token into its requests. When you set up a token in a VM, claude setup-token prints that VM’s placeholder, not the token, because devvm already saved it.

A VM gets either ~/.claude/.credentials.json or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN from devvm, never both, because Claude Code would use the token in its environment over the login in its file. A VM that started with the login devvm replaced keeps working, because its proxy puts the login devvm keeps now in place of either placeholder. A CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in devvm’s own environment on this machine wins over both, as it does in Claude Code, so VMs get that token, and devvm agent login claude warns you when it’s set. The VM gets placeholders whatever its network tier.

Anthropic doesn’t document the requests that Claude Code’s login sends, so devvm follows the ones Claude Code sends today, and a new Claude Code release can change them. When a login in a VM stops working, run devvm agent login claude again, or save a Claude Code token instead.

Codex and opencode logins

On every network tier, the VM’s auth.json holds placeholders, and its proxy holds the real API keys and logins. The proxy reads them from the login files in devvm’s store as it needs them and refreshes ChatGPT logins there, so when the agent in the VM stops getting answers, the proxy’s own log, proxy.log in ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/logs/, may say that refreshing a login failed or that you’re no longer logged in that way. To log in again, run devvm agent login codex or devvm agent login opencode in the VM’s folder, which also gives that VM the new login’s placeholders, and the other VMs get them on their next launch. The proxy puts in opencode’s API keys for the providers that API keys the proxy puts in lists, and its OpenAI and GitHub Copilot logins. The VM’s entry for such an API key holds only its type and the placeholder, so the entry’s other fields, such as its metadata, stay on this machine.

The VM’s copy of Codex’s auth.json holds only what Codex needs for its API key and its ChatGPT login: the placeholders, how it logs in, when it last refreshed, and the IDs of the account and the login. devvm keeps every other field on this machine, because the VM’s proxy can’t put it in, and it names those fields at every launch. That includes Codex’s other ways to log in, such as a personal access token or an Amazon Bedrock key, so Codex in a VM can’t use them. To use Codex in a VM, log in with ChatGPT or an OpenAI API key (logging in with devvm agent login). devvm treats Claude Code’s account state in ~/.claude.json the same way, so the VM gets only the account fields that Claude Code writes there today, and devvm names any other field at every launch.

devvm keeps every other entry of opencode’s auth.json on this machine too, because devvm doesn’t know which hosts it’s for, so the VM gets that entry without its key or its tokens, and devvm warns you about each at every launch. That’s an API key for any other provider, such as Azure’s or a local model server’s, a well-known login, which an organization’s own opencode config sets up, and any other OAuth login, such as Copilot Enterprise’s. The VM keeps only the fields of a withheld entry that name the account or how it logs in, such as its type, its enterpriseUrl and its expiry, so opencode in the VM doesn’t use that provider. To use an OAuth login’s provider in the VM, log in to it with an API key on this machine and import the login again.

To give the VM one provider’s API key as it is, such as a local model server’s that the VM’s proxy can’t put in, list the provider under opencode in config.toml’s [pass-keys] table (config.toml), as you would for pi. The provider is its entry’s name in opencode’s auth.json, such as ollama. Every VM with opencode then gets that entry whole, its metadata included, and opencode 2 in the VM imports it into its database too, and devvm says so at each launch. It applies only to entries with an API key, because a VM never gets a login’s tokens, and only to providers whose keys the proxy doesn’t put in, because a key the proxy puts in is always its placeholder:

[pass-keys]
opencode = ["ollama"]

So when opencode in a VM can’t reach a provider whose key works on this machine, such as a local model server’s, and devvm’s warning at launch names that provider, add it to [pass-keys] and run devvm in the folder again.

Logging in with devvm agent login

devvm agent login logs Codex or opencode in from inside this folder’s VM, so this machine never needs either agent, and devvm’s agent store keeps the login for every VM with that agent. Claude Code’s login is devvm agent login claude (Claude Code login), and pi’s is an API key alone (pi logins):

devvm agent login codex # log Codex in to ChatGPT in a browser on this machine
devvm agent login opencode --device-code # log opencode in with a code, in a browser on any machine
devvm agent login codex --api-key # save Codex's OpenAI API key, asking for it
devvm agent login opencode --api-key --provider anthropic # save opencode's Anthropic API key

devvm starts the folder’s VM first if it’s stopped, as devvm host does, and the VM must have the agent, which devvm tools add codex gives it. Then devvm runs the agent’s own ChatGPT login in the VM, on your terminal: codex login for Codex, and opencode auth login openai --method chatgpt-browser, opencode’s Codex browser login, for opencode. The agent shows an address, which you open in a browser on this machine. When you approve the login there, the browser comes back to localhost:1455, where the agent’s own server in the VM waits, so devvm forwards this machine’s localhost:1455, and localhost:1457, which Codex uses when 1455 is taken in the VM, to the same ports in the VM. The forward lasts only while the login runs, and it ends when the login ends, fails or you press Ctrl+C, which ends the agent’s login in the VM too. When another program on this machine has port 1455, devvm refuses and names --device-code.

With --device-code, the agent shows a code instead, which you type into a browser on any machine, and devvm forwards nothing. Codex’s device code login is codex login --device-auth, which your ChatGPT account’s security settings must allow, and opencode’s is opencode auth login openai --method chatgpt-headless, its Codex device code login.

When the agent logs in, the VM’s proxy saves the login in the store, and the agent in the VM gets placeholders, as the next section describes. devvm then says what the store saved and the account’s email, and the VM uses the login at once. When the login ends without a new login in the store, for example because you chose another way to log in, devvm says so and fails, and devvm network log shows each login the proxy saved. Codex in a VM keeps its login in ~/.codex/auth.json, never in a keyring, because devvm sets cli_auth_credentials_store = "file" in the VM’s ~/.codex/config.toml on every launch.

With --api-key, devvm asks for the API key without showing it, or reads it from a line of input with --stdin, and saves it in the store itself, so the key never goes into the VM. Codex’s key is an OpenAI key, and it replaces Codex’s ChatGPT login in the store, as codex login --with-api-key does. opencode’s key is for the provider that --provider names, by one of the IDs in API keys the proxy puts in, and the store keeps opencode’s other providers beside it. devvm then gives the running VM its copy of the login, with a placeholder in place of the key, and the VM’s proxy puts the key in at once. opencode keeps its logins in its own database in the VM, and it reads its auth.json only when it first makes that database, so when opencode has already run in the VM, devvm also gives it the key’s placeholder with opencode auth import. devvm reads at most 1 MiB of what that import prints in the VM, and when it prints more, devvm stops it and fails, so running devvm in the VM’s folder tries again. Every other VM with opencode gets the key’s placeholder at its next launch, the same way, and any credentials that you added to opencode in a VM yourself stay in its database.

opencode’s Anthropic login is an API key, because opencode itself has no other way to log in to Anthropic. opencode’s Claude Agent provider uses Claude Code’s own login instead, so it works in a VM that has Claude Code too, with the login that devvm agent login claude saves.

Logins made in a VM

When Codex or opencode in a VM logs in to OpenAI, whether devvm agent login runs it or you run it yourself, the VM’s proxy saves the login in devvm’s store, in the agent’s own auth.json, and the agent in the VM gets only placeholders, so on every tier but open the VM never holds the login’s tokens. The VM you logged in from uses the login at once, and every VM with that agent gets it from its next launch. opencode reads its auth.json only when it first makes its database, so in a VM where opencode has already run, devvm adds the store’s logins to opencode’s database at each launch when they changed since the VM last got them, and makes them the ones opencode uses. Credentials that you added to opencode in the VM yourself stay in its database, labeled with your names rather than devvm, and opencode auth switch changes back to one of them. A login that shows a code to type into a browser on any machine works in a VM as it is, such as codex login --device-auth and opencode’s Codex device code login. opencode’s Sign in with ChatGPT doesn’t work in a VM, because it gets its tokens from another endpoint, whose replies the VM’s proxy refuses so that they never reach the VM, so choose one of opencode’s Codex logins instead, as devvm agent login opencode does. A new login replaces the one in the store, together with Codex’s API key, so every VM with the agent uses the account you logged in to last. A VM saves a login only for an agent that it has, so a VM without Codex can’t replace the store’s Codex login, and a VM without opencode can’t replace opencode’s. When a VM sends a login for an agent it doesn’t have, such as one that a program installed in the VM itself, its proxy refuses the login, devvm saves nothing, and the proxy’s own log says so. In a VM with both Codex and opencode, devvm tells their logins apart by the program that sends them. devvm network log shows a login line for each login it saved. On the open tier, a program that goes around the VM’s proxy gets the login’s tokens itself, and devvm saves nothing (logins made in a VM). Claude Code’s logins in a VM are saved in the same way (Claude Code login).

pi logins

pi in a VM uses API keys that devvm keeps on this machine, for the providers whose keys the VM’s proxy puts in, which API keys the proxy puts in lists. You save one with devvm agent login pi --api-key --provider PROVIDER, because pi’s login always takes both flags, or you import the API keys in your own ~/.pi/agent/auth.json with devvm agent import pi:

devvm agent login pi --api-key --provider anthropic # save pi's Anthropic API key, asking for it
devvm agent import pi # copy pi's settings and auth.json from this machine

The login saves the key in the store’s ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/pi/.pi/agent/auth.json, in pi’s own format, beside pi’s other providers, as opencode’s --api-key does (logging in with devvm agent login). It needs a VM with pi in this folder, which it gives its copy of the login at once, and every other VM with pi gets it at its next launch. The VM’s ~/.pi/agent/auth.json holds a placeholder in place of each of those keys, and the VM’s proxy puts the key into pi’s requests to that provider’s hosts, on every network tier, and allows those hosts, as the table in API keys the proxy puts in describes. The VM’s entry for such a provider holds only its type and the placeholder, so it gets none of the entry’s other fields, such as its env, whose values pi uses before the environment’s, and the store keeps them on this machine.

devvm keeps every other entry of pi’s auth.json on this machine too, and the VM gets that entry without its key, its env or its tokens, and devvm warns you about each. That’s an API key for any other provider, such as a local model server’s, a key that’s a command for pi to run, such as !security find-generic-password, and a key that pi fills in from a variable, such as $KEY or ${KEY}, even for a provider whose key the proxy puts in, because devvm can’t tell what pi would send. The VM keeps only the fields of a withheld entry that name the account or how it logs in, such as its type, its accountId and its expiry.

To give the VM one provider’s API key as it is, such as a local model server’s that the VM’s proxy can’t put in, list the provider under pi in config.toml’s [pass-keys] table (config.toml). Every VM with pi then gets that entry whole, its env included, and devvm says so at each launch. It applies only to entries with an API key, because a VM never gets a login’s tokens, and only to providers whose keys the proxy doesn’t put in, because a key the proxy puts in is always its placeholder:

[pass-keys]
pi = ["ollama"]

pi’s own logins with an account, which /login and pi auth login make for a subscription, such as Claude’s, ChatGPT’s or GitHub Copilot’s, aren’t among the logins devvm keeps, so save the provider’s API key instead. Don’t log pi in with an account inside a VM either. pi’s Claude and ChatGPT logins use the same token endpoints as Claude Code’s, Codex’s and opencode’s logins, whose replies the VM’s proxy captures for those agents, and devvm never keeps such a login as pi’s. In a VM that also has the matching agent, Claude Code for a Claude login and Codex or opencode for a ChatGPT login, the proxy saves pi’s login as that agent’s own, in place of the one devvm keeps for every VM with that agent. In a VM with none of them, the proxy refuses pi’s login and devvm saves nothing (logins made in a VM).

pi’s settings

The VM’s copy of pi’s settings.json leaves out three keys, because each would undo what devvm sets in the VM, and devvm names the ones it left out. httpProxy would send pi around the VM’s proxy, sessionDir would keep pi’s sessions outside ~/.pi/agent/sessions, where history exports look for them, and selfUpdateCommand would run a command of the file’s on pi update. When devvm agent save pi saves the VM’s settings.json, its diff shows those keys as taken out, so save it only when you mean to drop them from the store’s copy too.

When the store’s settings.json sets defaultProjectTrust to always, devvm warns you at each launch. That setting makes pi load a project folder’s own .pi extensions, settings and MCP servers without asking, and they run in the VM with pi, so set it to ask in devvm’s agent store unless you trust every project you open.

API keys the proxy puts in

The VM’s proxy puts in opencode’s and pi’s API keys for the providers in this table. The ID is the provider’s entry in the agent’s auth.json and the value that devvm agent login --provider takes. The VM’s copy of the login holds a placeholder in place of each of these keys, and on every network tier the proxy swaps it for the key in the headers that the table names, in requests to the provider’s hosts alone, so any other host gets only the placeholder. Where the table names a path, the proxy swaps it only in requests for paths that start with it, so the rest of that host gets the placeholder too. The proxy also allows those hosts on port 443, as it allows the hosts of every secret it puts in, so you don’t allow them yourself:

ID Provider Hosts Paths Headers
anthropic Anthropic api.anthropic.com any x-api-key
deepseek DeepSeek api.deepseek.com any Authorization
google Google Gemini generativelanguage.googleapis.com any x-goog-api-key
groq Groq api.groq.com any Authorization
mistral Mistral api.mistral.ai any Authorization
openai OpenAI api.openai.com any Authorization
openrouter OpenRouter openrouter.ai /api/ Authorization, x-api-key
xai xAI api.x.ai any Authorization

OpenRouter’s key goes in either of its two headers, because pi sends it in x-api-key for OpenRouter’s Anthropic models, as Anthropic’s own API takes a key, and in Authorization for every other model. The proxy swaps the placeholder only when the header holds the placeholder and nothing else, or for Authorization, Bearer, one space and the placeholder, which is how opencode and pi send each of these keys. A header that holds anything else beside the placeholder, or a second header of the same name, keeps the placeholder, so code in the VM can’t surround your key with text of its own, which a provider that quotes part of a key it refuses could show back to it.

The placeholder for an OpenAI key starts with sk-, as an OpenAI API key does, because pi takes an OpenAI key that starts any other way for a Sign in with ChatGPT login and then leaves settings such as the longest reply it wants out of its requests. The Google Gemini key is the Gemini API’s, for Google AI Studio. Vertex AI logs in with a Google Cloud account or a service account instead, so devvm withholds its logins, as it does any other provider’s. These providers’ keys never need [pass-keys], and when it lists one of them all the same, the VM still gets the key’s placeholder, not the key, and devvm notes at each launch that you can take the provider out.

The placeholder keeps a key out of the VM only from the launch that first gives the VM the placeholder. A VM that was given one of these keys as it was before then, such as through [pass-keys] when the proxy didn’t put that provider’s key in, may still hold copies of it. They can be in opencode’s database, its write-ahead log and its freed pages, in the disk’s free space and anywhere that the VM’s own code copied the key. While opencode in the VM fails to import the placeholder, devvm’s record of opencode’s last import, ~/.local/state/devvm/opencode-import.json, holds the key too. Those copies still work wherever they are, so when you don’t trust that VM, make a new key at the provider, save it with devvm agent login AGENT --api-key --provider PROVIDER and revoke the old one.

With some of these keys, code in the VM can make a credential of its own that works without the proxy. Google Gemini’s key gets an ephemeral token for Gemini’s Live API, which lasts up to about 20 hours and allows as many uses as the VM asks for. xAI’s key gets a realtime client secret that lasts as long as the VM chooses, and OpenAI’s key gets one that lasts up to 2 hours. opencode’s experimental voice mode asks for these itself, so the proxy allows those requests (attack vectors). Some of these providers’ own tools also fetch the URLs that a request names, such as Google Gemini’s URL context and Search grounding, xAI’s live search, Groq’s compound models and Mistral’s agents with web search, so code in the VM can reach hosts that the allowlist doesn’t have through them, as it can through Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s.

Pasting images

An agent in the VM can’t see this machine’s clipboard, so an image you copied, such as a screenshot, gets to it through devvm paste, which sends the image into the VM and copies its path there for you to paste:

  1. Copy an image on this machine, such as a screenshot, copy pages in a PDF viewer such as Preview, or copy a file in Finder or your file manager.
  2. In a terminal on this machine, run devvm paste in the project folder. devvm says where the image is in the VM, such as /tmp/devvm-paste/paste-20261109-153012-7f3a9c01.png, and puts that path on your clipboard. If putting it there fails, devvm warns you and still says where the image is, so you can paste that path yourself.
  3. Paste the path into the agent with your terminal’s paste shortcut, which is Cmd+V on macOS and usually Ctrl+Shift+V on Linux. Ctrl+V on its own asks the agent to read the VM’s clipboard, and the VM has none. Claude Code, Codex and opencode attach an image whose path you paste, and pi reads it with its read tool.

The VM must be running, because devvm paste is for an agent that runs in it, and devvm refuses a stopped one.

devvm paste # send what you copied, asking first about a copied file
devvm paste --send-file # send a file in the project folder without asking, as a script must
devvm paste --json # the same, and print what it sent
devvm paste rm # delete the files devvm paste left in the VM, after asking

What devvm paste sends

devvm reads only an image, a PDF or a copied file’s reference from the clipboard, never text, so a password you copied never reaches it:

  • An image: PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, and on macOS also a TIFF, which many Mac apps copy, sent as a PNG.
  • A PDF, such as pages you copied in Preview, sent as it is, as a .pdf file, because most models read PDFs.
  • One copied file, after devvm asks you about it.
  • Nothing over 64 MiB, whether it’s an image, a PDF or a file.

devvm checks that an image’s or a PDF’s bytes are the type the clipboard claims (how). Text is never sent, so paste text, such as an error message, into the agent’s terminal yourself. The app you copied from hands over what you copied when devvm asks for it, and devvm waits for it at most 30 seconds, then stops waiting, sends nothing and says so, so copy it again, or wait until the app responds, then run devvm paste again. On macOS, devvm reads the clipboard of the session you’re logged in to, so run devvm paste in a terminal on that Mac, not over ssh.

What devvm gets depends on the app you copied from:

  • A browser’s Copy Image hands over a PNG, never the original JPEG, GIF or WebP, and Safari hands over a TIFF, which devvm makes a PNG, so an animated GIF arrives as one still frame. To send the original, save it and copy the saved file instead.
  • A PDF viewer puts a picture of what you copied beside the PDF, and devvm sends the PDF, never the picture. When you copy a page’s thumbnail in Preview, Preview also puts a temporary file of its own on the clipboard, and devvm sends the PDF without asking about that file.
  • Finder, on macOS, puts the copied file’s icon on the clipboard as an image beside the file, and devvm sends the file, not the icon. If the file is gone by the time you run devvm paste, devvm says so and sends nothing, rather than the icon. Text is never taken for a file, even when it’s a path, so copy the file itself in Finder.
  • Photos puts a file of the Photos library beside a photo you copy, so devvm asks about that file, as it does about any copied file.

Copied files

Before devvm sends a copied file, it shows the file’s path on this machine and asks, [y/N], because the clipboard can name any file of yours, such as a key in ~/.ssh that you didn’t mean to copy. Answer no and nothing is sent. An image or a PDF is sent without a question, because it’s only what you copied.

devvm sends a copied file under a name of its own that keeps only the file’s extension, when it’s letters and digits alone and at most 16 of them, so my shot (1).png becomes paste-20261109-153012-7f3a9c01.png, and Makefile becomes paste-20261109-153012-7f3a9c01 (why). It sends one file at a time, and it refuses:

  • several files;
  • a folder;
  • a file with a symbolic link anywhere in its path, your own included, because a link the VM planted in the project folder could point at a file of yours. The only links devvm follows are the system’s own, which root owns, such as macOS’s /tmp, so copy the file from the folder it’s really in.

devvm paste --send-file answers the question for a file in the project folder, which it sends without asking, as a script must, because the VM can read that folder already. It doesn’t answer for the rest:

  • A file anywhere else is still asked about, so only you can send it, at a terminal.
  • A file whose path goes through a symbolic link is asked about too, even through one of the system’s that devvm follows, because the file may not be where its path says.
  • A clone VM’s files, because a clone VM, made with --clone, doesn’t mount the folder.

Where devvm can’t ask, such as without a terminal, it sends nothing, and it names --send-file for a file in the folder, the file and the folder for one outside it, and the file for one reached through a link. So don’t bind devvm paste --send-file to a hotkey to send files from outside the project, because a hotkey has no terminal to ask in, and devvm refuses those files.

devvm paste –json

devvm paste --json does the same and prints what it sent as one object, with "version": 1 first. It has whether anything was sent, which is false when you answered no about a file, the VM, and the file’s path in it ("" when nothing was sent). Then its kind (image, pdf or file), an image’s or a PDF’s type (image/png, image/jpeg, image/gif, image/webp or application/pdf, and "" for a file), and a copied file’s source, its path on this machine ("" otherwise). Last come its size in bytes, and whether the path was copied to the clipboard:

{"version": 1, "sent": true, "vm": "devvm-website-3f9a1c2b4d5e6f", "path": "/tmp/devvm-paste/paste-20261109-153012-7f3a9c01.png", "kind": "image", "type": "image/png", "source": "", "bytes": 48213, "copied": true}

The paste folder and your agent’s settings

The files go into the VM’s paste folder, /tmp/devvm-paste unless config.toml’s paste-dir names another (the paste folder), and they keep their mode, 600, so only the VM’s user reads them. The folder is a fixed path so that you can allow it once in an agent’s settings. Claude Code refuses to read a path outside the project folder when its permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories setting is on, until you add the folder in Claude Code:

/add-dir /tmp/devvm-paste

Or list it in permissions.additionalDirectories in your settings, which devvm’s agent store keeps for every VM, in ~/.config/devvm/agents/claude/.claude/settings.json:

{ "permissions": { "additionalDirectories": ["/tmp/devvm-paste"] } }

Anything in the VM can read what you send, as it can read any file in the project folder, so paste nothing you wouldn’t put in the folder.

Deleting pasted files 

devvm paste rm # delete the files devvm paste left in the folder, after asking in a terminal
devvm paste rm --force # delete them without asking, as a script must

devvm never deletes a pasted file on its own, because Codex reads the image when you submit your message and pi when the model calls read, which may be some time after the paste. devvm paste rm deletes only the files devvm paste named, and nothing else in the folder, so a paste-dir of your own, such as /home/USER/pastes where USER is your user in the VM, can hold other files. The VM’s /tmp is emptied when the VM boots, so with the default folder the files are gone after a restart anyway. With a paste-dir of your own, they stay, and a command that starts a stopped VM and opens its shell offers to delete them, [y/N], once the VM is set up. Those commands are:

  • devvm and devvm restart;
  • devvm tools, devvm tools add, devvm tools rm and devvm tools update;
  • devvm layer add and devvm layer rm;
  • devvm update;
  • devvm clone on and devvm clone off.

Without a terminal, devvm keeps the files and says nothing, and if deleting them fails, it warns you and opens the shell anyway. Commands that start a VM without opening its shell, such as devvm code and devvm agent save, don’t ask, so run devvm paste rm when you want the files gone.

On Linux

devvm reads and writes the clipboard with wl-paste and wl-copy in a Wayland session, which WAYLAND_DISPLAY names, and with xclip in an X11 session, which DISPLAY names. It tells you which one is missing, and installs nothing itself, so install wl-clipboard or xclip with your distribution’s package manager:

sudo apt install wl-clipboard # or xclip for X11; dnf, pacman and zypper have both

devvm looks for them only in the system’s folders, never elsewhere on your PATH (which folders, and why). Run devvm paste from a terminal in your desktop session, because without either variable there’s no clipboard to read. If WAYLAND_DISPLAY or DISPLAY names a session that’s over, as in a tmux window left from an earlier login, devvm tells you that wl-paste or xclip failed and what it said, rather than that the clipboard is empty. Copying the path leaves wl-copy or xclip running until you copy something else, because a Linux clipboard’s contents live in the program that copied them.

History

Each VM’s transcripts and sessions stay in that VM. devvm history export [FILE] saves them, and devvm rm saves them before it deletes a VM that has an agent. The export is a .tar.gz of ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.local/share/opencode, ~/.local/state/opencode and pi’s sessions, ~/.pi/agent/sessions, in the VM, written to FILE or to ~/.local/share/devvm/exports/<vm>-<date>-<time>.tar.gz. An export in that folder gets a <vm>-<date>-<time>.folder file beside it, which names the VM’s project folder and the VM’s network tier when devvm wrote the export.

devvm history lists the exports in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports, oldest first, in a table with a header. It shows each export’s file, the VM it’s of, that VM’s folder, the date and time devvm wrote it, and its size, with - for a folder devvm has no record of. Exports you wrote to a FILE of your own aren’t listed, and devvm history changes nothing and starts no VM.

devvm history –json

devvm history --json prints the same list as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. Each of the exports has its file, its vm, the VM’s folder, which is "" when devvm has no record of it, the date devvm wrote it in RFC 3339 with this machine’s time zone, and its size in bytes.

{
 "version": 1,
 "exports": [
 {
 "file": "/Users/you/.local/share/devvm/exports/devvm-website-71a99b1076d92c-20261001-120000.tar.gz",
 "vm": "devvm-website-71a99b1076d92c",
 "folder": "/Users/you/code/website",
 "date": "2026-10-01T12:00:00+02:00",
 "size": 1048576
 }
 ]
}

After devvm rm, an export is the only copy of that VM’s history, so devvm keeps the exports until you ask it to delete them. devvm gc --history deletes the exports in that folder, and devvm gc --history --older-than 30d deletes only those written 30 days ago or more. An export’s age counts from the date and time in its name, which is this machine’s local time when devvm wrote it, so across a change to or from daylight saving time an export reaches an age such as 30d an hour earlier or later, for --older-than and for the history.age retention setting alike. gc lists each one by its VM and date first, and in a terminal it asks. Exports you wrote to a FILE of your own stay where they are.

The agents’ logins aren’t in the export, which leaves out ~/.claude/.credentials.json, ~/.codex/auth.json, and opencode’s auth.json, account.json, mcp-auth.json and bin, and holds nothing of ~/.pi/agent but its sessions, so pi’s auth.json stays out too. opencode keeps its sessions and its logins together in one database, ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db, so the export holds a copy of that database without its logins. The VM makes the copy with sqlite3, which every base image has, and the copy has no logins, API keys or opencode account in any part of the file, not even a key you typed into opencode in the VM, while the VM’s own database keeps them (how). The export never holds the database’s -wal, -shm or -journal files, which can hold logins that opencode saved last. When the VM has no sqlite3, such as a VM made from an image built without it, the export leaves the database out, so opencode’s sessions aren’t in it, and the run log says so. devvm starts a stopped VM for the export as a launch does, so it locks the folder’s .git again and checks the VM’s confinement first, and the VM stays running. devvm writes the file only once the export is complete, so a failed export leaves no file and leaves an existing FILE as it was. An export holds at most 2 GiB, because a VM could otherwise write until this machine’s disk is full. When the VM sends more, devvm stops the export and keeps nothing of it, so devvm history export fails, while devvm rm and the commands that make a VM again warn that they kept no export and go on without one. Only you can read the file, and devvm makes the exports folder yours alone each time it writes one there, whatever its mode was before. When FILE is in a folder of your own, that folder keeps its mode. If the export fails, devvm rm keeps the VM, and devvm rm --no-export deletes it without exporting. devvm rm VM, for a VM whose folder is gone, exports in the same way, but only from a running VM or a --clone VM, because starting any other would make its folder again (a VM whose folder is gone).

Importing history

devvm history import [FILE] puts an export back into this folder’s VM, so the agents’ transcripts and sessions carry over when you delete a VM and make it again. Without FILE, it imports the newest export in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports that devvm saved for this folder, going by the .folder file beside each one, and it never picks an export made for another folder. With FILE, it imports that .tar.gz, such as one you saved with devvm history export FILE. devvm starts a stopped VM for the import, as it does for an export. The import works on every VM, whether its base is Ubuntu’s image or a Debian-, Ubuntu- or Alpine-based container image (starting from a container image), because it unpacks the export with GNU tar, which Debian and Ubuntu always have and which devvm installs in every base made --from alpine.

When devvm makes a new VM that has an agent, and it saved an export for the same folder before, it offers that export. In a terminal it asks whether to import it into the new VM, with no as the default. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, it doesn’t ask, and it says which export it found and that devvm history import in the folder puts it into the VM. devvm imports the export once the VM has started and before its setup, and if the import fails, devvm warns and makes the VM anyway, so you can run devvm history import later.

An export holds what a VM wrote, so devvm treats it as untrusted. Its transcripts can hold what the old VM’s agents read, and a VM on a less strict tier reaches more, such as your local network on the open tier. So when the export comes from a VM on a less strict tier than the VM you import it into, going from open to internet, allowlist and none, devvm warns you before it imports. devvm knows an export’s tier only from the .folder file beside it in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports, so it warns about an export with no tier recorded, or any FILE elsewhere, such as in the project folder that a VM can write, as if it came from an open VM. devvm never unpacks an export on this machine. It streams the file into the VM as it is, and the VM’s own tar unpacks it there as the VM’s user, so it can only write what that user can write. Before unpacking anything, the VM lists the paths in the export, and when one of them is outside ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.local/share/opencode, ~/.local/state/opencode and ~/.pi/agent/sessions, starts with / or has a .. part, devvm imports nothing and says so. The import keeps no owner or mode from the export, so the VM user’s umask applies and no file is set-user-ID. It also takes out every symbolic link that points outside the folder it’s in, which is any link to an absolute path or one with a .. part, so an agent writing to a session file can’t follow a link out of its history. An export that devvm didn’t write, such as a .tar.gz you made yourself, can hold opencode’s database with its logins, so the import takes out the database’s -wal, -shm and -journal files and puts in a copy of the database without its logins, as the export makes it, or leaves the database out when the VM has no sqlite3. opencode in the new VM then reads the logins that devvm gave the VM, as it does when it first makes its database. When the VM already has an opencode database, it keeps its own, and opencode’s sessions from the export aren’t imported.

The import leaves out what devvm puts in the VM itself. That’s the agents’ logins, ~/.claude/.credentials.json, ~/.codex/auth.json, and opencode’s auth.json, account.json, mcp-auth.json and bin. It’s also ~/.claude.json, whose copy in the old VM held that VM’s own placeholders, and every agent’s mounted folders and copied files, which the new VM’s setup links and copies from devvm’s agent store. A file or folder the VM already has stays as it is, so importing into a VM that has history of its own adds the export’s files without replacing any of its own.

The VM’s setup

Besides the agents’ config, every launch sets the VM up from this machine’s settings:

  • its hostname, which is the folder’s part of the VM’s name;
  • the timezone (TZ, else this machine’s) and, when it’s UTF-8, the locale (LC_ALL, else LANG);
  • git’s user.name and user.email, as git has them in the project folder;
  • telemetry off where an environment variable can’t turn it off, which is Go’s, and Codex’s analytics and metrics;
  • every agent’s environment variables, which turn off its self-update and its telemetry (supported agents);
  • every toolchain’s environment variables, such as the ones that turn off .NET’s telemetry and send npm i -g into your home, and the folders where the toolchains’ global installs go, on the PATH (toolchains);
  • (devvm) at the start of the prompt.

On every network tier, the launch also installs the VM’s own CA and the next one, points apt, sudo, ssh, the docker layer’s Docker and the nix layer’s Nix at the proxy, and adds devvm-why, which shows what the proxy blocked lately. It also tells the agents, in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, why a request may fail (inside the VM). The VM’s secrets go in ~/.config/devvm/env in the VM, which login shells read, and that file holds their placeholders.

item.title: Toolchains
item.description:
devvm has these toolchains:

Toolchain What it brings
node Node 24, with npm, pnpm, yarn and bun
python CPython, with pip and uv
rust rustup, cargo and the stable toolchain
go Go
dotnet the .NET SDK and its runtimes

A new VM gets the ones its folder’s files call for, which the summary of the new VM shows, unless you customize the VM and check others in the list or give others with --tools, as in devvm --tools node,python (what a new VM gets). Each section below says what the toolchain brings and which files make devvm choose it. A project that gets its toolchain from Nix uses the nix layer, which Nix projects covers.

node

node brings the newest release of Node 24, with npm, pnpm, yarn through corepack, and bun. devvm stays on Node 24 because newer releases drop corepack.

  • Files. devvm chooses node for a folder with package.json, bun.lock or bun.lockb at its top level.
  • Versions. A project’s .nvmrc or .node-version picks its Node version, which installs into the VM the first time it’s used.
  • Global installs. npm i -g installs into ~/.npm-global in the VM, which is on the PATH.
  • Allowlist. On the allowlist tier, the VM can reach npm’s, yarn’s, pnpm’s and bun’s registries and Node’s downloads, which are registry.npmjs.org, registry.yarnpkg.com, repo.yarnpkg.com, nodejs.org and bun.sh.

python

python brings a prebuilt build of the newest CPython release, and uv, so pip and uv work as usual.

  • Files. devvm chooses python for a folder with pyproject.toml, requirements.txt, uv.lock, setup.py or Pipfile at its top level.
  • Versions. A project’s .python-version picks its Python version, which installs into the VM the first time it’s used.
  • Global installs. The shared Python is read-only, so packages go into a project’s virtual environment or into your home in the VM, and ~/.local/bin is on the PATH.
  • Allowlist. On the allowlist tier, the VM can reach PyPI and the Python downloads that uv uses, which are pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org and releases.astral.sh.

rust

rust brings rustup, cargo and the newest stable toolchain, with the rust-src and rust-analyzer components already added.

  • Files. devvm chooses rust for a folder with Cargo.toml at its top level.
  • Versions. A project’s rust-toolchain.toml picks its toolchain, which rustup installs into the VM next to the shared one the first time it’s used.
  • Global installs. cargo install installs into ~/.cargo/bin in the VM, which is on the PATH. rustup component add can’t change the shared toolchain, which is why it comes with rust-src and rust-analyzer.
  • Allowlist. On the allowlist tier, the VM can reach crates.io and Rust’s toolchain downloads, which are crates.io, index.crates.io, static.crates.io and static.rust-lang.org.

go

go brings the newest Go release, and devvm turns Go’s telemetry off in the VM.

  • Files. devvm chooses go for a folder with go.mod at its top level.
  • Versions. The toolchain line in a project’s go.mod picks its Go version, and Go itself downloads that version into the VM the first time it’s used.
  • Global installs. go install installs into ~/go/bin in the VM, which is on the PATH.
  • Allowlist. On the allowlist tier, the VM can reach Go’s module proxy, its checksum database and Go’s downloads, which are proxy.golang.org, sum.golang.org, go.dev and dl.google.com.

dotnet

dotnet brings the newest release of the .NET SDK, with the .NET and ASP.NET Core runtimes that come with it, and devvm turns off .NET’s telemetry and its first-run banner in the VM.

  • Files. devvm chooses dotnet for a folder with a solution (*.sln or *.slnx), a C# or F# project (*.csproj or *.fsproj) or global.json at its top level.
  • Versions. The sdk.version in a project’s global.json picks its SDK, which installs into the VM the first time it’s used. mise installs exactly that version and doesn’t follow rollForward, so a global.json that allows a newer SDK still gets the one it names, and a global.json without an SDK version keeps the shared one. mise installs that SDK with Microsoft’s install script, which checks only the download’s size, while devvm checks the shared SDK against the SHA-512 that Microsoft publishes for it.
  • Global installs. dotnet tool install -g installs into ~/.dotnet/tools in the VM, which is on the PATH, and NuGet keeps its packages in ~/.nuget/packages. The shared SDK is read-only, so dotnet workload install installs workloads into ~/.dotnet in the VM instead of the SDK’s folder.
  • Allowlist. On the allowlist tier, the VM can reach NuGet, the revocation lists that NuGet checks packages’ signatures against, and the SDK downloads that a global.json asks for, which are api.nuget.org, crl3.digicert.com on port 80, dot.net and builds.dotnet.microsoft.com. Microsoft’s telemetry isn’t on the allowlist.

Nix projects

A project whose toolchain comes from Nix gets the nix layer, which brings Nix, direnv and nix-direnv into its VM. For a folder with flake.nix, shell.nix or devenv.nix at its top level, or with a default.nix that makes a shell with mkShell, the list devvm shows when you customize a new VM names that file in the nix row, and you choose it there. A layer isn’t chosen by default, so a VM made as its summary shows, or without a terminal, gets it only with --layers nix, as in devvm --layers nix in a folder with package.json and flake.nix, which gives node on the nix layer.

  • Dev shells. Put use flake (or use nix for a shell.nix) in the project’s .envrc and run direnv allow in the VM once. From then on, each shell that changes into the folder loads the dev shell, and leaving the folder unloads it. This works in your terminal and in the terminals of editors connected over SSH.
  • The flake’s tools come first. While the dev shell is loaded, its tools are ahead of the shared tools on the PATH, so a flake’s node wins over the shared node, and the shared tools come back when you leave the folder.
  • Files in the project. nix-direnv keeps its cache of the dev shell in your home in the VM, so the project gets no .direnv folder. Nix itself writes a flake.lock next to a flake.nix that has none, and in a git repository it marks that file to be added, as it does on any machine.
  • One store per VM. Each VM has its own Nix store, so a package one VM builds isn’t in another’s. nix run nixpkgs#hello works in any VM with the layer.
  • Shared downloads. VMs share their downloads from Nix’s binary cache, on every network tier, an open VM’s included, because every VM’s Nix goes through its proxy. The first VM that needs a package gets it from cache.nixos.org through devvm, which keeps a copy on this machine, and the other VMs get that copy, so each package downloads once per machine instead of once per VM. Only devvm adds to this shared cache, and only what cache.nixos.org signed, so no VM can change what another VM gets. When the cache doesn’t have a package or can’t get it, Nix goes to cache.nixos.org itself. The cache keeps to 10 GiB, deleting the packages used least recently first, unless you set another size with devvm retention nix-cache.size=20G (retention). devvm space shows what it takes, and devvm gc --nix-cache empties it (how it works).
  • Trust. Only root is a trusted Nix user, so the VM’s user can’t add caches or signing keys of their own, and Nix ignores --option substituters from them. sudo nix works. Nix builds every package in its sandbox, and a build fails rather than run without it.
  • Allowlist. On the allowlist tier, the VM can reach Nix’s binary cache and its channels and flake registry, which are cache.nixos.org, channels.nixos.org and releases.nixos.org, and GitHub, where most flakes’ inputs come from. A package that isn’t in Nix’s binary cache builds from source, which downloads its sources from their own hosts, and those are blocked until you allow them (Nix through the proxy).

Sharing a team’s packages

When your team’s projects use one flake for their dev shell, you can put that dev shell’s packages into an image, so every VM made from the image starts with them in its store and downloads none of them. VMs made from one image share its disk, because on macOS each VM’s disk is a copy-on-write clone of the image’s, and on Linux hosts it’s an overlay of the image’s, so the packages take their space once. This works with the stable Nix that the nix layer installs, on every network tier.

To do it, make a layer of your own that builds the dev shell while the image builds, and give it after nix, so that it runs on top of the nix layer:

devvm layer new myteam
$EDITOR ~/.config/devvm/layers/myteam.sh
devvm --layers nix,myteam # a new VM of the image nix+myteam

Put these lines in ~/.config/devvm/layers/myteam.sh, below the starter’s set -euo pipefail, with your team’s flake at the commit you want:

# The team's flake at a commit, so the image holds exactly that dev shell.
flake=github:myorg/devshell/0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567
bin=/nix/var/nix/profiles/default/bin
"$bin/nix" develop "$flake" --profile /tmp/myteam-shell --command true
# A garbage collector root in the VM's home keeps the dev shell's packages in the store.
mkdir -p ~/.cache/myteam
"$bin/nix-store" --add-root ~/.cache/myteam/dev-shell --realise "$(readlink -f /tmp/myteam-shell)"
rm -f /tmp/myteam-shell /tmp/myteam-shell-*-link

nix develop builds or downloads every package of the flake’s dev shell into the image’s store and records the dev shell in a profile. nix-store --add-root then makes ~/.cache/myteam/dev-shell a garbage collector root, so nix-collect-garbage in a VM never deletes those packages. A project that loads the same dev shell, with use flake github:myorg/devshell/<commit> in its .envrc, finds every package already in its VM’s store, and so does most of a project whose own flake pins the same nixpkgs revision. The image is built without your credentials, because credentials never go into images, so the flake has to be one that anyone can fetch, such as a public repository.

What this doesn’t cover:

  • Packages a VM gets after it’s made stay on that VM’s own disk. The shared downloads at least save downloading them again.
  • A new version of the flake needs a new image. Moving flake to another commit edits the script, so devvm builds the image again the next time it’s used, while VMs made earlier keep the packages they have. When the script names a branch instead of a commit, a changed flake.lock upstream doesn’t change the script, so run devvm rebuild myteam to build the image again.
  • A flake that pins another nixpkgs revision shares few packages with the image, and its VM downloads the rest.
  • Nix’s local overlay store, which would let VMs share one store as it changes, is left out until Nix makes it stable.

How toolchains are shared and updated

The toolchains are shared tools, like the coding agents, so they aren’t part of any image. devvm builds each version once and mounts it read-only into every VM that has it, and mise runs it, so each toolchain’s commands, such as node or cargo, work from any shell in the VM, including bash -c from agents and from editors over SSH. Because the shared copy is read-only, a toolchain can’t update itself, and anything you install globally goes into your home in the VM, as each section above says.

devvm follows each toolchain’s newest release, and Node 24 for node. Which bases they run on says what each one needs from a VM’s base. Adding and removing tools explains how devvm update and devvm tools update move a VM to newer versions, how devvm tools add adds a toolchain to an existing VM, and how devvm tools rm takes one out. What a new VM gets explains what happens when a folder calls for more than one toolchain.

Which bases they run on

Every toolchain runs on base from Ubuntu’s own image, and on an Alpine-based image with --from, which gets musl builds of the tools. dotnet also needs ICU, the Unicode library that .NET’s globalization uses, so devvm installs ICU in base, whether it’s made from Ubuntu’s image or --from a container image. On a Debian- or Ubuntu-based image, each tool needs at least the glibc version that its prebuilt release was built against. devvm measures that version from the tool’s files whenever it builds a new version, and it refuses a tool whose version is newer than the image’s glibc (shared tools and glibc). Today the shared tools need these glibc versions, so Debian 10 and Ubuntu 20.04 and newer images run all of them:

Shared tool arm64 amd64
node 2.28 2.28
pnpm and bun, with node 2.18 and 2.17 2.18 and 2.17
python 2.17 2.17
uv, with python 2.28 2.17
rust, with rustup 2.17 2.17
go none, because its programs need no glibc none
dotnet 2.27 2.27
claude, opencode and pi 2.17 2.17
codex 2.28, for its voice helper 2.28

Adding and removing tools

A new VM gets the shared tools chosen when devvm makes it, the toolchains and the coding agents, and keeps those versions. On each launch, devvm warns when there are newer ones and names devvm update, which moves the VM to them, and also makes the VM again when its image has changed, after asking (outdated VMs).

In a terminal, devvm tools shows the same list as for a new VM, with this folder’s VM’s toolchains and agents already chosen and its layers greyed out, because they’re built into the VM’s image, which keeps them until devvm layer add or devvm layer rm makes it again. The Layers heading names devvm layer add and devvm layer rm, which change a VM’s layers by making it again (adding layers to a VM). Choose the tools and confirm, and devvm adds and takes out what changed, as devvm tools add and devvm tools rm do, then opens a shell in the VM. When a new agent’s config folders need the running VM to start again, devvm asks first. When nothing changed, devvm says so and opens nothing.

Without a terminal, or with --no-input or --json, devvm tools shows the tools of this folder’s VM in a table, one row per tool, with node’s pnpm and bun and python’s uv in rows of their own:

Column
TOOL the tool’s name, such as node or pnpm
VERSION the version the VM has
NEWER the version in devvm’s tools lock when the VM has another build, which is usually a newer version, or - when the VM has the lock’s build
BUILT yes when that newer version is built, no when devvm tools update builds it first, or -

The table changes nothing and starts no VM. devvm reads the tools lock as it is, without going online, so a release that came out since devvm last checked isn’t in it yet.

devvm tools –json

devvm tools --json prints the same table as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. Each of the tools has the tool’s name and the VM’s version. A tool that the lock has another build of also has newer, which is the lock’s version, and newer_built, which says whether that version is built.

{
 "version": 1,
 "tools": [
 {
 "tool": "node",
 "version": "24.10.0",
 "newer": "24.11.0",
 "newer_built": false
 },
 {
 "tool": "pnpm",
 "version": "10.18.0"
 }
 ]
}

The commands below change the VM’s tools from a script or the command line. They don’t change the VM’s disk, because its tools are mounted, so a change takes effect when devvm then opens a shell in the VM. Each takes the tools’ names as separate words, as in devvm tools add python claude, and devvm refuses names joined with + or a comma.

  • devvm tools add TOOL... builds the tools that the share lacks, and they join the VM’s list at once. It says which of the tools the VM has already and leaves those as they are. A new agent’s config folders are mounted too, which needs the VM to start again. A stopped VM gets them as it starts, and for a running VM devvm asks before restarting it, because anything running in it stops (restarting). If you answer no, there’s no terminal or you pass --no-input, the VM gets them at its next start.
  • devvm tools rm TOOL... takes tools out. What the VM installed itself, such as other versions or global packages, stays.
  • devvm tools update checks upstream for newer versions, builds what’s missing, and moves the VM to them. When the VM already has the newest versions, it builds any of them that are missing. It changes only the shared tools, and never makes the VM again.
  • devvm update does the same first, without asking, and then asks to make the VM again only when the VM’s image has changed (outdated VMs), or its devcontainer.json has (updating a VM from the file).

--tools, --agents and --layers choose only what a new VM gets, so on a VM that exists they change nothing, and devvm warns and names devvm tools. Layers aren’t shared tools, so devvm tools can’t add or take out a layer such as docker or nix. A VM gets its layers when devvm makes it, so devvm layer add and devvm layer rm change them by making the VM again, after asking (adding layers to a VM).

item.title: SSH and editors
item.description:
You can reach each running VM by name from ssh and from editors such as VS Code, and you choose for each VM whether it can use your SSH keys. ssh into VMs explains how devvm’s ssh entries keep a VM away from the rest of this machine.

SSH access by name

Each running project VM can be reached as devvm-<folder>, as in ssh devvm-website or VS Code’s Remote-SSH: Connect to Host. devvm chooses this alias once, when it makes the VM, and records it, so it never changes. A VM gets devvm-<folder> unless another VM already has that alias, and then its alias is its full name. So when two folders share a name, the first VM made keeps devvm-website, and the second one’s alias is its full name, whichever of them you delete first. The VM’s full name (devvm-website-<hash>) always works as well.

devvm writes these entries to ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config each time it launches or stops a VM, because a VM’s SSH port can change each time it starts. To use them, add this line to the top of ~/.ssh/config, before any Host block:

Include ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config

You can also point ssh at the file, as in ssh -F ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config devvm-website. devvm host, devvm code and a new --clone VM offer to add the line in a terminal, and without one, they show it.

  • Only running VMs are listed. A stopped VM’s port is free for any program on this machine to take, so an entry for it could hand your connection, and your agent, to that program. Start the VM with devvm host or devvm before you connect from an editor.
  • Each entry checks the VM’s own host keys, which devvm reads from the VM once each time it starts and keeps in the VM’s folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/known_hosts. ssh refuses a host key that doesn’t match, and a VM whose keys devvm can’t read gets no entry.
