  • Each entry reaches the VM on this machine’s loopback, 127.0.0.1, as the VM’s user with the VM’s own key. A VM whose backend names any other address, or no user or key, gets no entry, so ssh never takes your connection somewhere else.
  • The entries need OpenSSH 8.7 or newer (ssh -V), and an older ssh refuses them.
  • Keep remote forwards out of Host *. The entries turn off what else your ssh config could share with a VM, but they can’t turn off a RemoteForward of yours.

devvm host and devvm code

devvm host gets this folder’s VM ready for ssh and editors, then shows its host name (devvm-website) and its folder in the VM. It does what a launch of an existing VM does, without opening a shell. It checks .git, applies the size, ports and agent forwarding that a stopped VM’s state asks for, starts the VM if it’s stopped, runs the self-check, sets the VM up and writes the ssh config. A VM whose tier isn’t enforced is stopped, and it gets no name.

devvm code does the same, then opens the folder in VS Code over Remote-SSH with VS Code’s code command, as in code --remote ssh-remote+devvm-website ~/website. VS Code gets the SSH agent that devvm was started with, not the one that devvm’s own connections to the VM carry. Without code on PATH, devvm names the host to connect to with Remote-SSH: Connect to Host.

VS Code

Over Remote-SSH, VS Code reaches further than ssh:

  • Ports. It forwards the ports that programs it starts in the VM listen on to this machine’s localhost, whatever devvm ports says. Those programs include its terminals, its tasks and an agent.
  • Git sign-in. It answers git’s credential prompts in the VM with your GitHub sign-in in VS Code.

devvm turns both off in VS Code’s settings for the VM, ~/.vscode-server/data/Machine/settings.json in the VM. Each time devvm sets the VM up, it sets remote.autoForwardPorts, git.terminalAuthentication and github.gitAuthentication to false and keeps the file’s other settings. A file with comments isn’t plain JSON, so devvm leaves it as it is and says so in the run log.

The VM can change that file back, so for a VM you don’t trust, also set the three in your own VS Code settings on this machine. Programs in the VM can also open URLs in this machine’s browser ($BROWSER).

Agent forwarding

SSH agent forwarding is off by default. While it’s on and you’re connected, anything in the VM, coding agents included, can use the agent’s keys, for example to push or to log in to servers. It can’t copy them. Turn it on for one VM when you need git over SSH there.

flowchart TD
choice{{"devvm ssh-agent"}}
choice -- "off, the default" --> off["no agent:<br>git over SSH fails"]
choice -- "on" --> on["your agent, while<br>you're connected"]
choice -- "devvm" --> own["devvm's own agent,<br>with only the keys<br>you added"]
  • devvm --ssh-agent creates the VM forwarding your agent. devvm ssh-agent on, devvm or off changes it for an existing VM from its next start, and devvm ssh-agent shows it. For a running VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart it now, as devvm restart does, and otherwise, or without a terminal or with --no-input, the change waits for devvm restart or the VM’s next start. Until then, each time devvm opens the running VM it asks in a terminal whether to restart it with the change, with no as the default unless an agent’s new folders wait too (restarting).
  • The choice applies to devvm’s shells and to the ssh entries alike, both as the VM’s current start was made with, so a change reaches neither until the VM next starts, whichever folder devvm runs from. For a VM started outside devvm, such as with limactl start, they follow the current choice. When forwarding is off, an entry says ForwardAgent no, whatever your own Host * settings say, and none of devvm’s own connections to the VM carry your agent.
  • With forwarding off, git over SSH in the VM fails. devvm says so when it creates a VM for a repo whose origin is an SSH URL. Use an HTTPS remote with a GitHub token instead, or turn forwarding on.
  • No keys loaded. When a VM forwards your agent, the agent has no keys and ~/.ssh has one, devvm offers to load it (ssh-add --apple-use-keychain on macOS). To keep it loaded across reboots, add AddKeysToAgent yes, and UseKeychain yes on macOS, under Host * in ~/.ssh/config.
  • You can also use an agent that asks you to approve each use, such as 1Password’s or Secretive.

GitHub’s host keys are preinstalled in every VM, so a first connection to GitHub doesn’t prompt.

devvm’s own agent

devvm’s own agent keeps your other keys out of reach, because it holds only the keys you add to it, such as a deploy key or a key with access to fewer repos.

  • devvm ssh-agent add ~/.ssh/deploy_key starts the agent and loads the key. The agent’s socket is ~/.local/share/devvm/agent.sock. devvm ssh-agent devvm makes this folder’s VM forward that agent instead of yours, in devvm’s shells and in the ssh entries alike. The entries name it as the agent, so an editor forwards it however the editor was started.
  • devvm ssh-agent shows this folder’s VM’s choice, and once you’ve added a key, it then lists the keys devvm’s agent holds, as ssh-add -l does, and each key you added, with its file, its fingerprint and how it’s loaded. It loads the keys the agent lacks before it lists them.
  • devvm ssh-agent rm ~/.ssh/deploy_key takes the key out of devvm’s agent and out of ~/.local/share/devvm/agent-keys.json, so devvm doesn’t load it again. devvm finds the key in the agent by the fingerprint it recorded, so the key file can have changed or be gone, and devvm leaves the file itself as it is. devvm refuses a key you didn’t add, and devvm ssh-agent lists the ones you did.
  • devvm loads a key again when a VM that uses the agent launches without it, such as after a reboot or once the key’s lifetime ran out, and it asks for the key’s passphrase if it has one. It does so only while the file holds the key you added. add records the key’s fingerprint, so devvm doesn’t load a file that was replaced since, or a link that was swapped to another key. A key you replaced in place needs devvm ssh-agent add again.
  • devvm refuses a key inside a folder a VM mounts, and doesn’t load it, because that VM could read it. That’s every folder that a VM’s state says it mounts, whether the VM is running or stopped: its project folder, its agents’ config folders and the shared tools. Keep the keys for devvm’s agent outside project folders.
  • An encrypted key in the old PEM format needs converting first, with ssh-keygen -p -f KEY, because devvm can’t read its fingerprint without the passphrase.

The agent drops each key 12 hours after it loads it, so a VM can’t keep using the key indefinitely. --lifetime 30m changes that for one key, and it takes a duration in minutes, hours, days or weeks, such as 30m, 8h or 1d, or forever. --confirm makes the agent ask you before each use, such as each push or each login, through an ssh-askpass program. macOS doesn’t include one, so install one and put it on your PATH, or set SSH_ASKPASS to it. devvm keeps the keys and their options in ~/.local/share/devvm/agent-keys.json, and running devvm ssh-agent add on the same key again replaces its options.

devvm ssh-agent –json

devvm ssh-agent --json prints what devvm ssh-agent shows as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. mode is this folder’s VM’s choice, off, on or devvm. Each of the keys is a key you added to devvm’s agent, with its file, the fingerprint devvm recorded, confirm, its lifetime and loaded, which says whether the agent holds it. As without --json, devvm loads the keys the agent lacks first, and with no key added, keys is [] and devvm doesn’t start its agent. With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses on, devvm or off with it.

{
 "version": 1,
 "mode": "devvm",
 "keys": [
 {
 "file": "/Users/you/.ssh/deploy_key",
 "fingerprint": "SHA256:mVPwvezndPv/ARoIadVY98vAC0g+P/5633yTC4d/wXE",
 "confirm": false,
 "lifetime": "12h",
 "loaded": true
 }
 ]
}

item.title: Ports and size
item.description:
This page covers the ports a VM forwards to this machine and the CPUs, memory and disk it gets. You choose both when devvm makes a VM, and you can change both later with devvm ports and devvm size. Port forwarding explains how devvm’s forwarder works.

Size and ports

A new VM gets its image’s size unless you set one with --cpus, --memory and --disk, as in devvm --cpus 6. For base that’s 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk. On a machine with fewer than 4 CPUs, base gets as many CPUs as the machine has, and when 8 GiB would leave the machine less than 2 GiB of its own, base gets half of the machine’s memory, which is 4 GiB on an 8 GiB machine. When devvm builds base on such a machine, it says how many CPUs and how much memory base gets, and devvm size -g sets the size that new VMs get instead.

  • --cpus takes a whole number. --memory and --disk take a size in GiB, written 16, 16G or 16GiB, and decimals are allowed.
  • What the flags leave unset comes from the [size] table of config.toml when it sets it, else from what devvm size -g and devvm setup saved (choosing new VMs’ size).
  • devvm refuses more CPUs than this machine has, and a disk smaller than the image’s, because disks can’t shrink. It refuses them before it builds anything.
  • devvm also refuses more memory than a VM can have, because a VM that asks for all of this machine’s memory doesn’t start. A VM can have this machine’s memory less 2 GiB, counted in whole GiB, so 6 GiB on an 8 GiB machine. On a machine with 4 GiB or less, it can have half, so 2 GiB on a 4 GiB machine. When you ask for more, devvm says how much memory this machine has and the most you can give a VM, so you can run the command again with that.

A new VM forwards every TCP port from 1024 up that it listens on, unless --ports says otherwise, as in devvm --ports 5173.

  • --ports takes all, none, or ports and ranges such as 5173,8000-8010.
  • Without --ports, the default comes from ports in config.toml when it sets it, else from what devvm ports -g saved, and without either, a new VM forwards every port.
  • When you customize a new VM without --ports, devvm asks whether it forwards every port, none or the ports you type, starting from the default, and saves the answer for that VM alone (what a new VM gets).

devvm refuses a default that isn’t a valid value, as it refuses a bad flag, and for one in config.toml it names the file and the line (when devvm can’t read it).

Ports

A VM forwards the TCP ports it listens on to the same port on this machine’s localhost, so a server on :5173 in the VM is at localhost:5173 here. To change which ports a VM forwards:

devvm ports # what this folder's VM forwards: all, none or a list
devvm ports 5173,8000-8010 # only these ports and ranges
devvm ports add 5432 # one more
devvm ports rm 5173 # one fewer, as listed; the last leaves none
devvm ports none # nothing; devvm ports all forwards every port again
devvm ports -g none # what new VMs forward (default: all)
  • A change applies at once. A stopped VM forwards the new ports from its next start. On a running VM, devvm starts its forwarder again with the new ports while the VM runs on, so a server on an added port reaches this machine within a few seconds. The connections that were open through the old forwarder close, so a client that was connected through it has to connect again.
  • add and rm take ports and ranges, not all or none. devvm refuses rm on a VM that forwards every port, because there’s no list to remove from. -g also works with add and rm.
  • devvm ports -g shows what new VMs forward, followed by where it came from after a #, and devvm ports -g --json adds it as source. When config.toml sets ports, devvm ports -g refuses to change it and names the file, so edit config.toml instead (where a default comes from).
  • devvm forwards ports on every network tier, and it forwards no ports from builds.

When a VM forwards every port, devvm forwards each TCP port from 1024 up that a server in the VM listens on, whether on the VM’s loopback or on all its addresses. When a VM lists its ports, devvm forwards those ports alone, however many there are, ports below 1024 included. A port reaches this machine within a few seconds of the server starting, only on localhost (127.0.0.1 and ::1), and the forward goes away when the server stops. At most 256 ports are forwarded at once. Your browser sends the cookies of every app you use on localhost to a forwarded port as well, so the server in the VM gets them (your browser).

A VM never takes a port that a program on this machine already has, a port that another VM lists, or a port that devvm uses for its VMs’ ssh and proxies. When a port you listed is taken by a program on this machine as the VM starts, or as you change its ports, devvm warns you and the VM runs on without that port. The next start or change that finds the port free forwards it. A program that starts on a port after the VM’s forward does can still bind it on all addresses, as most servers do, and then that program’s localhost connections reach the VM.

If the forwarder can’t start, devvm warns you and names its log, and the VM runs on without forwarded ports.

UDP isn’t forwarded, on any backend. Run the UDP client in the VM instead, or tunnel it over a forwarded TCP port with socat, installed on both sides. For a UDP server on port 8125 in the VM, with TCP port 9125 forwarded:

socat TCP-LISTEN:9125,fork,reuseaddr UDP:127.0.0.1:8125 # in the VM
socat UDP-LISTEN:8125,fork TCP:127.0.0.1:9125 # on this machine

TCP is a stream, so datagrams can arrive merged or split. This suits low-rate request and response traffic, such as DNS, statsd or syslog, but not high-rate or latency-sensitive traffic, such as games, QUIC or WebRTC media.

Size

To see or change a VM’s size:

devvm size # what this folder's VM has: cpus=4 memory=8GiB disk=100GiB
devvm size --cpus 6 --memory 16 # change it; what isn't given stays
devvm size --disk 200 # a bigger disk; never a smaller one
devvm size -g --memory 16 # the size new VMs get (default: the image's)
devvm size -g # cpus=, memory= and disk= lines, empty for the image's, each with its source
  • The flags take the same values as for a new VM and have the same limits, so devvm refuses more CPUs than this machine has and more memory than a VM can have (size and ports). devvm size -g checks a default size in the same way when you set it. A VM that already has more memory keeps it and still starts, because devvm checks a size only when you set one.
  • devvm size -g ends each line with where its value came from, after a #: the path of config.toml, devvm: settings.json for what devvm size -g or devvm setup saved, or devvm: default for the image’s. When config.toml sets cpus, memory or disk, devvm size -g refuses to change that one and names the file, so edit config.toml instead (where a default comes from).
  • A stopped VM gets its new size when it next starts, such as with devvm, and until then devvm size shows what the VM has now and says what changes. For a running VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart it now, which stops anything running in it, and if you answer yes, devvm restarts it as devvm restart does. Otherwise, and without a terminal or with --no-input, the VM keeps its size until it next starts, for example with devvm restart. When devvm opens the running VM while its new size still waits, it asks once more in a terminal, with no as the default unless an agent’s new folders wait too, and a yes restarts the VM with its new size before the shell opens (restarting).
  • Disks grow but never shrink, so devvm refuses a disk smaller than the VM’s.

Choosing new VMs’ size

devvm asks for the CPUs and memory that new VMs get on your first run, before it asks which features base gets, and again whenever you run devvm setup:

devvm setup # asks its questions, the size among them
devvm size -g --cpus 6 --memory 16 # only the size, without asking

Before the two questions, devvm says how many CPUs and how much memory this machine has. Each question shows in brackets the value new VMs get now. That’s what config.toml sets or devvm size -g saved, or else base’s own size fitted to this machine: 4 CPUs and 8 GiB, or less on a machine that doesn’t have room for them (size and ports). Confirm to keep the value, or enter another one. devvm checks what you type as it checks --cpus and --memory, and when this machine can’t give it, devvm says why and asks again.

devvm doesn’t ask for a value that config.toml sets, and says so. It saves only the values you type, where devvm size -g saves them, and keeps a saved disk size as it is. When you keep both values, devvm saves nothing, so new VMs go on getting the image’s size. Either way, devvm prints the size new VMs get. A new size changes only the VMs made after it, and nothing is rebuilt, so existing VMs keep their size until you change it with devvm size.

The first run asks only in a terminal, and only when no size is set and you didn’t give --cpus or --memory. It asks once, because that run also chooses base’s features, and devvm asks only before they’re chosen. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm asks nothing, and new VMs get the image’s size. devvm setup asks only in a terminal, without --no-input, and only when you give it no flags (devvm setup). To set the size without asking, use devvm size -g --cpus N --memory GiB, which takes the same values and has the same limits.

Disk use

A VM’s disk size is how far the disk can grow, not how much space it takes. A project VM starts as a copy of its image’s disk that shares the image’s blocks, so a new VM takes almost nothing until it writes (clones and overlays):

  • macOS: the copy is an APFS clone. du counts the shared blocks as the clone’s own, so it overcounts.
  • Linux: the copy is a qcow2 overlay of the image’s disk, which holds only the VM’s changes, about 12 MB for a new VM instead of 2 GB.

Free space

Before devvm builds an image or makes a VM, it checks the free space on the disk that will hold it, and it refuses to start the step when there’s less free than the step needs:

Step macOS Linux
building base 8 GiB 8 GiB
building any other image 2 GiB 8 GiB
building shared tool images 3 GiB, and 0.5 GiB for each tool 9 GiB, and 0.5 GiB for each tool
making a VM 2 GiB 2 GiB

devvm rounds each number up to whole GiB, so building one shared tool with Lima on macOS needs 4 GiB, and building all ten needs 8 GiB. Each build checks again before it starts, so the first VM on a Mac, which builds base, needs 8 GiB free.

The numbers leave a margin over what each step took when devvm’s tests measured the free space before, during and after it. Most of a step’s space is only needed while it runs. On Lima on macOS, base took about 1 GiB with Ubuntu’s cloud image already downloaded, and downloading the image takes up to another 0.9 GiB. base’s features add up to 2.5 GiB. A build of all ten shared tools took 6 GiB at its peak and kept 1.5 GiB of images. On macOS, an image built on another and a new VM take only what they write. On Linux hosts, an image and the VM that builds shared tools start as a full copy of their parent’s disk, but a new VM’s disk holds only its own changes. A VM then grows as you work in it, and its disk never shrinks.

devvm checks the disk that holds the images and VMs, which is the disk of devvm’s Lima home. Shared tool images come out into devvm’s data folder, so a tools build also checks that folder’s disk, which needs 0.5 GiB and 0.25 GiB for each tool, rounded up: 1 GiB for one tool and 3 GiB for all ten. When devvm’s data folder is on a small temporary disk, such as a tmpfs /tmp on Linux, devvm checks that disk.

devvm doctor also warns when that disk has less free space than building base needs, but the warning doesn’t make doctor fail. When devvm refuses, see Not enough free space for how to make room.

As JSON

devvm size --json and devvm ports --json print what the commands show as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. With -g, they print the same fields for new VMs. With --json they only show, so devvm refuses --cpus, --memory, --disk or a list of ports with it.

devvm size --json has cpus, memory_gib and disk_gib, and leaves out what isn’t set. For -g, that’s what new VMs take from the image. When the VM’s size changes at its next start, pending has the cpus, memory_gib and disk_gib that change.

{
 "version": 1,
 "cpus": 4,
 "memory_gib": 8,
 "disk_gib": 100,
 "pending": {
 "memory_gib": 16
 }
}

With -g, devvm size --json also has sources, which says where each of cpus, memory and disk came from: config.toml, settings.json for what devvm saved, or built-in for the image’s (where a default comes from).

{
 "version": 1,
 "cpus": 6,
 "memory_gib": 16,
 "sources": {
 "cpus": "settings.json",
 "disk": "built-in",
 "memory": "config.toml"
 }
}

devvm ports --json has ports, which is all, none or a list of ports and ranges, written as devvm ports takes it. With -g, it also has source, which is config.toml, settings.json or built-in.

{
 "version": 1,
 "ports": "5173,8000-8010"
}

item.title: Managing VMs
item.description:
This page covers a VM from the time devvm makes it until you delete it: opening, restarting and stopping it, deleting it, listing your VMs, and what devvm does when you run a command in a subfolder or when the project folder is made again, moved, deleted or on a disk that isn’t connected. Overview has each step devvm takes for a new VM and an existing one.

Opening a VM

devvm makes a new VM from its image of base and the layers you chose, building the image first if it isn’t built yet, then starts the VM and opens a shell in it in devvm’s place, so devvm ends when the shell does. The VM mounts only the project folder, read-write, and the shared tools and its agents’ config folders, read-only, or with --clone it gets its own clone of the repo instead of the folder. devvm also locks the .git hooks and config of the folder and of the repos nested in it against changes from the VM. On macOS it locks them with a file flag, and on Linux it makes them read-only in the VM where the kernel lets it and only watches them where it doesn’t (.git protection). For a VM that exists, devvm starts it if it’s stopped and opens it as it is.

A VM is running or stopped from the time devvm makes it until you delete it.

flowchart TD
none(["no VM"]) -- "devvm" --> running(["running"])
running -- "devvm restart,<br>devvm update" --> running
running -- "devvm stop" --> stopped(["stopped"])
stopped -- "devvm,<br>devvm restart,<br>devvm update" --> running
running -- "devvm rm" --> deleted(["deleted"])
stopped -- "devvm rm" --> deleted
outdated@{ shape: braces, label: "When its image changes, a VM<br>is outdated, and it keeps<br>its image until devvm update." }
running ~~~ outdated

Restarting and stopping

devvm restart stops this folder’s VM, then starts it and opens a shell in it as devvm does. Some changes apply only when a VM starts, such as a new size for a running VM, a change into or out of the open tier, a change to its SSH agent forwarding, or the config folders of an agent that devvm tools add added, and a restart applies them.

When you make one of these changes to a running VM with devvm size, devvm network into or out of open or devvm ssh-agent, or change its .git protection on macOS with devvm git-protect, which waits for the VM to stop, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart the VM now, because anything running in it stops. If you answer yes, devvm restarts it as devvm restart does and opens a shell in it. If you answer no, devvm keeps the change and says that devvm restart applies it, and it does the same without asking when there’s no terminal or you pass --no-input.

When devvm opens a running VM that still has changes waiting for its next start, it names them, such as its size and its agent folder mounts, and asks in a terminal once whether to restart the VM now. It names each change on a line of its own, and when more than two wait, it names the first and says how many more there are. When the VM’s agent folder mounts are among the changes, the default answer is yes ([Y/n]), because an agent you just added needs its folders. Otherwise the default is no ([y/N]), because the VM is already running and you may only want its shell. If you answer yes, devvm stops the VM, starts it with the changes and opens a shell in it. If you answer no, or there’s no terminal, or you pass --no-input, devvm warns about each change and opens a shell in the running VM.

devvm stop stops this folder’s VM and its proxy (stopping a VM). Once the VM is stopped, devvm locks its .git again and checks it, as a launch that finds the VM stopped does, and it takes the VM’s entry out of devvm’s ssh config. devvm, devvm restart, and the commands that need the VM running, such as devvm host, start it again.

Deleting a VM

devvm rm deletes this folder’s VM together with what devvm keeps for it. That’s the VM’s state, its own allowlist, its network log, its .git locks or, for a --clone VM, the repo’s devvm remote, and its ssh config entry (deleting a VM). It asks first in a terminal, and --force deletes without asking, which devvm rm needs when there’s no terminal.

When the VM has an agent, devvm first exports the agents’ history, unless you give --no-export, and when the export fails, devvm keeps the VM (history). For a --clone VM, devvm offers to fetch the branches this repo hasn’t fetched, and it deletes the VM’s uncommitted changes only after you confirm. --no-clone-check skips that check and warns you that the clone’s unfetched commits and uncommitted changes go with the VM (deleting the VM).

devvm deletes the VM made for an earlier folder at this path only after you confirm (a folder made again). In a folder without a VM of its own, devvm rm acts on the VM of the nearest folder with one that this folder is inside, and it names that VM and deletes it only after you confirm (a subfolder). devvm asks these questions only in a terminal, and --force never answers them. To delete a VM whose folder you deleted or moved, give its name, as in devvm rm devvm-web-71a99b1076d92c (a VM whose folder is gone).

Listing VMs

devvm ls prints a table of the project VMs, sorted by name, with a header first. Images and build VMs aren’t in it.

Column
NAME the VM’s name, devvm-<folder>-<hash>
STATUS its state as its backend reports it, such as Running or Stopped
IMAGE its image, base and its layers, with a base from a container image as base (from node:24) (details)
TOOLS its shared tools, joined with commas, such as node,claude, or - for none
GIT its .git protection, on or off, or clone for a --clone VM
NET its network tier, open, internet, allowlist or none, or unenforced (the self-check), and internet (learning) while it learns the hosts it needs
LINKS how many links it has to ports of your other VMs, or - for none
FOLDER its project folder, with (gone) after it when nothing is at that path, which devvm rm VM deals with (a VM whose folder is gone), or (not connected) when the folder was on a disk that isn’t connected (details)

A value the VM’s state doesn’t have shows as -, so a VM whose creation didn’t finish shows only its name and status.

devvm ls –json

devvm ls --json prints the same list as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. vms has a VM’s columns as fields, sorted by name. image is the image alone, tools is the list of its shared tools, [] for none, and from is the container image its base started from, which is left out for a base from Ubuntu’s cloud image. A value the VM’s state doesn’t have is "". folder is the folder alone, and folder_state is there when something is at its path, gone when nothing is, and not_connected when the folder was on a disk that isn’t connected. links is how many links the VM has, 0 for none. net is the tier alone, and a VM that’s learning the hosts it needs also has learning_since, the time it started learning.

{
 "version": 1,
 "vms": [
 {
 "name": "devvm-website-71a99b1076d92c",
 "status": "Running",
 "image": "base",
 "tools": ["node", "claude"],
 "from": "node:24",
 "git": "on",
 "net": "internet",
 "learning_since": "2026-11-07T10:00:00Z",
 "backend": "lima",
 "folder": "/Users/you/code/website",
 "folder_state": "there",
 "links": 0
 }
 ]
}

A subfolder

A VM mounts its whole project folder, so the folders inside it are in the VM at the same paths. When the folder you run a command in has no VM of its own, devvm looks for one in the folders it’s inside, starting with the nearest. It stops before your home folder and the filesystem root, so it never uses a VM made for either. It stops at the nearest folder that has a VM, and when that VM was made for an earlier folder at its path (a folder made again), or its backend has lost it, the folder you’re in has no VM, so devvm never reaches past it to a VM further out. Using a parent folder’s VM mounts nothing new, because the subfolder is already inside the folder that VM mounts.

When you run devvm in such a subfolder, such as ~/some-project/src, devvm opens the parent folder’s VM there, with the shell at the subfolder’s path, and first prints a line that names the VM and the folder it was made for. It does the same with or without a terminal, and it asks nothing. --tools, --agents and --layers change nothing on the parent folder’s VM, as on any VM that exists, and devvm warns that they don’t (adding and removing tools). devvm --here makes a new VM for the subfolder instead, and so does devvm --clone, which makes the subfolder’s own clone VM. Once the subfolder has its own VM, devvm opens that one. In a parent folder’s --clone VM, the shell opens in the subfolder when the clone has it (subfolders).

The other commands that act on this folder’s VM, such as devvm stop, restart, tools, size, ports, host and code, use the parent folder’s VM in the same way, without asking. Each one first prints a line that names the VM and the folder it was made for. devvm rm is the exception, because it never deletes a parent folder’s VM unasked. In a terminal, it names the VM and its folder and asks before deleting it, with no as the default, and --force never answers that question. Without a terminal, it refuses and tells you to run devvm rm in the parent folder instead. The commands that give the VM more access ask in the same way, because the parent folder’s project may not expect them. They are devvm secret use, devvm ssh-agent on and devvm ssh-agent devvm, devvm network with a lower tier, such as devvm network open, devvm network allow, devvm network rm when it removes a deny, and devvm git-protect off. In a terminal, each one names the VM and its folder and asks before it changes the VM, with no as the default. Without a terminal, it refuses and tells you to run it in the parent folder, or in a terminal to confirm. The commands that take access away, such as devvm secret unuse and devvm network deny, ask nothing. devvm host gives the subfolder as the folder to open in the VM, and devvm code opens the subfolder. devvm adopt acts only on the VM made for this folder’s own path, never on a parent folder’s.

A subfolder that is a git repo of its own is treated as a separate project, and so is a subfolder inside such a repo, when the repo is below the folder with the VM. That covers a nested repo, a submodule and a worktree, which each have a .git folder or file of their own. When you run devvm there, devvm makes a new VM for the subfolder, with or without a terminal, and asks nothing. The other commands don’t use the parent folder’s VM there, and they say this folder has no VM, as in any folder without one.

Every command that acts on this folder’s VM, devvm included, takes --here and --parent, and each finds the VM in the same way. --here uses only this folder’s own VM, so devvm --here makes one when the folder has none, and the other commands say this folder has no VM. --parent uses the VM of the nearest folder with one that this folder is inside, even across a git repo of its own and even when this folder has a VM of its own, so devvm --parent in a repo of its own opens the project’s VM there. When no folder that this folder is inside has a VM, a command given --parent fails and changes nothing. You can’t give the two together, or either of them with -g, and devvm --clone doesn’t take --parent, because a clone VM is always the folder’s own. devvm rm VM takes neither, because it deletes the VM you name, and neither does devvm adopt, because it acts only on this folder’s own path. With --parent, devvm rm and the commands that give the VM more access still ask before they change the parent folder’s VM.

A nested project replaced

A project with a VM of its own inside a folder with another VM, such as a nested repo, is in both VMs, because the parent folder’s VM mounts everything inside its folder. Code in the parent folder’s VM can change the nested project’s files, though not the hooks and config of its .git while the parent folder’s VM protects it, as .git protection does for the repos nested in a VM’s folder. It can also move the nested project folder aside and put a link in its place, or another folder. On Linux, if devvm then started the nested project’s VM, the VM would mount whatever the link points to, such as your home folder. On macOS the VM mounts the project folder itself, wherever it was moved, and never what a link at its path points to. On both, devvm checks the nested project folder just before it starts the VM and again once the VM runs. If the folder is now a link, sits below a link, or is another folder, devvm doesn’t start the VM, or it stops the VM again, and it tells you which. Find what replaced the folder, move the project folder back to its path, and run the command again. Replacing the folder while the VM runs never shows the VM what the link points to. On Linux the VM keeps the folder it mounted when it started, and on macOS the VM gets “Operation not permitted” for its project folder, as it does when the folder was moved aside while the VM started and put back later, so run devvm restart once the folder is back. To keep a nested project out of the parent folder’s VM altogether, move it out of the parent folder.

Each time devvm makes or opens the nested project’s VM, it warns once and names the VM of the nearest parent folder that mounts the project. It warns whether that VM runs or not, because the VM can write to the folder whenever it runs. A --clone VM mounts nothing, so devvm doesn’t warn when you open one, and a parent folder’s --clone VM never counts. The other commands, devvm restart included, don’t warn.

A folder made again

A VM belongs to the folder it was made for, which devvm knows by its path and by the folder itself (one VM per folder). When that folder was deleted and a new one made at the same path, every command that opens, stops or changes the VM refuses it, such as devvm, devvm stop, devvm restart and devvm tools. Two commands deal with it, and each acts only after you confirm in a terminal:

  • devvm rm deletes the VM and never exports its history, because its folder is gone. The VM may hold that project’s work, so --force never answers this question.
  • devvm adopt gives the VM to this folder, with its files, secrets and allowlist. Its .git protection starts again, as if .git had just appeared. devvm adopt --force gives it without asking, which devvm adopt needs when there’s no terminal.

A moved or renamed folder

When you move or rename a project folder on the same disk, as with mv ~/code/app ~/work/app, the folder keeps its VM once you say so. The first time you run a command on this folder’s VM at the folder’s new path, such as devvm or devvm stop, devvm finds the VM made for the folder at its old path, names the VM and that path, and asks whether to move the VM here, with no as the default. When you answer yes, the VM belongs to the folder at its new path, with its home folder, secrets, allowlist, links and settings, and devvm finds it there from then on without asking. When you answer no, the folder has no VM, so devvm makes a new one, and the old VM stays with the old path, where devvm rm VM deletes it (a VM whose folder is gone). Without a terminal, devvm refuses and tells you to run devvm adopt in a terminal, or devvm adopt --force, which moves the VM without asking.

The VM mounts the folder at its new path from its next start. When the VM is running as you move it, it still mounts the old path, so devvm stops it before it moves it, and devvm then starts it with the folder at its new path. If a VM runs with its folder at another path all the same, devvm asks whether to restart it as it opens the VM, with yes as the default, and when you answer no, it warns that the VM mounts the folder at its new path only when it next starts. The folder’s .git moves with it, locks and all, so its .git protection goes on as before. Links to the VM and its group go by the VM’s name, so they stay, and a link whose TARGET is the folder’s path finds the VM at its new path. The folder’s path in the VM changes with it.

Claude Code’s history follows the folder. Claude Code keeps a folder’s sessions and its settings for that folder, such as whether you trust it and the MCP servers you added there, by the folder’s path. At the VM’s next start, devvm moves them in the VM from the old path to the new one, so claude --continue and claude --resume offer the sessions from before the move. When Claude Code already has sessions at the new path, the old path’s sessions join them, and a session the new path already has stays as it is. Settings that Claude Code already keeps for the new path stay as they are, and the old path’s stay under the old path. devvm moves only what Claude Code keeps for the project folder itself, so sessions you started in one of its subfolders stay under that subfolder’s old path.

Codex records each session’s folder in the session, and codex resume and codex resume --last look only at the current folder’s sessions, so they miss the ones from the old path. codex resume --all lists the sessions of every folder, the old path’s included, and codex resume with a session’s ID resumes that session wherever it started. opencode keeps the sessions of a git repo by the repo’s first commit, so they follow the folder without any change. In a folder that isn’t a git repo, opencode keeps sessions by the folder’s path, so they stay under the old path.

devvm offers the move only when the folder at the new path is the folder the VM was made for, which devvm knows by its device, inode and birth time (one VM per folder), and when nothing is at the old path any more, or only a symlink to the new path. It never offers a VM to a copy of the folder, which is another folder, or to a folder on a file system that may give a new folder the inode number of a deleted one. That leaves folders whose file system records a birth time: on macOS, folders on APFS and HFS+, and on Linux, folders on ext4, XFS, Btrfs, tmpfs, ZFS, F2FS and bcachefs. Folders on network shares, FUSE file systems and USB drives formatted with FAT or exFAT never get the offer. devvm also offers no VM for a folder that another user owns, or a --clone VM, which keeps its own clone of the repo at the old path inside the VM. When more than one VM was made for the folder at paths it had before, devvm moves none of them and names them, so you can choose one with devvm adopt VM. devvm refuses to move a VM to a folder that it wouldn’t make a new VM for, such as your home folder (project folders devvm refuses). A new folder at the old path gets a new VM of its own, with another name.

Moving a folder to another disk copies it, so the folder at the new path is another folder, which devvm never offers the VM to on its own. To give the copy the VM, delete the folder at the old path or disconnect its disk, then run devvm adopt VM in the copy, with the VM’s name as devvm ls lists it. devvm names the VM and its old path and asks first, with no as the default, and --force moves it without asking, which devvm adopt VM needs when there’s no terminal. The VM’s .git protection starts again, as if .git had just appeared, because the copy’s .git is another folder too. devvm refuses a VM whose folder is still there, a --clone VM, and a folder that has a VM of its own, which you delete first with devvm rm.

A VM whose folder is gone

When you delete or move a project folder, its VM stays, because the VM may hold work that’s nowhere else and devvm never deletes a VM on its own. A folder you moved gets its VM back at its new path once you say so (a moved or renamed folder), and until then the VM’s folder counts as gone. devvm ls writes (gone) after the folder of each VM whose folder is gone (listing VMs), and devvm space names each one with its folder. A folder on a disk that isn’t connected isn’t gone, and a folder on a disk that isn’t connected covers it. A folder that was deleted and made again at the same path isn’t gone, and devvm handles it as a folder made again. A VM whose folder is gone explains how devvm tells.

devvm rm VM deletes a VM whose folder is gone, and you can run it in any folder. VM is the VM’s name, as devvm ls lists it, or the alias that ssh reaches it by. In a terminal, devvm names the VM and its folder and asks before deleting it, with no as the default. --force deletes it without asking, which devvm rm VM needs when there’s no terminal. Like devvm rm, it deletes what devvm keeps for the VM, and when the VM has an agent, devvm first exports the agents’ history unless you give --no-export (history).

The export reads the history from the running VM. Starting a stopped VM would make its folder again, because Lima makes a missing folder that a VM mounts, so for a stopped VM with an agent devvm refuses and tells you to run devvm rm VM --no-export. If you moved the folder and want the history, run devvm history export or devvm rm in the folder at its new path, which moves the VM there first (a moved or renamed folder). A --clone VM mounts no project folder, so devvm starts it to export the history. Its clone’s work can’t be fetched into a repo that’s gone, though, so devvm refuses to delete it unless you give --no-clone-check, which deletes the VM and that work with it.

devvm rm VM refuses a VM whose folder is still there, including a VM made for an earlier folder at that path, and tells you to run devvm rm in that folder. Given this folder’s own VM, it does what devvm rm does. It also refuses a name that isn’t one of your VMs, and a VM that its backend no longer has, for which devvm gc --orphans deletes what devvm keeps (leftovers of a VM deleted outside devvm). When the VM’s state names this folder but the folder has a VM of its own, which only a state changed by hand can do, devvm refuses it as a VM whose folder is still there, so devvm rm VM never deletes the folder’s own VM in its place.

A folder on a disk that isn’t connected

When a project folder is on an external disk, a USB stick or a network share that isn’t connected, nothing is at its path, but the folder may still hold the project’s work, and so may the VM. devvm tells this apart from a deleted folder by the disk: it finds the nearest folder above the path that’s still there, and when that folder is on another disk than the project folder was, the project folder isn’t connected. devvm ls writes (not connected) after such a folder, and devvm space names each such VM with its folder. To use the VM again, connect the disk.

devvm rm VM refuses such a VM when there’s no terminal, even with --force, and tells you to connect the disk, or to run devvm rm VM in a terminal to delete the VM anyway. In a terminal, devvm names the VM and its folder and asks before deleting it, with no as the default, and --force never answers that question. Otherwise it deletes the VM as it deletes one whose folder is gone. A folder that you moved to another disk and then deleted counts as not connected too, so devvm asks in that case as well.

item.title: Images and tools
item.description:
Every VM is a copy of an image. An image is base with your choice of layers on it, and nothing else. A VM also gets the shared tools you chose for it, such as node or Claude Code, which are mounted into it and are never part of an image. This page covers what base and the layers bring, adding layers to a VM, how the shared tools work, what a new VM gets, and how to rebuild, list and delete images. Images and caching explains how devvm builds, pins and caches them, and toolchains and coding agents list the shared tools.

flowchart TD
ubuntu["Ubuntu's cloud image,<br>or a --from image"] --> base["base, with<br>the features you chose"]
base --> docker["docker, a layer<br>on base"]
base -. "a copy" .-> vm1["VM of base,<br>with node"]
docker -. "a copy" .-> vm2["VM of docker,<br>with node and claude"]
tools[("shared tools:<br>node, claude…")] -- "mounted<br>read-only" --> vm1 & vm2

Base

base is the image that every other image is built on. It is Ubuntu 26.04’s cloud image with git, build-essential, ripgrep, jq, sqlite3 and mise added, followed by the optional features you chose, such as oh-my-bash and fzf. Docker comes as a layer of devvm’s, so you choose it when you customize a new VM, or give devvm --layers docker. With --from, base starts from a container image instead of Ubuntu’s (details).

A VM made from base gets 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk unless you give it another size, and on a small machine it gets fewer CPUs and less memory (size and ports).

base drops the server extras that Ubuntu’s cloud image comes with, which are snapd, multipath, ModemManager, udisks, firmware updates, crash reporting, tracing tools, kernel headers, and apt’s background updates and upgrades. That saves 0.9 GB of disk and 100 MB of memory per VM. The everyday tools stay, such as htop, tmux, lsof, strace, tcpdump, rsync and nano.

The first time devvm builds base on this machine, it starts from the newest release of Ubuntu’s cloud image and installs the newest packages from Ubuntu’s archive, or first from a mirror you set. devvm keeps a copy of each package it installed, so building the same base again, such as after devvm images rm base, installs exactly those packages from the copies, with no network for them. devvm rebuild base starts again from the newest image and packages. Your VMs use Ubuntu’s live archive, and base keeps no package lists, so run sudo apt update in a VM before you install a package, and apt upgrade then gets the current updates.

Layers

An image is base with layers on it, named bottom first and joined with +, so foo+bar is bar on foo on base. You can leave base itself out, which makes base+foo the same as foo. An image name never holds shared tools, which aren’t layers, so devvm build, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm refuse a shared tool’s name, such as node, and point you to devvm tools.

A layer is a script that bash runs in the image’s VM as the VM’s user, who has sudo. It is either one of devvm’s built-in layers or one of yours, at ~/.config/devvm/layers/<name>.sh. A layer’s name is made of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starts with a letter or digit, and is neither base, a built-in layer’s name nor a shared tool’s name. devvm refuses any other name in an image, and it refuses a layer whose script is missing. devvm layer new NAME starts a layer of your own (details).

devvm build foo+bar # builds base, foo and foo+bar, unless they're built
devvm rebuild foo # builds foo again, and deletes the old foo and foo+bar

Built-in layers

devvm ships three layers, desktop, docker and nix. You choose them like any other layer, in the list devvm shows for a new VM or as in devvm --layers docker, and you build one with devvm build nix. To give every new VM one, choose it with devvm setup --layers, and to give a VM you have one, run devvm layer add (adding layers to a VM). Their names are reserved, so devvm refuses devvm layer new docker and never reads a desktop.sh, docker.sh or nix.sh of yours. The hosts that each layer needs are in its own allowlist.

desktop

The desktop layer installs an Xfce desktop with TigerVNC’s server, which devvm desktop opens in Screen Sharing, and adds about 370 MB to the image. Its packages come from the distribution’s archive as it is when the layer builds, which on a base made --from alpine means Alpine’s own packages, and they aren’t pinned. It needs no hosts of its own on the allowlist tier, and a VM without the layer has no desktop.

docker

The docker layer installs Docker’s engine, CLI, BuildKit and Compose from Docker’s apt repository, adds the VM’s user to the docker group, and starts the daemon at each boot. On a base made --from alpine, it installs Alpine’s own packages instead. A VM without the layer has no Docker. A VM with the layer can be on any network tier like any other, because its containers’ connections go through the VM’s network, which devvm confines from outside the VM (network tiers). devvm gives every container the VM’s proxy settings, and on a confined tier, a container that ignores them, or was made without them through Docker’s API, reaches the hosts the VM’s rules allow by name through transparent mode, on Docker’s default bridge and on networks that docker network create and Compose make. Such a container doesn’t trust the VM’s CA, so a blocked HTTPS host gives it a certificate error rather than the proxy’s 403, and the block is logged all the same. A container run with --network none, or on an --internal network, reaches nothing.

nix

The nix layer installs Nix with flakes and the nix command turned on, and direnv with nix-direnv, so a project’s flake.nix, shell.nix or devenv.nix can supply its toolchain. Each VM has a Nix store and daemon of its own, which no other VM and nothing on this machine shares. VMs share their downloads from Nix’s binary cache through a cache on this machine that only devvm fills. Nix projects explains that cache, and how a flake’s dev shell and the shared tools work together.

The nix layer works on a base from Ubuntu, Debian or Alpine. On a base made --from alpine, it installs Alpine’s xz package, which isn’t pinned, and runs Nix’s daemon as an OpenRC service.

Adding layers to a VM

A VM keeps the layers devvm made it with, because a layer’s script changes the VM’s disk. devvm layer add LAYER... gives a VM more layers by making it again. devvm builds an image with the new layers on top of the VM’s own, in the order you give them, and gives the VM a new disk, copied from that image. A VM of docker with desktop added is made again from docker+desktop, so the images it already uses stay as they are. devvm names the layers the VM has already and leaves them where they are, and when the VM has all of them, devvm says so and changes nothing.

devvm layer add desktop # make this folder's VM again with the desktop layer on top
devvm layer add docker nix # docker, then nix on top of it
devvm layer add desktop --force # the same without asking, as a script must

Everything on the VM’s disk that devvm doesn’t keep is lost, so in a terminal devvm names the image and asks first, with no as the default. Without a terminal, it refuses unless you give --force. When the VM has a coding agent, devvm first exports the agents’ history, as devvm rm does, unless you give --no-export (history). In a subfolder of a folder with a VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to make that folder’s VM again, and refuses without one.

devvm refuses before it changes anything when a name isn’t a layer, or is a shared tool’s name, which devvm tools add adds instead. It also refuses when the VM’s backend can’t run one of the layers, when the VM’s creation didn’t finish, and for a --clone VM, whose clone of the repo is on its disk. To give a --clone VM more layers, run devvm clone off, which offers to fetch the clone’s work first, then devvm layer add and devvm clone on (switching a VM that exists).

devvm then works in this order:

  1. It builds the new image, so a build that fails leaves the VM as it was.
  2. It exports the agents’ history and saves the VM’s home folder on this machine.
  3. It stops the VM and sets its old disk aside under another name.
  4. It makes the VM again from the new image, with the same name and settings, and starts it.
  5. It copies the home folder onto the new disk and deletes the old disk, then opens a shell in the VM.

Until the new VM has started with its home folder, a step that fails, or Ctrl+C, deletes the new disk and puts the old one back as it was. While one devvm makes a VM again, another devvm that would make the same VM again refuses, and so does devvm in its folder, so wait for the first to finish. While devvm makes the VM again, the old disk, the new one and the saved home folder take room on this machine at the same time, and devvm checks for free space before it starts.

What a VM made again keeps

devvm keeps the project folder, which is on this machine, and everything it keeps for the VM: its name, its shared tools, its size, its ports, its network tier and allowlist, its secrets’ bindings, its SSH agent choice and its .git protection. It also keeps the VM’s links, group and published ports, its desktop’s password and port, and what its devcontainer.json gave it. The commands in its devcontainer.json that run once, such as postCreateCommand, run again on the new disk. The VM gets new SSH host keys, which devvm pins as it does for any new VM, and it keeps its identity, so links to it still reach it.

devvm keeps the VM’s home folder too. It reads the folder as the VM’s user before it stops the VM, and copies it onto the new disk before devvm’s own setup runs there. What other shells in the VM write after devvm reads the folder is lost, so close them first. A file that the new image puts in your home itself, such as ~/.bashrc, stays the image’s, so put shell settings of your own in a file of yours in ~/.bashrc.d. devvm leaves out what the new VM gets from devvm itself: ~/.config/devvm, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, the agents’ logins, and the agents’ folders and files that devvm links or copies from this machine. It leaves out ~/.cache too. devvm keeps only files, folders and symlinks, without setuid bits, and nothing from a filesystem mounted inside your home. --clean-home gives the VM the new image’s home folder instead.

Everything else on the VM’s disk is lost: the packages you installed with apt, programs installed outside your home, Docker’s images, containers and volumes, the Nix store, and the processes that ran in it. When saving the home folder fails, devvm keeps the VM as it was, and --clean-home goes ahead without it.

A remake that stops halfway

If devvm itself is killed while it makes a VM again, such as when this machine loses power, the VM’s state records the remake. The next devvm, devvm layer add, devvm layer rm, devvm update, devvm clone on or devvm clone off in the folder finishes it without asking. When the new VM already has its home folder, devvm only deletes the old disk. When the old disk is still set aside otherwise, devvm puts it back and makes the VM again from the start, and when it’s gone, devvm makes the new VM with the home folder it saved. Until then, other commands on the VM refuse and name devvm, and devvm rm deletes the VM together with its old disk.

Taking layers out of a VM

devvm layer rm LAYER... takes layers out of a VM by making it again, in the same way that devvm layer add puts them in. devvm builds an image of the VM’s other layers, in the order they had, and gives the VM a new disk, copied from that image. A VM of docker+nix+desktop without nix is made again from docker+desktop, and a VM without any of its layers is made again from base. devvm names the layers that the VM doesn’t have and leaves them out, and when the VM has none of them, devvm says so and changes nothing.

devvm layer rm desktop # make this folder's VM again without the desktop layer
devvm layer rm docker nix # take out docker and nix
devvm layer rm desktop --force # the same without asking, as a script must

The VM keeps what a VM made again keeps, its home folder included, and everything else on its disk is lost, such as what the layers you took out installed and Docker’s images. So devvm asks first in a terminal, with no as the default, and refuses without one unless you give --force. It takes the same flags as devvm layer add, works in the same steps and refuses the same VMs, before it changes anything: a --clone VM, one whose creation didn’t finish, and one whose backend can’t run the layers left. It also refuses base, a shared tool’s name, which devvm tools rm takes out instead, and a name that isn’t a layer. You can still take out a layer of yours whose script you deleted, and that’s the one way to make such a VM again with its home folder and settings, because devvm layer add and devvm update need every layer’s script to build the VM’s image.

Shared tools

The toolchains and coding agents are shared tools, not image layers. A VM of any image can have them, in any mix, such as node and Claude Code on base, or go and Codex on foo. A VM’s state lists its shared tools apart from its image. Toolchains lists the toolchains, with what each brings, and supported agents lists the coding agents.

devvm builds each tool version once and mounts it read-only into every VM that has it, so any mix of tools works without building anything new, and ten VMs with node share one copy of it. The builds are in ~/.local/share/devvm/tools. Each C library gets a build of its own, so when an Alpine VM and an Ubuntu VM both have node 24, devvm images lists two builds of that version (what devvm keeps). An Alpine VM’s builds are only ever shared with VMs on the same container image, as shared tools and glibc explains. mise runs the tools:

  • They work as usual. Each toolchain’s commands, such as npm i -g (into ~/.npm-global) or go install (into ~/go/bin), work from any shell, including bash -c from agents and from editors over SSH. Global installs go into your home, as each toolchain’s section says.
  • A project’s own version files win. A toolchain’s version files, such as .nvmrc for node, pick its version, which installs into the VM the first time it’s used, and each toolchain’s section names its files. mise also reads a mise.toml in the project folder, and devvm trusts it without asking, because the folder is yours.
  • They’re read-only. A VM can’t change the shared tools, even as root. The tools can’t update themselves, and rustup component add can’t change the shared toolchain.
  • They’re mounted, or the launch stops. When one of a VM’s tools is missing or the VM can’t mount it, devvm stops the launch and names the tool, and the VM never downloads its own copy in its place (a shared tool doesn’t mount). Only the versions that a project’s own version files pick install into the VM.

devvm doesn’t pin the tools’ versions, because agents like Claude Code release several times a week. It follows the newest release of each tool, with Node 24 for node and opencode 2 for opencode. The first time a tool is needed, devvm looks up its newest release, which needs this machine to be online once. When it makes a new VM, devvm also checks for newer releases if its last check was more than a day ago, and DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK=1 turns that check off.

A new VM gets the tools chosen for it when devvm makes it, and keeps those versions. devvm tools shows them, and in a terminal lets you choose them. devvm tools add, devvm tools rm and devvm tools update change them too, as does the first step of devvm update, and changing them never changes the VM’s disk (adding and removing tools).

What a new VM gets 

flowchart TD
run["devvm in a folder<br>without a VM"] --> defaults["the defaults: the folder's toolchains,<br>devvm setup's agents and layers"]
defaults --> flags["each flag given replaces its part:<br>--tools, --agents, --layers, --network, --cpus, --memory"]
flags --> summary["the summary says what the VM gets"]
summary --> term{{"a terminal, without --no-input,<br>and something left to choose?"}}
term -- "no" --> copy
term -- "yes" --> ask{{"Customize it? [y/N]"}}
ask -- "Enter" --> copy
ask -- "y" --> pick["the list, then the tier,<br>then the CPUs, memory and disk"] --> copy
copy["its image built if it isn't,<br>and the VM is a copy of it,<br>with its shared tools mounted"]

Before devvm makes a new VM, it shows a summary of what the VM gets. The summary names each toolchain, coding agent and layer with why the VM gets it, such as for package.json, from devvm setup or from --tools, and then the VM’s size, its network tier, its ports and the folder’s devcontainer.json, when there is one:

==> This folder's new VM, devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c, gets:
 toolchain node, for package.json
 agent claude, from devvm setup
 layers: none
 size: 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk
 network tier: allowlist
 ports: all
 devcontainer.json: .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, which devvm --no-devcontainer skips
Customize it? [y/N]

In a terminal, devvm then asks whether to customize the VM, with no as the default, so confirming makes it as shown. When you customize it, devvm shows the three parts in one list under three headings, Toolchains, Coding agents and Layers, with what the summary showed already chosen (choosing in a list). The Layers heading says that a layer is extra software built into the VM’s image:

Choose what devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c gets. Use up and down to move, space to toggle and enter to confirm.
Toolchains
> [x] node for package.json
 [ ] python
 [ ] rust
 [ ] go
Coding agents, which you start in the VM's shell
 [x] claude from devvm setup
 [ ] codex
 [ ] opencode
 [ ] pi
Layers: extra software built into the VM's image, such as docker, nix or desktop
 [ ] desktop an Xfce desktop, which devvm desktop opens
 [ ] docker Docker's engine, CLI, BuildKit and Compose
 [ ] nix Nix, direnv and nix-direnv

Then devvm lists the four network tiers, with learn after internet for a VM that learns the hosts it needs, each with what it reaches, unless you gave --network, and you choose one, starting from the tier the summary showed: allowlist, or the tier you saved for new VMs with devvm network -g (choosing a tier). Next, unless you gave --ports, devvm lists the ports the VM can forward: every port, none, which you add later with devvm ports add, or the ports you type, which devvm checks as --ports checks them and asks for again when they aren’t a list. The list starts on what the summary showed, every port unless config.toml or devvm ports -g set another (size and ports), and the ports you choose are this VM’s alone. Last, it asks for the VM’s CPUs, memory and disk, starting from the summary’s, and confirming keeps each one. Each question is skipped when you gave its flag, --cpus, --memory or --disk. Before the disk’s question, devvm says that the disk can grow later with devvm size --disk but never shrinks, and that it takes up only the space the VM writes. A disk smaller than the image’s, 100 GiB for base, is refused as --disk refuses it, and devvm asks again, as it does for a value that isn’t a size. The size you type is this VM’s alone, and devvm saves it for no other VM.

Each part has a default:

  • Toolchains: the ones the folder’s files call for, each naming its file in the summary and the list, such as package.json.
  • Coding agents: the ones you chose with devvm setup, which the summary and the list say. The summary says from config.toml for the ones that config.toml sets. Until you choose some, there are none.
  • Layers: the ones you chose with devvm setup, bottom first, which the summary and the list say in the same way. Until you choose some, there are none. A layer that a project file calls for, such as nix for a flake.nix, names the file in its row of the list but isn’t chosen unless devvm setup chose it, so you choose it when you want it.

Three flags choose the parts on the command line. --tools takes the toolchains, as in --tools node,python, --agents takes the coding agents, as in --agents claude,codex, and --layers takes the layers bottom first, as in --layers docker,mine. Each is the exact list for its part and replaces that part’s default, and none chooses none of it, as in --agents none. A part whose flag you leave out takes its default. devvm checks each name before it does anything. For a name that belongs to another part, such as --tools claude, it names the flag that takes it, and for a name it doesn’t know, it suggests the closest one.

A part, tier or size that a flag gives is taken as given, and the summary says so. devvm still asks whether to customize the VM while anything is left to choose, because a flag answers only its own part. When you customize it, the list shows a part that a flag gave greyed out, and the cursor skips it. devvm skips the list when --tools, --agents and --layers give all three parts, skips the tier when you give --network or saved a tier, skips the ports when you give --ports, and skips the CPUs, the memory or the disk when you give --cpus, --memory or --disk. devvm doesn’t ask at all when the flags give every part, the ports, the CPUs, the memory and the disk, and the tier is given or saved. It doesn’t ask about the tier on a backend whose VMs can only be open, either.

Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm asks nothing and doesn’t fail. The VM gets what the summary shows, and the summary ends with the flags that choose others.

devvm looks at the folder’s top level for the files that call for a toolchain, in this order:

Toolchain Files
node package.json, bun.lock, bun.lockb
python pyproject.toml, requirements.txt, uv.lock, setup.py, Pipfile
rust Cargo.toml
go go.mod

If more than one toolchain matches, the VM gets them all, so package.json and pyproject.toml give node and python. A Nix project’s files call for the nix layer, whose row names them. Those files are flake.nix, shell.nix and devenv.nix, and a default.nix that makes a shell with mkShell. In a folder with none of these files, the default is no toolchains, so a VM made without a terminal or flags gets devvm setup’s layers and agents.

A folder’s devcontainer.json adds what its features map to, such as toolchains or the docker layer, to the defaults, each naming the file in the summary and the list (devcontainer.json). Its layers go on top of devvm setup’s.

The VM’s image is base with its layers, in the order you give them, bottom first, so --layers docker,mine makes the image docker+mine. When you check layers in the list, devvm setup’s stay in their order at the bottom, and the ones you add go on top in the list’s order. Its shared tools are a list of their own, the toolchains first, then the agents.

If the image isn’t built yet, devvm builds it first, then the shared tools the share lacks, and the VM is a copy of the image with its shared tools mounted. A VM keeps the image and tools it was made from, and the options for a new VM change nothing on a VM that exists, which ignores them with a warning. The warning names the command that changes the same on that VM, such as devvm tools, which changes its shared tools, for --tools, devvm layer add, which adds layers, for --layers, and devvm size for --cpus, and for --from and --no-devcontainer it names none. Only devvm takes these options, and another command given one fails as it does for any flag it doesn’t know (flags and values).

Choosing in a list

devvm’s lists work the same way everywhere: the new VM’s list, its network tiers and ports, devvm tools, base’s features in devvm setup, and the hosts in devvm network lock. Up and down, or k and j, move. In a list where you choose several, such as the toolchains, coding agents and layers, space chooses or unchooses the row under the cursor, and a chooses every row, or unchooses them all when they’re all chosen already. In a list where you choose one, such as the network tiers, moving chooses it. Enter confirms. A row that’s greyed out, such as a part a flag gave or a VM’s layers in devvm tools, can’t change, and the cursor skips it. A list longer than the terminal scrolls with the cursor, with a line above and below that says how many more rows there are, and each row is cut to the terminal’s width. At a question with a value in brackets, such as a size, Enter keeps that value.

Rebuilding

When you edit a layer’s script, devvm builds that layer again the next time it’s used, together with every layer built on it, and it reuses the layers below. A new choice of base’s features rebuilds base and everything on it in the same way.

devvm rebuild IMAGE builds an image again from its parent as the parent is now, where IMAGE is base or a stack of layers, such as docker or foo+bar. That’s how you get the newest packages that a script installs without a pin. On Lima, devvm rebuild base also starts base again from the newest release of Ubuntu’s cloud image, which devvm otherwise picks only the first time it builds base on this machine. devvm also builds the images on it again, on the new image, the next time they’re needed. When there are such images, devvm lists them first and, in a terminal, asks before it goes on. After the build, devvm deletes the old images that no VM uses.

Shared tools aren’t images, so devvm rebuild refuses a shared tool’s name, and devvm update and devvm tools update get their newer versions. Rebuilding explains how devvm tells which images to build again.

Outdated VMs

A VM keeps the image it was made from. When that image, or one it’s built on, changes after an edited script, another choice of base’s features or a rebuild, the VM is outdated. devvm then warns on each launch, names the images that changed and devvm update, and leaves the VM as it is.

devvm update brings this folder’s VM up to date in two steps. First it moves the VM to the newest shared tools, as devvm tools update does, and that needs no question, because the shared tools aren’t part of the image and nothing on the VM’s disk changes (adding and removing tools). Then, when the VM is outdated, devvm makes it again from its own image as it builds now, with the same layers, in the same way that devvm layer add makes a VM again with more layers. devvm builds the image first, then gives the VM a new disk copied from it, and keeps its home folder, the project folder and its settings (what a VM made again keeps). Everything else on its disk is lost, such as the packages you installed with apt and Docker’s images, so in a terminal devvm names the images that changed and asks first, with no as the default. When the folder’s devcontainer.json changed since devvm made the VM, or is gone, or has appeared, devvm also makes the VM again, after asking, as the file says now (updating a VM from the file).

devvm update # move the VM to the newest shared tools, and to its image's new build after asking
devvm update --force # the same without asking, as a script must
devvm update --clean-home # the same, with the new image's home folder

When only the shared tools are newer, devvm moves the VM to them and opens a shell in it without asking, because newer tools don’t need the VM made again. When you answer no, devvm keeps the VM with any newer shared tools it moved to, and opens a shell in it if there were some. Without a terminal, devvm refuses an outdated VM unless you give --force, and it refuses before it changes anything, the VM’s shared tools included.

When the VM has the newest shared tools and nothing it was made from has changed, devvm says that the VM is current and changes nothing. To make a current VM again with the newest packages that a script installs without a pin, run devvm rebuild on its image first, which makes the VM outdated, then devvm update (rebuilding). devvm update takes the same flags as devvm layer add, and it refuses the same VMs, before it changes anything: a --clone VM, one whose creation didn’t finish, and one whose backend can’t run its layers. It exports the agents’ history first unless you give --no-export, and --clean-home gives the VM the new image’s home folder instead of its own. In a subfolder of a folder with a VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to make that folder’s VM again, and refuses without one. The steps, and what happens when one fails, are those of adding layers to a VM.

For a VM made with --from, devvm tells whether the VM is outdated from the container image’s digest that it last recorded, without looking anything up. When devvm makes the VM again, the build looks up the digest as every build does, so a tag that has moved since gives the VM the container image’s newer version too, and a pinned digest stays as it is (--from).

devvm tools update moves the VM to newer shared tools alone, and it never makes the VM again, even when the VM is outdated (adding and removing tools).

Listing images

devvm images prints two tables, each with a header, and it shows what a row lacks as -. The first table lists the images by name, with unfinished builds last:

Column
IMAGE its name, such as base or foo+bar
FROM what its base started from: the --from image, or Ubuntu’s cloud image with its release’s date, ubuntu 26.04 (20261001)
DIGEST the first 12 hex digits of that image’s SHA-256
KEY its key, which devvm images rm also takes
STATE current, stale when what it’s built from has changed since it was built, unfinished for a build that didn’t finish, or building while another devvm builds it
SIZE the disk it takes, in powers of 1024 (2.1G). On macOS an image is a clone of its parent’s disk, and the blocks they share count for both

The second table lists the shared tools that devvm has built, by the name you choose them by, such as node for node, pnpm and bun. The toolchains come first, then the agents, with each tool’s versions newest first:

Column
NAME a toolchain’s name, such as node, or an agent’s, such as claude
TOOL, VERSION the tool and its version
LIBC the C library (gnu, or musl for an Alpine base) that this build is for, because each gets a build of its own, or - when devvm can’t tell
SIZE the disk it takes
VMS how many VMs have it
STATE current for the version new VMs get, in use for another version a VM has, unused for neither, not built for the current version of a tool devvm has other versions of, and not installed when devvm has no version of it

After the tables, devvm says on stderr how many images are stale or unfinished and how much disk the unused tools take, when there are any. It ends with the disk that the images and shared tools take together, and when the shared Nix cache holds anything, the disk it takes of its cap. devvm space shows the rest of what devvm keeps (what devvm keeps).

devvm images –json

devvm images --json prints the same as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes, and devvm still says the same on stderr. images and tools have the tables’ columns as fields, with sizes in bytes, and each also names the backend that has it or built it, lima. An image’s digest is the full SHA-256 of what its base started from, and sized says whether devvm knows its size. A tool image’s built says whether devvm has built it, and only a built one has backend and libc. A value an image lacks, such as an unfinished build’s name, is "". total is the disk the images and shared tools take together, unused_tools is the part the unused tool images take, and nix_cache has the shared Nix cache’s files, the disk they take and its cap.

{
 "version": 1,
 "images": [
 {
 "name": "base",
 "from": "ubuntu 26.04 (20261001)",
 "digest": "sha256:8eb876c2ccc4b6ff89e4a65d511815923b285e04503ba465809bf587f763da24",
 "key": "7a76021c46ef",
 "state": "current",
 "size": 2254857830,
 "sized": true,
 "backend": "lima"
 }
 ],
 "tools": [
 {
 "name": "node",
 "tool": "node",
 "version": "24.11.0",
 "built": true,
 "backend": "lima",
 "libc": "gnu",
 "size": 125829120,
 "vms": 1,
 "state": "current"
 }
 ],
 "total": 2380686950,
 "unused_tools": 0,
 "nix_cache": {
 "files": 0,
 "size": 0,
 "cap": 10737418240
 }
}

Deleting images

devvm images rm IMAGE|KEY... deletes images. You name each one by its name or by the key that devvm images shows:

  • A name means its image as it is now, on base from --from when you give it. A stale or unfinished image has only its key.
  • Each image must be built, or devvm deletes nothing. Shared tools aren’t images, so devvm refuses a name that has one, such as node+foo, and devvm gc deletes the shared tools no VM has.
  • devvm also deletes nothing while another devvm is building one of the images, so run the command again once that build ends. devvm gc and devvm rebuild leave such an image alone too.
  • A deleted image is built again the next time it’s needed. VMs made from it keep working, because on macOS they’re clones of its disk. On Linux hosts, devvm refuses to delete an image whose disk VMs are overlays of, and names those VMs.

Cleaning up

devvm gc deletes four things. The first is what devvm images lists as stale or unfinished. The second is the shared tools it lists as unused. The third is the older versions of the mise that devvm runs on this machine to look up the tools’ versions, which an upgrade of devvm leaves behind, except one that changed in the last hour, because another devvm may be downloading it. The fourth is the shared Nix cache’s least recently used files, while it takes more than its cap, the nix-cache.size retention setting, which is 10 GiB when it’s off. devvm’s mise and the shared Nix cache are both in cache/ in devvm’s data folder, which holds only what devvm makes again when it needs it, so you can also delete that folder yourself at any time. gc lists them all first and, in a terminal, asks. Without a terminal, it deletes nothing unless you give --force, which deletes without asking, in a terminal too.

  • devvm gc --tool-images also deletes the current shared tools that no VM has, such as a toolchain you tried once, for every C library. devvm gc --tool-images node claude deletes only those tools’ builds, by the names you choose them by, so node also covers pnpm and bun. A tool that a VM’s state lists stays, including a stopped VM’s, and a tool that no VM has goes however recently it was built. While devvm is making a VM, or giving one new shared tools through devvm tools add or devvm tools update, that VM may not list the tools it picked yet, so gc keeps every current shared tool that no VM has, names them, and deletes the rest of what it would. Run it again once that’s done. A tool that devvm is still building never reaches gc, because gc waits for the build to finish before it lists anything. A VM that has a deleted tool builds it again when it needs it.
  • The devvm making a VM holds a lock from before it picks the VM’s tools until the VM’s state lists them, and the system lets go of that lock as soon as that devvm ends, so one that crashed or that you killed never leaves gc keeping tools. A devvm that starts to make a VM while devvm gc --tool-images runs, or while retention deletes shared tools, waits for it to finish and says it’s waiting. In a terminal, gc holds that lock while it asks you, so answer it first.
  • When a shared tool that a new VM’s state lists is gone before the VM’s first shell, for example because you deleted it by hand, the VM’s setup can’t mount it. devvm then names the tools it couldn’t mount and stops, and the VM stays. Run devvm tools update in the folder, which builds the missing tools again and opens the VM.
