  • devvm gc --history also deletes the exports of agents’ history that devvm history export and devvm rm saved, which are the only copy of a deleted VM’s history, and --older-than DURATION keeps those newer than that duration, such as 12h, 30d or 2w. gc never deletes exports without --history.
  • devvm gc --nix-cache also deletes the rest of the shared Nix cache. VMs download its packages again when they need them.
  • devvm gc --orphans also deletes what devvm keeps for VMs that their backend no longer has, such as one you deleted with limactl delete instead of devvm rm, and with it the hold their state has on their shared tools (leftovers).
  • devvm gc --caches then frees devvm’s share of Lima’s own caches, such as its downloads of Ubuntu’s cloud image, after asking, or without asking with --force, which it needs without a terminal (Lima’s caches).
  • devvm gc --retention then applies the retention settings at once, which devvm otherwise applies at most once a day. They’re all off until you set them.
  • When Lima can’t list its images while one of your VMs uses it, for example because Lima isn’t installed, gc warns and leaves Lima’s images, shared tools, VM leftovers and caches alone. It also leaves the shared tools whose record doesn’t name the backend that built them, because they may be Lima’s. gc still succeeds, so run devvm doctor to see what’s wrong with Lima, then run gc again once it answers. devvm images fails instead, because it lists all the images or none.
  • gc never deletes VMs, and it keeps current images, which devvm images rm deletes (deleting images). Without --tool-images it keeps the current shared tools. It always keeps every shared tool that any VM has, including a stopped VM’s and that of a VM deleted outside devvm whose state is left, until --orphans deletes that state.
  • On Linux hosts, a stale image whose disk VMs are overlays of stays, and devvm says which VMs use it.
  • After an Alpine VM is gone, the shared tools built for Alpine are unused, unless you give gc that --from.

Images and caching has the details of what counts as current and unused. To see what gc would free before you run it, and what takes the rest of the space, run devvm space (what devvm keeps).

item.title: Customizing images
item.description:
You customize images with your own layers, which add what a project needs, and by choosing base’s features, which are devvm’s optional extras that every VM gets. Your layers live in ~/.config/devvm ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/devvm), not next to devvm’s binary, so upgrading devvm keeps them. To give every new VM something of your own, write it as a layer and make it one of the layers new VMs get (extras of your own).

Your own layers 

devvm layer new mailpit # writes ~/.config/devvm/layers/mailpit.sh and mailpit.policy
$EDITOR ~/.config/devvm/layers/mailpit.sh
devvm --layers mailpit # a new VM with your layer; or devvm build mailpit

When you customize a new VM, its list also shows your layers under Layers, so you can choose mailpit there instead of giving --layers (what a new VM gets). To give every new VM your layer, choose it with devvm setup --layers mailpit, or add it to the layers key in config.toml (layers for new VMs). When you delete a layer’s script that you chose there, new VMs are made without it, and devvm warns you.

A layer is a script, ~/.config/devvm/layers/<name>.sh, that bash runs once as the VM’s user, who has sudo, in an image on top of its parent. devvm layer new NAME writes a starter script, and also NAME.policy next to it unless that file exists. It refuses to overwrite a script that exists.

  • Names are made of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, and start with a letter or digit. A name can’t be base, a built-in layer’s name (desktop, docker or nix) or a shared tool’s name (node, claude and so on). A command’s name, such as log, is fine, because devvm takes layers only through --layers, the list and image names.
  • Built-in layers go in the same image names as yours, bottom first, as in devvm --layers docker,mailpit, which makes the image docker+mailpit.
  • Put interactive shell setup in ~/.bashrc.d/<name>.sh, which every VM’s ~/.bashrc reads, and PATH changes in ~/.profile.
  • Download files with devvm-fetch URL SHA256 OUT, which base installs. It fails when the file’s checksum doesn’t match.
  • NAME.policy lists the hosts that VMs with the layer can reach on the allowlist tier, one rule per line.
  • Editing the script rebuilds its image, and the ones built on it, the next time they’re used (rebuilding).
  • A layer’s script changes the VM’s disk, so devvm layer add mailpit gives a VM you have the layer by making the VM again, keeping its home folder and settings (adding layers to a VM), and devvm layer rm mailpit takes it out again in the same way (taking layers out of a VM).

To edit layers with an agent in a VM, keep them in a repo of their own and copy them in, because devvm refuses a VM for a folder inside ~/.config/devvm (details).

Example: mailpit

This layer installs Mailpit, which catches the emails your app sends while you develop it, and starts it with the VM. Point your app’s SMTP settings at localhost:1025, and read the emails at localhost:8025 in your browser, because devvm forwards both ports to your machine. Put these lines in ~/.config/devvm/layers/mailpit.sh, below the starter’s set -euo pipefail:

mailpit_version=1.32.0
mailpit_sha256_amd64=4b5993c978e8604c70d43927e2ad103b311bba3b1822fa0cf1d4ee4ec890a93c
mailpit_sha256_arm64=e1e45d1dc72bd497fb262a1e4100178eee057c42c5fc36d143eb8621769e1137

case "$(uname -m)" in
 x86_64) arch=amd64 sha256=$mailpit_sha256_amd64 ;;
 aarch64) arch=arm64 sha256=$mailpit_sha256_arm64 ;;
 *) echo "mailpit: no build for $(uname -m)" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
devvm-fetch "https://github.com/axllent/mailpit/releases/download/v$mailpit_version/mailpit-linux-$arch.tar.gz" \
 "$sha256" /tmp/mailpit.tar.gz
sudo tar -xzf /tmp/mailpit.tar.gz -C /usr/local/bin mailpit
rm /tmp/mailpit.tar.gz

printf '%s\n' '[Unit]' 'Description=Mailpit' '[Service]' 'ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/mailpit' \
 'DynamicUser=yes' '[Install]' 'WantedBy=multi-user.target' |
 sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/mailpit.service >/dev/null
sudo systemctl enable --now mailpit

The version and each download’s SHA-256 sit at the top, so devvm-fetch refuses a download that doesn’t match. To update Mailpit, change all three and rebuild the image. The downloads come from GitHub’s releases, which base’s allowlist has, so mailpit.policy can stay empty. On a base made --from an Alpine image, start it with OpenRC (rc-update, rc-service) instead of systemd.

Base image features

Features are optional extras that devvm builds into base after base’s own setup, so every VM has them.

Feature What it adds
omb oh-my-bash: a themed prompt, completions and aliases, with auto-update off
fzf fuzzy Ctrl-R history and Ctrl-T file search
cli-tools bat, fd, eza, zoxide (z), btop, tree, tldr

The desktop that devvm desktop opens isn’t a feature but a built-in layer, desktop, so only the VMs you choose it for get it.

Choosing features

On its first run, devvm asks which features base gets, after the size and coding agents that new VMs get and before it shows what the folder’s new VM gets. devvm build and devvm rebuild ask too, until the features are chosen. The list starts with every feature chosen, and you choose in it as in any of devvm’s lists. Without a terminal, devvm chooses every feature. devvm prints the choice and saves it, in the order the features run. When features in config.toml chooses them, devvm doesn’t ask.

To change the choice:

devvm setup # asks again, starting from the current choice
devvm setup --features fzf,omb # without asking
devvm setup --features none # without asking, and base gets no features

In a terminal, devvm setup asks for the features among its other questions, which devvm setup lists in order. --features asks for none of the others. Without a terminal, devvm setup keeps the choice. devvm refuses a name that isn’t a feature, and an empty --features '', and then nothing changes. You can also choose them by hand with features in config.toml, such as features = ["fzf", "omb"], which wins over what devvm setup saved, and then devvm setup --features refuses to change them. features = [] chooses none, and devvm skips a name without a script, with a warning.

A new choice makes base and the images built on it rebuild the next time they’re used, and devvm setup says so. The old images are then stale, and devvm gc deletes them.

Extras of your own

Base’s features are the ones in the table above, and devvm ships all of them. To give every new VM an extra of your own, such as your shell setup or a tool you always use, write it as a layer of your own and choose it as one of the layers new VMs get:

devvm layer new dotfiles # writes ~/.config/devvm/layers/dotfiles.sh
$EDITOR ~/.config/devvm/layers/dotfiles.sh
devvm setup --layers dotfiles # every new VM gets it

A new VM’s summary then shows dotfiles, and when you customize the VM, its list shows dotfiles under Layers, already chosen because devvm setup chose it, so you can leave it out of that VM (layers for new VMs). A layer is an image built on top of base, so the images that have it are named with it, such as dotfiles or docker+dotfiles, and editing its script rebuilds only those images, never base.

item.title: Settings and files
item.description:
devvm writes nothing into your project folders. It keeps the settings you edit in ~/.config/devvm and everything it writes itself in ~/.local/share/devvm, and it reads a few environment variables. Your settings lists the files you edit, devvm’s data folder lists the ones devvm writes, and Overview explains how devvm keeps them.

Your settings

~/.config/devvm ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/devvm) holds what you edit, and it’s the only folder of devvm’s that you should change by hand. devvm never rewrites a file of yours there. It reads config.toml and your own layers and CAs, it creates a new layer’s files when you run devvm layer new, it changes single lines of policy when you add or remove a rule for every VM, and it writes version when the folder has none and when it changes its folders to a newer layout.

File What it holds Written by
config.toml the defaults that new VMs get and the retention settings, which win over what devvm’s commands save, the company proxy and an Ubuntu mirror (config.toml) you
policy your network rules for every VM devvm network allow -g, deny -g, rm -g, or you
layers/ your own layers and their allowlists devvm layer new, then you
agents/ your agents’ settings in devvm’s agent store, one folder for each agent devvm agent import, devvm agent save, or you
ca/ your company’s CA certificates, which VMs and builds trust you
version the folder’s layout version, which says how devvm keeps its files here devvm, when it’s missing or older

Edit the files in ~/.config/devvm, and never edit the ones in ~/.local/share/devvm. devvm writes those itself and rewrites them whole, so a change you make there can be lost, or can stop devvm from reading the file. To set a default by hand, put it in config.toml instead.

Upgrading devvm keeps this folder as it is. Back it up, such as in a dotfiles repo, to keep your settings and layers.

config.toml

~/.config/devvm/config.toml sets the defaults that new VMs get, the retention settings, the company proxy, an Ubuntu mirror, the release check, transparent mode and the API keys that VMs get as they are, in a file you write by hand. devvm reads it and never writes it. Every key is optional, and devvm has no config.toml until you write one. This example sets every key:

# The network tier new VMs get: open, internet, allowlist or none.
network = "allowlist"

# The ports new VMs forward: all, none, or ports and ranges.
ports = "5173,8000-8010"

# The features base gets, in the order they run, or [] for none.
features = ["cli-tools", "fzf", "omb"]

# The coding agents new VMs get, or [] for none.
agents = ["claude", "codex"]

# The layers new VMs get, bottom first, or [] for none.
layers = ["docker"]

# A mirror of Ubuntu's archive that base's first build tries first.
ubuntu-mirror = "http://mirror.example.com/ubuntu-ports"

# Whether a launch checks once a day for a newer devvm release.
release-check = true

# Whether confined VMs send tools that ignore the proxy settings to their proxy.
transparent-proxy = true

# The folder in every VM that devvm paste puts images and files in.
paste-dir = "/tmp/devvm-paste"

# New VMs' CPUs, and their memory and disk in GiB.
[size]
cpus = 4
memory = 8
disk = 100

# What devvm deletes on its own, with the keys devvm retention takes.
[retention]
logs.runs = 20
history.age = "90d"
history.count = 10
tools.unused-age = "30d"
orphans.age = "30d"
nix-cache.size = "20G"

# The company proxy, when the shell you run devvm in sets none.
[proxy]
https = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
http = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
no-proxy = "localhost,.example.com"

# Providers whose API keys an agent's VMs get as they are.
[pass-keys]
opencode = ["ollama"]
pi = ["ollama"]

Each key takes what its command takes. network is a tier, open, internet, allowlist or none, as devvm network -g sets it (choosing a tier), and never learn, because each VM learns the hosts it needs on its own. ports is all, none or a list, as devvm ports -g takes it (size and ports). features lists the features that base gets, agents the coding agents that new VMs get, and layers the layers that new VMs get, bottom first. cpus is a whole number, and memory and disk are a number of GiB, such as 8, 8.5 or "8G", as devvm size -g takes them. The [retention] keys are the retention settings, with a duration such as "90d" or a size such as "20G" in quotes, and a count as a number.

The [proxy] table is the company proxy that every VM’s proxy, builds and devvm’s own downloads go through when the shell you run devvm in sets neither HTTPS_PROXY nor HTTP_PROXY, whatever the VM’s tier. No VM gets the company proxy’s settings itself. That shell’s settings win over the whole table. https and http take what HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY take, an http:// URL or host:port, and no-proxy takes what NO_PROXY takes. A URL never holds a password, and devvm refuses one that does, so put only the user in it and save the password with devvm secret set proxy. No command saves the proxy, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

The [pass-keys] table names, for an agent, the providers whose API keys its VMs get as they are, which devvm otherwise keeps on this machine because the VM’s proxy can’t put them in, such as a local model server’s. It takes opencode and pi, each with a list of the agent’s provider IDs as its auth.json names them, in lower case, such as ["ollama"] (opencode logins, pi logins). devvm refuses another agent, a name that isn’t a provider’s ID and a repeat (config.toml names the line). A provider whose key the VM’s proxy puts in (API keys the proxy puts in) never needs the table, because the proxy puts its key in without it. When the table lists one all the same, the VM gets that key’s placeholder from its next launch on, not the key, and devvm notes at each launch that you can take the provider out. A VM that got such a key as it was before then may still hold copies of it, which keep working, so make a new key when you don’t trust that VM (API keys the proxy puts in). Every VM with the agent gets the change at its next launch. No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

An Ubuntu mirror

ubuntu-mirror is a mirror of Ubuntu’s archive, such as one your company or university runs, which the first build of base gets its packages from before it tries Ubuntu’s own. It must mirror the archive for this machine’s architecture: archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu on an Intel or AMD machine, or ports.ubuntu.com/ubuntu-ports on an Apple silicon Mac or another arm64 machine. Give it as an http:// or https:// address without a user, a query or spaces, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line). A package that the mirror doesn’t have, or a mirror that doesn’t answer, falls back to Ubuntu’s archive for that file.

A mirror can’t give base a package that Ubuntu didn’t publish. apt checks every list and package against Ubuntu’s archive key whichever server sends it, and refuses one that doesn’t match, and devvm checks them against that key again on this machine before it keeps any package. A mirror that’s behind, or one that’s lying, can still serve lists older than Ubuntu’s, because Ubuntu’s signed lists don’t expire. devvm refuses lists more than a day older than the Ubuntu cloud image base starts from, and it names the mirror and keeps none of the build’s packages (old package lists). devvm compares the lists with the cloud image’s date, not with today’s, so a mirror that fell behind after that date can still give base packages older than Ubuntu’s, and you should only set a mirror you trust to keep up. Only the first build of each base uses the mirror, because a later build of the same base installs the packages devvm kept from that first build (base). VMs don’t use it, and neither do layers or a --from base. No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

The paste folder

paste-dir is the folder in every VM that devvm paste puts images, PDFs and copied files in, /tmp/devvm-paste unless you set it. Each launch makes the folder in the VM when it’s missing, mode 700 and the VM’s user’s own. It leaves a folder that’s there as it is, so a folder of your own, such as /home/USER/pastes where USER is your user in the VM, keeps its mode and its other files. A launch warns, and goes on, when:

  • what’s at the path is a symbolic link, isn’t a folder or isn’t the VM’s user’s, and devvm paste then refuses the folder;
  • it can’t make the folder, as under a file.

It’s one fixed path for every VM so that you can allow it once in an agent’s settings. Give it as an absolute path without a trailing slash, made of letters, digits and ., _ and -, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line), because the path goes into a shell in the VM and onto your clipboard. A change applies to each VM at its next launch, which makes the new folder, and devvm paste uses the new folder at once. No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

The release check

When you run devvm in a terminal, it checks at most once a day for a newer devvm release, and when one is out it says so in one line before it opens the VM, naming the release, the version you have and devvm upgrade. devvm never installs anything on its own, so you upgrade with devvm upgrade when you choose to. release-check = false turns the check off, and so does setting DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK=1 in the environment, as CI can. release-check must be true or false, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line). No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

The check reads only where GitHub’s latest devvm release is, over HTTPS, and sends nothing about you or your machine. The latest release is never a prerelease, so the check never announces one (trying a prerelease). The exception is a devvm that Homebrew’s devvm-rc formula installed, which follows prereleases: its check reads GitHub’s list of devvm’s newest releases instead, and it announces a newer prerelease or release, whichever is newest. It runs beside the launch, so it never makes devvm wait, and when you’re offline it says nothing and tries again the next day. The line comes from what the last check found, so a release that came out since then shows up at the launch after the next check. devvm keeps what the check found in ~/.local/share/devvm/cache/release.json, and devvm doctor shows it. devvm says nothing without a terminal, with --no-input, for a devvm built from its source, or for a copy that neither the install script nor Homebrew installed, which devvm upgrade can’t upgrade.

Transparent mode

On every tier but open, devvm sends a tool that ignores the proxy settings to the VM’s proxy by the names it looks up, which is transparent mode. It’s on unless you turn it off. transparent-proxy = false turns it off for every VM that has no setting of its own, and devvm network transparent on or off gives one VM its own, which comes first. A change applies at each VM’s next launch. transparent-proxy must be true or false, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line). No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

Where a default comes from

For each default, devvm uses the first of these that sets it:

  1. A flag for one VM, such as --ports or --cpus.
  2. config.toml.
  3. What devvm’s commands saved: devvm setup, devvm size -g, devvm ports -g, devvm network -g and devvm retention save in ~/.local/share/devvm/settings.json.
  4. devvm’s own default.

A command that would save a default that config.toml sets refuses, names the file and the key, and changes nothing, because the value in config.toml would still win. To change that default, edit it in config.toml, or delete it there to let devvm’s commands set it again. In a terminal, devvm setup doesn’t ask about what config.toml sets, and it says so.

devvm size -g, devvm ports -g, devvm network -g and devvm retention show where each value came from, after a #. They show config.toml’s path for a value from config.toml, devvm: settings.json for one that a command saved, and devvm: default for devvm’s own:

$ devvm ports -g
5173,8000-8010 # /Users/you/.config/devvm/config.toml
$ devvm network -g
allowlist # devvm: default

With --json, the same commands add source, or sources for each value of devvm size -g and devvm retention, which is config.toml, settings.json or built-in.

When devvm can’t read it

devvm reads all of config.toml each time it needs a default, and it checks every key and value. A key it doesn’t know, such as a typo, a value that a key can’t take, and a file that isn’t TOML each stop the command, and devvm names the file and the line. Fix the line, and run the command again. config.toml has no key for the backend, because every new VM runs on Lima, so a backend key stops the command as an unknown key.

devvm setup

devvm setup chooses what new VMs get. In a terminal, it asks five questions, each starting from the current choice, and saves each answer in ~/.local/share/devvm/settings.json, as the command for that setting saves it. It skips a question that config.toml answers, saying so, and it refuses a flag that would change what config.toml sets.

  1. The features that base gets.
  2. The CPUs and memory that new VMs get, as devvm size -g saves them.
  3. The network tier that new VMs get, as devvm network -g saves it: open, internet, allowlist, which is the default, or none. Each new VM’s summary shows that tier, and when you customize the VM in a terminal, devvm asks for its tier, with Enter keeping the one the summary showed (what a new VM gets). --network TIER chooses for one VM and wins over the saved choice.
  4. The coding agents that new VMs get.
  5. The layers that new VMs get.
devvm setup # asks all five questions
devvm setup --features fzf,omb # base's features, without asking
devvm setup --features none # base gets no features
devvm setup --agents claude,codex # new VMs' coding agents, without asking
devvm setup --layers docker # new VMs' layers, without asking

devvm setup has three flags of its own, and each one chooses without asking anything. --features LIST chooses base’s features, as a comma-separated list or none for none, and devvm refuses an empty --features ''. --agents LIST chooses new VMs’ coding agents in the same way, and --layers LIST chooses new VMs’ layers. With any of the flags, what the flags leave out stays as it is. Without a terminal and without flags, devvm setup asks nothing and keeps base’s features, saving every feature when none was chosen yet. To change new VMs’ size without asking, use devvm size -g (choosing new VMs’ size), and to change their network tier, use devvm network -g (choosing a tier).

Coding agents for new VMs

The coding agents you choose in devvm setup are the ones a new VM gets unless you choose others for it. The summary devvm shows before it makes the VM names each of them as coming from devvm setup, and when you customize the VM, they’re checked in the list (what a new VM gets). --agents chooses others for one VM. The choice is for new VMs only, so a VM that exists keeps its agents, and devvm tools changes them.

devvm asks for them on its first run in a terminal, together with the size and base’s features, until you’ve chosen them. Until then, and when you choose none, new VMs get no agents by default. devvm setup --agents claude,codex and devvm setup --agents none choose them without asking, and devvm refuses a name that isn’t an agent’s, suggesting the closest.

Layers for new VMs

The layers you choose in devvm setup are the ones every new VM gets unless you choose others for it. They can be devvm’s built-in layers, desktop, docker and nix, and your own, which is how you give every new VM an extra of your own (extras of your own). The summary devvm shows before it makes a new VM names each of them as coming from devvm setup. When you customize the VM in a terminal, they’re already chosen under Layers in the list, and you can leave any of them out of that VM (what a new VM gets).

devvm setup --layers docker,desktop # every new VM gets docker, with desktop on top
devvm setup --layers none # new VMs get no layers
devvm --layers nix # this VM gets nix alone, not setup's layers
devvm --layers none # this VM gets no layers

devvm setup --layers takes the layers bottom first, in the order the image’s name joins them, so --layers docker,desktop gives new VMs the image docker+desktop. It refuses a name that isn’t a layer’s, suggesting the closest, and changes nothing. Until you choose some, new VMs get no layers by default, and devvm doesn’t ask for them on its first run. In a terminal, devvm setup asks for them last, after the coding agents. To set them by hand, use the layers key in config.toml, which devvm setup --layers then refuses to change.

--layers on devvm is the exact list of one VM’s layers, so it replaces setup’s layers, and --layers none makes a VM without any. A devcontainer.json’s layers go on top of setup’s (devcontainer.json).

The choice is for new VMs only. A VM that exists keeps the layers it was made with, and devvm setup says so when it saves the choice. To give that VM more layers, run devvm layer add in its folder (adding layers to a VM), and to take some out, devvm layer rm (taking layers out of a VM).

When a layer of yours that you chose in devvm setup has no script in ~/.config/devvm/layers, such as after you delete it, a new VM is made without it, and devvm warns, naming the layer. Run devvm setup --layers to choose the layers again. When the VM’s backend can’t run a layer you chose, such as docker on a backend without Docker’s engine, devvm makes no VM and names the layer. Then choose other layers for that VM with --layers, or change new VMs’ layers with devvm setup --layers.

Retention

devvm keeps what it makes until you delete it, and the retention settings tell it to delete some of it on its own. Every setting is off until you set it, so first run devvm space to see what each one would free: its RETAIN column shows each setting that’s on, beside the row it applies to, with what it would delete now (devvm space).

devvm retention shows every setting and its value, and off for each one that isn’t set. devvm retention KEY=VALUE... sets them, and devvm retention KEY=off turns one off, for example devvm retention history.age=90d tools.unused-age=30d. devvm refuses a key or value it doesn’t know, and a key with no value such as history.age=, and then it writes nothing. devvm saves the settings in ~/.local/share/devvm/settings.json. The [retention] table of config.toml sets them too, and a setting there wins over the saved one, so devvm retention refuses to change it. Each line that devvm retention shows ends with where its value came from, after a #. When devvm can’t read a file that sets them, it names the file, and the line for config.toml, and applies none of them.

Key What devvm deletes
logs.runs the run logs beyond the newest this many, which is 20 when it’s off
history.age the exports of agents’ history written this long ago or more, such as 90d
history.count the exports of agents’ history beyond the newest this many
tools.unused-age the current shared tools that no VM has had for this long, counted from when devvm first found that no VM has them. While a VM is being made or is getting new shared tools, retention deletes none of them in that run, because that VM may not list the tools it picked yet, and it still applies the other settings
orphans.age what devvm keeps for VMs that their backend no longer has, once their state hasn’t changed for this long, as devvm gc --orphans does
nix-cache.size the shared Nix cache’s least recently used files, while it takes more than this, such as 20G; it’s 10 GiB when it’s off

Ages are durations, a whole number of minutes, hours, days or weeks, such as 30m, 12h, 30d or 2w. Sizes are a whole number of K, M, G or T, each 1024 of the one before, such as 500M or 20G, as devvm space shows them. The shared Nix cache also keeps to its size while VMs fill it, because a VM’s proxy deletes the cache’s least recently used files before a new file would take it past that size. A size you set applies to each VM from its next start. devvm applies the settings at the start of a command, at most once a day, except for orphans.age, which needs to ask each backend about its VMs, so only devvm gc --retention applies it. devvm gc --retention applies all of them at once. When it deletes something, devvm says what in one line. Retention never deletes a VM, an image, a shared tool that any VM’s state lists, or anything in the backends’ own caches, which only devvm gc --caches frees. In cache/, the folder in devvm’s data folder that holds what devvm makes again when it needs it, retention deletes only the shared Nix cache’s files. When two devvms start at once, only one of them applies the settings.

devvm retention –json

devvm retention --json prints the settings as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. settings has every key with its value as you wrote it, and off for each one that isn’t set. sources has every key with where its value came from: config.toml, settings.json for one that devvm retention saved, or built-in for one that’s off. With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses a KEY=VALUE with it.

{
 "version": 1,
 "settings": {
 "history.age": "90d",
 "history.count": "off",
 "logs.runs": "off",
 "nix-cache.size": "off",
 "orphans.age": "off",
 "tools.unused-age": "30d"
 },
 "sources": {
 "history.age": "config.toml",
 "history.count": "built-in",
 "logs.runs": "built-in",
 "nix-cache.size": "built-in",
 "orphans.age": "built-in",
 "tools.unused-age": "settings.json"
 }
}

A company’s CA

Some company networks inspect TLS through a proxy, such as Zscaler or Netskope, that shows its own certificates, signed by the company’s certificate authority (CA). This machine trusts that CA, but VMs and the VMs that devvm builds images in don’t, so their TLS connections fail. To make them trust it, put the CA’s certificate in ~/.config/devvm/ca:

mkdir -p ~/.config/devvm/ca
cp company-root.pem ~/.config/devvm/ca/

devvm reads every *.pem and *.crt file in that folder each time you open a VM, each time it builds an image and each time it resolves the shared tools’ versions, and it leaves other files alone. A file can hold one certificate or several, in PEM, the text form that starts with -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----. devvm accepts only CA certificates. When a file holds anything else, such as a private key, a certificate devvm can’t read or a certificate that isn’t a CA’s, devvm refuses the whole folder and names the file. It sends only the certificates it read out of a file, never the rest of the file. devvm doesn’t follow links there, so copy each certificate into the folder rather than linking to it. When a *.pem or *.crt file is a link, or the folder itself is one, devvm refuses the whole folder and names the link, because a link into a project folder would let that project’s VM replace the CA that every VM, build and proxy trusts. devvm also refuses the folder, naming the file, when it can’t read a file there or the folder itself.

Every project VM trusts these CAs in its system’s store from its next launch, and so does every VM that devvm builds an image or shared tools in. devvm takes them out of a build VM before the image is finished, so images never keep them, and adding or removing a CA rebuilds nothing. A layer script of yours that copies the system’s CA bundle somewhere else does keep that copy. On every network tier, the VM’s proxy also trusts them for the connections it makes itself, and so does the refresh of a coding agent’s login that the proxy makes on this machine when the login is due, so a company proxy that inspects TLS doesn’t make the refresh fail. devvm also resolves the shared tools’ versions on this machine, with a mise of its own that it downloads once, and that download trusts these CAs as well as this machine’s own store, and on Linux so does that mise. On macOS, mise trusts them for most of its connections, but the part of it that checks where each tool’s release was built trusts only the CAs that macOS trusts, which Keychain Access shows. So on macOS, a company’s CA that mise needs has to be there too, where a Mac that your company manages usually has it already. When mise doesn’t trust a server’s certificate, devvm says so and names this folder. devvm’s other connections from this machine, such as checking an image’s registry or Ubuntu’s image, trust this machine’s own store, as your other programs here do. When you take a certificate out of the folder, VMs stop trusting it at their next launch, and stores that copy the system’s CAs, such as Java’s cacerts, drop it too.

Most tools read the system’s store, among them apt, apk, curl, git and Python’s ssl module. For those that don’t, every VM’s environment points them at it:

Variable Value For
NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS /etc/ssl/devvm.pem, which holds only devvm’s CAs and is empty when there are none Node, npm and Bun
SSL_CERT_FILE /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, the system’s bundle Go programs, and Rust programs that read the system’s roots
REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, PIP_CERT the system’s bundle Python’s requests and pip, which use their own CA list otherwise
UV_SYSTEM_CERTS 1 uv

A CA in the folder can read every TLS connection a VM makes, as it can this machine’s, so put only CAs there that you trust as much as this machine does. How it works › Network tiers explains how the CAs reach VMs, and Images and caching how builds use them.

devvm’s state

~/.local/share/devvm ($XDG_DATA_HOME/devvm) holds what devvm makes and keeps for you, and devvm writes everything in it, so don’t edit it by hand. It holds the defaults that devvm setup, devvm size -g, devvm ports -g, devvm network -g and devvm retention save in settings.json, below config.toml’s, and a folder for each VM in vms/, with the VM’s state, its own allowlist and its network logs. It also holds the images and the shared tools, the run logs, the agents’ history that devvm history export and devvm rm save, the ssh config for your VMs, and devvm’s own Lima home (lima/), where the Lima backend’s VMs and images live. devvm’s data folder lists each file and folder in it, with how each one is cleaned up.

On Linux hosts this folder also holds your secrets, in files under secrets/ that only you can read, so keep that in mind when you back it up. On macOS they’re in the Keychain.

devvm’s Lima home is its own, whatever LIMA_HOME says, so Lima settings meant for other VMs never reach devvm’s. Set DEVVM_LIMA_HOME to move it, for example to a sandbox or to a shorter path.

Only you can read devvm’s files, in either folder, because each time devvm runs, it makes both folders yours alone (devvm’s data folder). When devvm can’t read one of its files, it names the file and the line (a file devvm can’t read).

Project folders devvm refuses

A VM mounts its project folder read-write, so devvm refuses to make a VM for a folder that would give the VM more than the project. It refuses a folder that is or holds your home folder, ~/.config/devvm, ~/.local/share/devvm or devvm’s Lima home. It also refuses a folder inside one of devvm’s own folders, because a VM there could rewrite the scripts that every image build runs, or the files that devvm runs on this machine.

When devvm refuses a folder, make the VM in a project folder inside it, or keep the project somewhere else. A --clone VM mounts nothing from the folder, so devvm doesn’t refuse its folder.

Warning

If you mean to give the VM the whole folder, pass --unsafe-folder when you make the VM, and devvm warns you that the VM gets read-write access to it (only the project folder).

Colors

In a terminal, devvm colors the labels and links around its messages, while the messages’ own text stays in your terminal’s usual color. The values a message fills in, such as a VM’s name, a path, a port or a count, are bold, so they stand out from the words around them. An error’s devvm: label is red and a warning’s is yellow, a doc link is blue and underlined, and the ==> before what devvm did is bold. When a step fails, the end of the run log that devvm prints is dim, and so is the log’s latest line on the status line and each line that -v shows. The mark a slow step leaves when it’s done is green.

The tables that devvm ls, devvm images, devvm space and devvm doctor print are colored too. Each table’s header row and the totals row are bold, and a state is green when it’s good, such as current, Running or native, yellow when it needs your attention, such as stale, unused, Stopped or emulated, and red when something is wrong, such as an unenforced tier or an unreviewed emulation. Digests, image keys and a feature a backend doesn’t have, which devvm doctor lists as none, are dim, and names, paths, sizes and counts stay in your terminal’s usual color. The columns line up the same with colors or without.

devvm uses only your terminal’s 16 base colors, so your theme picks shades that read well on its background, light or dark. It never sets a background color.

devvm decides for standard output and standard error apart, and colors one only when it’s a terminal, so output you pipe or redirect to a file stays plain, tables included. What a command prints with --json is plain even in a terminal, and the run log is never colored. These environment variables change when devvm colors, and the first one that applies decides:

  • NO_COLOR, set to anything but an empty value, turns colors off.
  • FORCE_COLOR or CLICOLOR_FORCE, set to anything but 0, turns them on even when the output isn’t a terminal.
  • TERM=dumb turns them off.

Environment

NO_COLOR, FORCE_COLOR, CLICOLOR_FORCE turn devvm’s colors off, or on when the output isn’t a terminal (details)
DEVVM_LIMA_HOME move devvm’s own Lima home (details)
DEVVM_FROM the container image that the base of new VMs and builds starts from when there’s no --from (details)
DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK=1 don’t check for newer shared tools once a day (details)
DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK=1 don’t check for a newer devvm release once a day (details)
DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE the Keychain service devvm saves and reads secrets in, instead of devvm (details)
CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN the Claude Code token that VMs get, over the saved Claude Code login, whichever it is (details)

item.title: Working on a clone
item.description:
devvm --clone gives the VM its own clone of the repo instead of mounting your folder, so nothing in the VM can touch your working tree or .git. Use it when you don’t trust what runs in the VM, such as an agent working unattended, and on Linux hosts that can’t lock .git, such as Ubuntu 23.10 and newer, where devvm only names what changed after the fact (when Linux can’t lock). On Linux hosts it’s also the way to use SQLite in WAL mode, or a program that maps its files for writing, such as LMDB or the mold linker, in the repo, because those fail in the 9p share that VMs there mount the folder with, while the clone is on the VM’s own disk, which is also far faster (programs that map files). Files the VM writes lists what --clone keeps away from this machine.

devvm --clone # create the VM, copy your branches into it and open a shell in its clone
git fetch devvm # later, on this machine, fetch the VM's work as devvm/<branch>
git log -p main..devvm/main
sequenceDiagram
participant R as Your repo
participant V as The VM's clone
R->>V: devvm --clone pushes<br>every local branch
Note over V: you or an agent<br>commit in the VM
V->>R: git fetch devvm gives<br>devvm/#lt;branch#gt;
Note over R: review,<br>then merge
R->>V: devvm rm looks for<br>commits not fetched
V->>R: fetched into<br>saved/devvm/#lt;branch#gt;
Note over R,V: the VM is deleted,<br>and its remote removed

When the folder holds several repos, such as a frontend and a backend beside each other, devvm --clone gives the VM a clone of each repo you choose, at the same paths as on this machine (folders of repos).

Requirements

  • The folder is the top folder of a git repo that has at least one commit and a branch checked out, not a detached HEAD, or it’s a folder of repos (folders of repos).
  • The repo is the folder’s own, or the folder is a worktree that git worktree add made. devvm refuses a .git that points into another repo, because the push would copy that repo’s branches into the VM. That includes a .git file that isn’t a worktree’s, a worktree whose link back to this folder doesn’t match, a commondir that leads to another repo, and objects or refs that are symlinks, or that sit in a folder that is one. devvm also refuses a repo that borrows objects from another repo through objects/info/alternates. To use such a repo, run git repack -a -d in it, then delete that file.
  • git is installed on this machine. The VM’s images already have it.
  • No other VM mounts the folder, such as the VM of a folder it’s in. Code in that VM could swap the repo under the git commands devvm runs here as it copies your branches, so devvm refuses --clone and devvm clone on there and names that VM. Delete that VM, or move the repo out of its folder.
  • You choose --clone when the VM is created, and once a VM is a --clone VM you don’t need to pass --clone again. devvm refuses --clone for an existing VM that mounts its folder, and devvm clone on switches that VM instead (switching a VM that exists).

What’s copied

From this machine, the VM mounts only the shared tools and its agents’ config folders. Once the VM is running, devvm creates a repo in it at the same path as your folder and pushes every local branch into it. When the folder is a git worktree, devvm pushes only the worktree’s branch and that branch’s upstream, if it has one, and leaves the repo’s other branches on this machine. The push goes over ssh to the VM itself and checks the host keys devvm pinned for it. No setting in your repo’s config, such as a url.*.insteadOf that rewrites the VM’s URL, can send the push anywhere else (how the push connects). devvm checks out your current branch in the clone, and your shell opens there.

Apart from a worktree’s upstream, which can be a remote-tracking branch such as origin/main, devvm copies only your local branches. Tags, uncommitted changes, and untracked or ignored files such as .env and node_modules stay on this machine. devvm warns you about uncommitted changes, so you can commit them and send them later with git push devvm BRANCH.

If the copy fails, for example because the VM can’t be reached, devvm tries again the next time you run it in the folder.

The remote

devvm adds a git remote for the VM to your repo. It’s named devvm, or devvm-<folder> if devvm is already taken, or the VM’s full name if both are. The remote’s URL is the VM’s full name followed by the clone’s path, so git connects through devvm’s ssh config, and fetching needs two things:

  • Your ~/.ssh/config needs devvm’s Include line (SSH access by name). devvm offers to add it when it creates the clone, and again when you run devvm host or devvm code. Until the line is there, or when devvm had no terminal to ask in, fetch with GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -F ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config' git fetch devvm.
  • The VM must be running. A stopped VM has no SSH entry, so git fetch fails because it can’t resolve the name. Run devvm or devvm host in the folder first.

Fetching the VM’s work

git fetch devvm in the repo fetches the VM’s branches as devvm/<branch>, as for any remote. devvm clone fetch does the same for every repo the VM has a clone of, which is one repo here, or each repo of a folder of repos, and then lists the branches that are new or have moved since the last fetch, each with the repos it’s in:

$ devvm clone fetch
agent/search: backend, frontend
main: backend
==> Review each branch in its repo before you merge it, such as with git log -p main..devvm/main.

devvm clone fetch starts the VM if it’s stopped. It connects to the VM itself, as the copy does, so it needs neither devvm’s Include line in ~/.ssh/config nor the VM’s name in your ssh config. It fetches every branch of each clone into its repo’s remote, as devvm/<branch>, and never changes your own branches or tags. When a repo’s remote is gone, devvm clone fetch adds it again. When you’ve pointed the remote at another URL, or the folder on this machine isn’t that repo any more, for example because its .git is gone, devvm leaves that repo alone and says so.

Fetching runs nothing from the VM on this machine. git only receives objects and updates the devvm/* branches, or creates new saved/devvm/* branches when devvm rm does the fetch. The commits themselves are untrusted, though, so treat them as you would a contributor’s branch and review them before you merge them, check them out or run anything they change.

Subfolders

When you run devvm in a subfolder of the repo’s folder, devvm uses the --clone VM as it uses any parent folder’s VM (a subfolder). The clone is at the repo folder’s path, so the subfolder’s path in the VM is the same subfolder in the clone. When the clone has that subfolder, the shell opens there, and devvm host and devvm code give it as the folder to open. When the clone lacks it, for example because the subfolder is untracked or ignored and so never copied, they use the clone’s top folder instead.

devvm --clone in a subfolder never uses a parent folder’s VM. It makes a new --clone VM for the subfolder, as devvm --here does, and doesn’t take --parent, so the subfolder must be the top folder of a repo of its own.

Several agents in one VM

Several agents can work in one --clone VM, each on a branch of its own in a git worktree of its own, so each agent edits its own copy of the files. Put the worktrees inside the clone, such as in .worktrees/NAME, because the clone’s parent folders in the VM belong to root, and so git worktree add ../NAME fails there. In the VM, in the clone:

echo .worktrees/ >> .git/info/exclude # once, so git status in the clone leaves the worktrees out
git worktree add -b agent/api .worktrees/api # a worktree on a new branch, agent/api
cd .worktrees/api # then start the agent here

Every worktree shares the clone’s repo, so the agents’ branches are all in it. One git fetch devvm on this machine brings every agent’s branch back, such as devvm/agent/api, and you review each one as you would any of the VM’s work (fetching the VM’s work). Before devvm rm deletes the VM, it also checks each worktree inside the clone for uncommitted changes (deleting the VM).

Install each worktree’s dependencies in that worktree, and never share one node_modules folder between worktrees, because each branch can need different packages, and two agents installing at once can break it. pnpm and bun keep one package store in the VM and hard-link packages from it into each worktree’s node_modules when both are on the same disk, so another worktree costs little download or disk.

The agents also share the VM’s ports, so two servers on the same port collide. Give each worktree’s server a port of its own, such as with PORT=3001. A VM that forwards every port, as new VMs do by default, forwards each of them to this machine’s localhost (ports).

The agents in one VM share its network tier and rules, its secrets, and its CPUs, memory and disk, and each agent can read and change every other agent’s worktree. When the agents need different network tiers or rules, secrets or sizes, or when one agent mustn’t reach another’s work, give each agent a folder of its own on this machine, such as a separate clone of the repo, and run devvm --clone in each, so each gets a VM of its own.

Folders of repos

A project is often several repos in one folder, such as a frontend that uses file:../shared in its package.json, or a .NET solution whose projects point at ../Lib/Lib.csproj. devvm --clone in that folder gives one VM a clone of each repo you choose, each at the same path as on this machine, so the paths between them work in the VM as they do here. The folder can be a repo itself or not, and when it is one, you ask for this with --repos, because without it devvm --clone there gives the VM a clone of the folder’s own repo alone, as for any repo, whatever repos are below it.

my-repos/
├── docker-compose.yml
├── frontend/ (a repo)
├── backend/ (a repo)
└── shared/ (a repo)
cd my-repos
devvm --clone # choose the repos, then create the VM and open a shell in my-repos
devvm --clone --repos frontend,shared # or choose them on the command line, as a script must

devvm looks for repos up to four folders below this one, as .git protection does, and skips the folders of packages and build tools, such as node_modules and vendor. In a terminal, it lists the repos it found in a picker, each ticked, and you untick those the VM doesn’t need. A repo that --clone can’t copy is listed under its own heading with the reason, such as a repo without commits or one whose .git points into another repo, and it can’t be ticked. devvm lists at most 100 repos, and it names how many more it found. A linked worktree of a repo in the folder, such as one in .worktrees/NAME, isn’t a repo of its own, so devvm doesn’t list it. Its repo’s clone gets that repo’s current and default branches only, not the worktree’s own branch, so push that one yourself with git push devvm BRANCH in the worktree once the VM is made. A repo whose folder’s name has a character a terminal can’t show, such as a line break or a bidi control, can’t be ticked.

A repo that another VM mounts, because that VM is a subfolder’s that holds the repo, or the repo’s own, or, for a linked worktree, the VM of the repo it belongs to, can’t be ticked either, because code in that VM could swap the repo for another while devvm’s git works in it. devvm names that VM, and devvm clone add refuses the repo too. Delete that VM, or move the repo out of its folder, to give this VM a clone of it. A folder of repos inside another repo’s working tree is refused, because devvm would copy that repo’s files. To clone repos in it, run devvm --clone --repos LIST in that repo’s top folder, and choose them there.

Without a terminal, or with --no-input, give --repos, or devvm refuses without creating anything. --repos all takes every repo --clone can copy, --repos none takes none of them, and a list such as --repos frontend,backend takes those repos, by their folders relative to this one, with . for this folder’s own repo. devvm names each repo you chose that it can’t copy, and leaves it out. devvm records your choice in the VM’s state, never in the folder.

When devvm finds no repo below this folder that it can copy, devvm --clone gives the VM a clone of this folder’s own repo, as for a folder that holds no other, and the folder must then be one (requirements).

When the folder’s own repo is one of those you choose, its clone in the VM leaves the other repos’ clones out of its git status, and what your repo’s .git/info/exclude leaves out too, such as .worktrees/, so the other clones aren’t changes devvm rm asks about.

Each repo’s clone gets the repo’s current branch and its default branch, which is the branch origin/HEAD points to, else main, else master, whichever the repo has, as a local branch or as origin’s. devvm copies no other branches, which keeps the copy fast for big repos, and you send any other branch later with git push devvm BRANCH in that repo. When a repo’s HEAD is detached, its clone checks out the default branch, and devvm says so. A repo with a detached HEAD and no default branch has nothing to check out, so --clone can’t copy it.

Each repo gets a remote of its own for the VM, named as for one repo’s clone (the remote): devvm, or devvm-<folder> when that repo already has a devvm remote, for example from a VM of its own. One repo’s remote names never change the others’. When a repo has all three names taken, devvm leaves that repo out and names it.

As the copy is made, a repo that no longer passes the checks, for example because its last commit went, is left out and named, and the others are copied. When the copy fails, devvm copies what’s left the next time you run it in the folder.

The folder’s own files

A folder of repos often has files of its own at its top, outside every repo, such as a docker-compose.yml, a Makefile or an .envrc. When the folder isn’t a repo itself, devvm copies these into the VM once, when it creates the clone, at the same paths. It never copies them again, and nothing comes back from the VM, so a later change on either side stays there. To change one in the VM, edit it there, and to bring a change back, copy it out yourself, for example with devvm host and scp.

devvm copies the files and folders outside every repo, whether the VM has a clone of that repo or not, and never a .git, a folder shaped like one, such as a bare repo’s, or the folders of packages and build tools, such as node_modules, vendor and .venv. It keeps each file’s permissions but its set-user-id and set-group-id bits, and a link that leads to a path in the folder, as a link. It reads only beneath the folder, one folder at a time, and never through a link, so a link that leads out of it stays on this machine, as do a bare repo, a file with another hard link, sockets and other special files, anything on another disk, a file over 10 MiB, and the files past 64 MiB or 5,000 entries in all. devvm says how many of the files it left out. When the folder is a repo itself, its files are its repo’s, so devvm copies none of them this way.

A secret in one of these files, such as an .env at the folder’s top, reaches the VM as any other file does, so move it out of the folder before devvm --clone when the VM mustn’t have it. devvm refuses the folders it refuses to mount, such as your home folder (folders devvm refuses), because it would copy their files.

Opening a repo’s folder

In a folder of one of the VM’s repos, such as my-repos/frontend, devvm opens the folder’s VM at that repo’s path, as it opens any parent folder’s VM in a subfolder. A repo of its own in a subfolder usually gets a VM of its own, but the folder’s VM has this repo’s clone at the same path and mounts nothing of this machine, so the VM can’t reach the repo’s folder here. devvm --here in the repo’s folder still creates or opens that repo’s own VM. In a repo the VM has no clone of, devvm doesn’t use the folder’s VM.

Adding a repo

devvm clone add PATH copies one more repo into the VM, such as a repo you cloned into the folder after the VM was made, or one that you left out. PATH is the repo’s folder, relative to the folder you run it in, and it must be inside the VM’s folder. devvm checks the repo as it checks each repo it copies, starts the VM if it’s stopped, copies the repo’s current and default branches to the same path in the VM and adds its remote. When the copy fails, for example because the VM can’t be reached, devvm keeps the repo in the VM’s list, so devvm rm still checks what reached the VM, and running devvm clone add PATH again copies it again.

git clone git@github.com:me/docs.git
devvm clone add docs

A repo made in the VM stays in the VM, because the VM can’t add a repo to this machine. To bring it out, clone it from the VM with git clone devvm-my-repos-<hash>:/path/to/my-repos/new, using the VM’s full name from devvm ls.

Agents across repos

An agent that works on one change across repos uses one branch name in each repo, such as agent/search in frontend and in backend, so devvm clone fetch lists that change as one line with both repos. For several agents at once, give each its own folder with a worktree of each repo, inside the VM’s folder:

for r in frontend backend; do git -C "$r" worktree add -b agent/search "../.worktrees/search/$r"; done
cd .worktrees/search # the change's own copy of the folder's repos, then start the agent here

devvm copies the folder’s own files only into the folder itself, so copy those the agent needs into the change’s folder too. devvm rm checks each worktree inside the VM’s folder for uncommitted changes, whichever repo it belongs to (deleting the VM).

Deleting the VM

Before devvm rm deletes a --clone VM, it checks the clone for work you’d lose. It starts a stopped VM for the check as a launch does, so the VM’s confinement is checked first:

  1. If the clone has branches with commits this repo hasn’t fetched, devvm names them and offers to fetch them into new local branches named saved/devvm/<branch>. It skips a branch whose name git on this machine refuses and names it, and that branch goes with the VM. To keep such a branch, rename it in the VM with git branch -m before you run devvm rm.
  2. If the clone or a worktree inside its folder has uncommitted changes, devvm lists the first 20 of them in all, with each worktree’s changes under its path, and asks before deleting them along with the VM. devvm skips a worktree whose folder is gone or that git would prune, and it doesn’t check worktrees outside the clone’s folder. When the clone has more than 100 worktrees inside its folder, devvm checks the first 100 and asks before deleting the VM, even if none of them has changes. Worktrees outside the folder don’t count towards the 100.

For a folder of repos, devvm checks every repo the VM has a clone of, reading them all from the VM at once, and names the repo of each branch and each change it lists. It asks once whether to fetch the unfetched branches of every repo, each into that repo’s saved/<remote>/<branch> branches, and once before the uncommitted changes go, with the first 20 changes in all the repos shown. When a repo’s clone isn’t at its path in the VM, for example because something in the VM moved it, devvm says so and asks before deleting the VM, as for uncommitted changes. A repo whose copy didn’t finish is checked too when its clone is in the VM. When another VM mounts one of the repos, devvm still reads its clone in the VM and checks every other repo, but it leaves that repo on this machine alone, so it can’t fetch the VM’s work in it: it names that VM and asks before deleting, as for uncommitted changes. When a repo on this machine isn’t the repo the VM has a clone of any more, for example because its .git is gone, devvm refuses and keeps the VM, because git there would read another repo; put the repo back, or give --no-clone-check. devvm doesn’t check the VM’s copy of the folder’s own files, nor anything else outside the repos, so copy out what you need of those first.

If either check finds something and there’s no terminal to ask in, or you give --no-input, devvm refuses and keeps the VM. These questions are asked only in a terminal, because only you can judge the work, so --force never answers them (questions devvm asks).

Without a terminal, when a folder of repos has unfetched branches, devvm’s refusal names devvm clone fetch: run it first, and the check finds them fetched.

Once the checks pass, devvm deletes the VM. If the remote still points at the VM, devvm then removes it with git remote remove, in each repo of a folder of repos too, which also deletes its devvm/* branches and their upstream settings. Before it does, devvm keeps every devvm/* branch that has commits no other branch has as a new local branch under saved/devvm/, whoever fetched it. devvm names each branch it creates, and they’re yours to review, merge or delete, as with git branch -D saved/devvm/main.

The saved branches are named after the remote, as saved/<remote>/<branch>, and devvm never overwrites a branch. When a branch is in the way, devvm uses saved/<remote>-2, then -3 and so on, and if it finds no free name, devvm rm refuses and keeps the VM (saved branches).

devvm rm --force skips only the question whether to delete the VM at all, and both checks still run. devvm rm --no-export skips the export of the agents’ history, and it also leaves both checks as they are.

When another VM mounts the repo, such as the VM of a folder the repo is in, code in that VM could swap the repo under devvm’s git, so devvm runs no git in it on this machine. It checks the clone in the VM, names that VM and asks before deleting, as for uncommitted changes, because it can’t fetch the clone’s work into the repo; without a terminal it refuses and keeps the VM. Fetch the work by hand first if you need it, then give --no-clone-check.

devvm rm --no-clone-check skips both checks, so the VM goes with the commits this repo hasn’t fetched and the uncommitted changes, and devvm warns you of that first. Use it when a check can’t read the clone, such as when git in the VM is broken, and devvm refuses and keeps the VM. Use it too when the VM doesn’t start for the check, such as when its tier isn’t enforced, because devvm then says what kept it from starting and keeps the VM. devvm still asks whether to delete the VM unless you also give --force, and it still keeps the devvm/* branches you fetched as saved/devvm/ branches.

Switching a VM that exists

devvm clone shows whether this folder’s VM has its own clone of the repo, which is on, or mounts the folder, which is off. devvm clone on and devvm clone off switch the VM by making it again from the image it has, as devvm layer add does, and then open a shell in it:

devvm clone # show on or off
devvm clone on # make the VM again with its own clone of the repo, after asking
devvm clone off # fetch the clone's work, then make the VM again with this folder mounted

The VM keeps its home folder and its settings, as a VM made again does, and everything else on its disk is lost. So in a terminal devvm asks first, with no as the default, and without one it refuses unless you give --force. --no-export skips the export of the agents’ history, and --clean-home gives the VM the image’s home folder instead of its own, as for devvm layer add. When the VM is in the mode you ask for already, devvm says so and changes nothing.

devvm clone on needs a folder that --clone takes (requirements), and devvm refuses before it changes anything when the folder isn’t one. In a folder of repos, devvm asks which repos the new VM gets in the picker before it asks to make the VM again, and devvm clone on --repos LIST answers that without a terminal. Your work is in the folder, so only the VM’s disk is lost. The new VM mounts nothing of the folder, and as it starts, devvm copies your branches into its clone and adds the remote, as for a new --clone VM (what’s copied). Once the new VM is ready and the old one is deleted, devvm takes the .git locks off the folder, because no VM mounts it any more. First it names what the old VM changed that the locks can’t stop, as a launch does (when devvm reports .git).

devvm clone off loses the clone, which is on the VM’s disk, so first it checks the clone as devvm rm does (deleting the VM), every repo of a folder of repos included. It offers to fetch the branches this repo hasn’t fetched into saved/devvm/<branch> branches, and it asks before the clone’s uncommitted changes go. Only a terminal can answer these questions, and --force never does, so without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm refuses and keeps the VM as it is. devvm clone off --no-clone-check skips the check after a warning, and the clone’s unfetched commits and uncommitted changes are lost. The new VM mounts the folder again with .git protection as a new VM gets it, which is on on macOS and off on Linux hosts. Before the new VM first starts, and before devvm locks .git, it removes the remote and keeps each devvm/* branch that has commits no other branch has as a saved/devvm/ branch, as devvm rm does. If the switch is then undone, devvm adds the remote back.

When a step fails, or you press Ctrl+C, before the new VM has its home folder, devvm puts the old VM back as it was, in its old mode, as it does for any remake.

A --clone VM keeps its clone on its own disk, so devvm layer add, devvm layer rm and devvm update refuse it. To change its layers or bring it up to date, run devvm clone off, then that command, then devvm clone on.

devvm clone –json

devvm clone --json prints one JSON object with clone, which is on or off, as output for scripts describes. With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses on or off with it, and the flags that go with them.

{
 "version": 1,
 "clone": "on"
}

devvm clone fetch –json

devvm clone fetch --json fetches as devvm clone fetch does, then prints one JSON object instead of the list. repos has each repo with new or moved branches, by its folder relative to this one (. for this folder’s own repo), with its remote and those branches. branches has the same by name, each with its repos, sorted by name. Both are empty when nothing is new.

{
 "version": 1,
 "repos": [
 {
 "path": "backend",
 "remote": "devvm",
 "branches": ["agent/search"]
 },
 {
 "path": "frontend",
 "remote": "devvm",
 "branches": ["agent/search"]
 }
 ],
 "branches": [
 {
 "name": "agent/search",
 "repos": ["backend", "frontend"]
 }
 ]
}

item.title: devcontainer.json
item.description:
devvm supports the Dev Container specification, so a project’s devcontainer.json sets up its VM. When you run devvm in a folder with a .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, or else a .devcontainer.json at the folder’s root, the new VM gets that file’s settings by default, as far as devvm supports them. To make the VM without reading the file, run devvm --no-devcontainer.

The settings devvm supports are the container image to start from, the features devvm has layers for, the ports, the environment and the commands. devvm says in one line which file it read.

{
 "image": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/javascript-node:22",
 "features": { "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/docker-in-docker:2": {} },
 "forwardPorts": [3000],
 "remoteEnv": { "PATH": "${containerEnv:PATH}:${containerWorkspaceFolder}/bin" },
 "postCreateCommand": "npm ci",
 "postStartCommand": "npm run db:start"
}

When it’s read

  • When the folder’s VM is made, and again by devvm update. Comments and trailing commas are allowed. devvm reads the file only within the folder, so it doesn’t follow a link out of the folder, and it reads only a regular file of up to 1 MiB. devvm never writes anything to the project folder.
  • What you give on the command line wins. --from wins over image, which wins over $DEVVM_FROM, and --ports wins over forwardPorts, and devvm says so in one line for each. The new VM gets the toolchains and layers that the features map to, which its summary shows, and when you customize the VM, they’re already chosen in its list, each row naming the file, so you can leave them out there. --tools and --layers replace them, as they replace any part’s default (what a new VM gets).
  • An existing VM changes only when devvm makes it again. Its state records the file’s SHA-256. When the file differs from it on a launch, or is gone, or has appeared since, devvm warns once and names devvm update. devvm doesn’t check a VM made with --no-devcontainer, and devvm update doesn’t read the file for it.

A new VM takes each of these from the first place that sets it.

flowchart TD
subgraph ports["Its ports"]
direction TB
flag["--ports"] -- "or else" --> fwd["your ports, with<br>forwardPorts added"]
end
subgraph base["Its base starts from"]
direction TB
from["--from"] -- "or else" --> image["the file's image"]
image -- "or else" --> env["$DEVVM_FROM"]
env -- "or else" --> ubuntu["Ubuntu's cloud image"]
end

When devvm refuses something in the file, it stops with one line that names the file, before it makes anything. For invalid JSON, it names the line and column.

Updating a VM from the file

When you change the file, run devvm update. devvm reads the file as it is now, and before it changes anything, it refuses what it would refuse for a new VM. Then it asks to make the VM again from the file, keeping its home folder, the project folder and its settings, as for an outdated VM, and everything else on the VM’s disk is lost. devvm update --force doesn’t ask, and without a terminal devvm refuses unless you give --force.

devvm replaces only what the file gave the VM, and it keeps what you chose:

  • Toolchains and layers. The ones the file’s features gave the VM go when the file no longer has those features, and the ones the file’s new features map to are added. The ones you chose yourself stay, whether you gave them with --tools or --layers, devvm setup chose them, or the folder’s other files call for them. One you left out in the list, or took out later, stays out.
  • The container image. The VM’s base starts from the file’s new image, pinned as for a new VM. When the file no longer has one, the base starts from $DEVVM_FROM, or else from Ubuntu’s cloud image. A VM made with --from keeps its base, and devvm says that it ignores image.
  • The ports. The ports the file added go when the file no longer lists them, and the ones it lists anew are added, as devvm ports add adds them. The ports you added with devvm ports add stay, and one of the file’s that you took out with devvm ports rm stays out. A VM made with --ports gets the ports the file lists anew, but not the ones --ports won over.
  • The environment and the commands. They’re the file’s new ones, and the commands that run once run again on the new disk.

When the file is gone, devvm makes the VM again without it, so what the file gave goes, and so do its environment and commands. When a file appears for a VM made without one, devvm makes the VM again as the file says, as it would a new VM.

Properties

Property What devvm does
image The VM’s base starts from it, as with --from. devvm uses only an image that its registry gives anyone who asks anonymously, pinned to that digest. It never uses an image only Docker has, one only your registry login reaches, or one on this machine or its network, which is localhost or a registry whose address is loopback, private or link-local, by name or as it resolves.
features ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/docker-in-docker is devvm’s docker layer. A feature under ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/ named after one of devvm’s toolchains, such as ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node, is that shared toolchain. devvm ignores their options and says so in one line. It refuses docker-outside-of-docker, which is this machine’s Docker, and every other feature. devvm never fetches or runs a feature’s script.
forwardPorts devvm forwards numbers, localhost:N and 127.0.0.1:N to this machine’s localhost alone, adding them to your ports as devvm ports add does (ports). With every port forwarded, which is the default, they’re among them already. devvm ports rm takes one out, as for any port. It ignores other hosts’ ports and says so in one line.
containerEnv, remoteEnv The VM’s environment, which login shells and the commands below get. remoteEnv wins over containerEnv, and devvm’s own variables, such as LANG and secrets, win over both. A remoteEnv of null sets nothing.
onCreateCommand, updateContentCommand, postCreateCommand They run once, in that order, once the VM is made and set up (commands).
postStartCommand It runs at each start, on the first launch after the VM started.
initializeCommand It never runs, because it would run on this machine, and devvm says so in one line.
build, dockerFile, dockerfile, dockerComposeFile Refused, because devvm starts a VM only from an image.
postAttachCommand, privileged, capAdd, securityOpt, mounts, runArgs, workspaceMount, workspaceFolder, remoteUser, containerUser, updateRemoteUserUID, init, shutdownAction, overrideCommand, hostRequirements, appPort, portsAttributes, otherPortsAttributes, userEnvProbe, waitFor, overrideFeatureInstallOrder, context, service, runServices Ignored, and named in one line.
name, customizations, $schema Ignored.
anything else Ignored, and named in one line.

Commands

A command is a string, which devvm runs with sh -c, an array, which it runs as it is, or an object of named commands, which it runs one by one, sorted by name. The commands run in the VM, as its user, in the project folder, in a login shell, and never on this machine. Their output goes to the run log.

When a command fails, devvm names it in one line, and the commands after it that would run once, or at that start, don’t run. devvm keeps the VM and opens it, because the command is the project’s and not devvm’s. The commands reach only what the VM’s network tier allows, like anything else in the VM.

Variables

Variable
${containerWorkspaceFolder}, ${containerWorkspaceFolderBasename} the project folder, at the same path in the VM, and its name
${containerEnv:NAME} in a string command and in containerEnv and remoteEnv, the VM’s own NAME
${localEnv:NAME}, ${env:NAME} refused, because devvm never puts this machine’s environment in a VM
${localWorkspaceFolder}, ${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}, ${devcontainerId}, ${containerEnv:NAME} elsewhere refused

devvm leaves any other ${…} as it is, for the VM’s shell, such as ${HOME} in a command.

Security

The file belongs to the project, so a VM can rewrite it for the folder’s next VM, or for itself when you run devvm update, and devvm never lets it run anything on this machine, reach this machine’s files or environment, add a mount or weaken confinement. An image from it can still be any public container image, whose own code runs as root while devvm builds the VM’s base, as with --from (security model).

Its forwardPorts open ports on this machine, even when you’ve narrowed your ports with devvm ports -g or devvm ports. devvm forwards them only to this machine’s localhost, never to its other addresses, and never takes a port that a program on this machine already has, just as for devvm ports add. Anything on this machine that connects to such a port reaches what the VM serves there, including a web page in your browser, so for a repo you don’t trust, check its file first, or run devvm --ports none or devvm --no-devcontainer (ports the VM listens on).

item.title: Links between VMs
item.description:
A link lets a program in one of your VMs reach a TCP service in another by name, as in postgres://db:5432/app or fetch("http://api:3000"). The VM with the service is the target, and you publish its port in its folder. The VM that reaches it is the client, and you add the link in the client’s folder. Links work on every backend, whatever the two VMs’ network tiers, as long as the target’s tier is the client’s or a stricter one. devvm carries each connection over ssh through this machine, so neither VM’s network changes, and How it works › Links between VMs explains how.

For a database in ~/code/db and an app in ~/code/app, both with VMs:

cd ~/code/db && devvm link publish 5432 # offer the database's port to links
cd ~/code/app && devvm link add db 5432 # programs in app's VM reach it as db:5432

Programs in the app’s VM then reach the database as db:5432 and as db.devvm.internal:5432. A link joins the two VMs’ trust, so add one only between VMs you’d trust with each other’s reach (below). To link several VMs to each other at once, put them in a group.

Publishing a port

Links reach only the ports a VM publishes, so you publish a port in the target’s folder before any VM can link to it:

devvm link publish # what this folder's VM publishes: none, or a list
devvm link publish 5432 # offer port 5432 to links
devvm link publish 8000-8010 # offer a range
devvm link unpublish 5432 # stop offering it
  • devvm link publish takes ports and ranges as devvm ports does, such as 5432,8000-8010, but not all or none. A port you publish is offered to links from any of your VMs, and each link is still made in its client’s folder with devvm link add.
  • devvm link unpublish takes ports as devvm link publish lists them, and it refuses a port that isn’t published. The server in the VM keeps running. When other VMs link to a port you take out, devvm names them, and their next connections to that port are refused, while connections that are open stay until they close. To remove those links, run devvm link rm in their folders.
  • A change applies at once, whether the VM is running or stopped.
  • Publishing forwards nothing to this machine, and it doesn’t change the ports the VM forwards.

A link connects to the target’s own 127.0.0.1, so the server in the target has to listen there or on all its addresses. A server that listens on ::1 alone isn’t reached.

Adding a link

In the client’s folder, devvm link add TARGET PORT links its VM to PORT of the VM that TARGET names, once that VM publishes the port:

devvm link add db 5432 # reach port 5432 of the VM for the folder db as db:5432
devvm link add db 5432 --as pg # reach it as pg:5432 instead
devvm link add ../api 8080 # name the target by its folder's path
devvm link add devvm-api-71a99b1076d92c 8080 # or by its VM's name

TARGET takes one of four forms:

  • A folder’s name, as VM names have it, such as db for devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c. devvm matches it against the folder that each VM was made for, so a VM whose backend needed a shorter name still matches its whole folder name. When more than one VM has a folder of that name, devvm refuses and lists each VM with its folder, so you can give the VM’s name or the folder’s path instead.
  • A folder’s path, which starts with . or holds a /, such as ../api or /Users/you/code/api.
  • A VM’s name, as devvm ls lists it.
  • A VM’s ssh alias, such as devvm-db, as you’d give it to ssh (SSH access by name).

devvm refuses a target that has no VM, the client’s own VM, and a port that the target doesn’t publish. It also refuses a link that the two VMs’ tiers don’t allow. When devvm makes the link, it says what the client reaches it as, and that the link joins the two VMs’ trust.

Names

Programs in the client reach a link at NAME:PORT and NAME.devvm.internal:PORT. NAME is the target’s folder name, as VM names have it, unless you give --as NAME. .internal is reserved for private networks, so NAME.devvm.internal never names a host on the internet, and it’s the name to use when the short one could clash with a name your network resolves.

  • A client has one name for each VM it links to. The first link to a target sets the name, and later links to that target take it too, so after devvm link add db 5432 --as pg, devvm link add db 8000 reaches pg:8000. To change the name, remove that target’s links and add them again.
