  • A name is one DNS label, made of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, which starts and ends with a letter or a digit and isn’t all digits. devvm refuses localhost, the client’s own hostname and a name that another of the client’s links has. When the target’s folder name isn’t a valid name, or it’s taken, give another with --as NAME.
  • A link is reached only by its names, never at the client’s localhost, so localhost:5432 in the client stays the client’s own.
  • A link’s name hides the same name from anywhere else in the client, such as a host db under your network’s search domain.

Ports

The client reaches the target’s port on the same port number, so devvm link add web 80 gives web:80, and ports below 1024 work like any other. Two targets can publish the same port, because the client reaches each one by its own name.

Links carry TCP over IPv4 alone. Each name resolves to an IPv4 address, so a program that connects only over IPv6 doesn’t reach it, and UDP isn’t carried.

Which VM a link reaches

A link stays with the VM it was made for, because devvm records the target VM’s identity with the link. A VM made again in the target’s folder after devvm rm, or another VM with the same folder name that appears later, isn’t the linked target. devvm layer add, devvm layer rm and devvm update keep the target’s identity as they make the VM again, so its links still reach it (adding layers to a VM).

A link joins the two VMs’ trust

Code in the client can often run code in the target through the target’s own service, such as Postgres’s COPY … TO PROGRAM. It then has whatever the target has: its network, the secrets it may use and its project folder. devvm doesn’t stop that, because it’s what the service itself allows. So add a link only between VMs you’d trust with each other’s reach, and publish only the ports that you mean other VMs to use. Network tiers explains what this means for each tier.

Links and network tiers

A client links only to a target on its own network tier or a stricter one, because a link to a target on a lower tier would let the client reach more through the target. So an allowlist client links to allowlist and none targets, but not to internet or open ones, and an open client may link to any target. When devvm can’t read a client’s or a target’s tier, because that part of its state was changed by hand, it refuses the link rather than take it as open (a file devvm can’t read).

devvm checks this rule when you add a link, at each launch of the client and on every connection. For a client on a confined tier, on every connection the target’s tier must also be in force as the target runs. If you move the target from open to a confined tier while it’s running, devvm ls shows it as unenforced until the target starts again behind its proxy, and devvm refuses the client’s connections to it until then, so start the target again with devvm restart in its folder. devvm also warns you of such a target when you add a link to it, when you publish a port in its folder that the client links to, and each time the client starts. The warning names the target and refuses nothing, and devvm doesn’t warn of a stopped target, because its tier applies when it next starts.

While such a link exists, devvm refuses to give the target a tier lower than a client’s, such as devvm network open in its folder, and names the clients that link to it, and it refuses to give the client a tier higher than a target’s, such as devvm network allowlist for a client that links to an open VM. Remove those links with devvm link rm first, or give the target the client’s tier.

Every VM has its proxy, so a program that uses the VM’s proxy settings, such as curl, sends its requests for a link to the VM’s proxy, and the proxy carries a request for one of the link’s names and its port, such as db:5432 or db.devvm.internal:5432, to the link. Other programs reach the link by its name directly. The proxy passes a link’s connection on as it is, so it doesn’t look into it and puts none of your secrets into it.

The network rules don’t apply to links. The allowlist doesn’t allow or block a link’s connections, and devvm network deny db doesn’t stop the link db. The rule above and the published ports decide which connections a link carries, and devvm network log shows them (the link log). To stop a link, remove it with devvm link rm, or unpublish its port in the target’s folder.

Listing links

devvm link lists this folder’s VM’s links, with one row for each port:

NAME PORT TARGET FOLDER STATUS APPLIES
db 5432 devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c /Users/you/code/db Running yes
db 8000 devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c /Users/you/code/db Running unpublished

STATUS is the target’s status as its backend reports it, such as Running or Stopped, and it’s empty when devvm can’t tell. APPLIES is yes for a link that works while the target runs, or else it says why the link doesn’t apply:

  • gone: the target VM no longer exists.
  • replaced: the target’s folder has another VM, made again since the link was.
  • unpublished: the target doesn’t publish the port.
  • policy: the target is on a lower network tier than the client.
  • ungrouped: a group made the link, and the two VMs aren’t in that group together any more. You can remove such a link with devvm link rm.

devvm ls shows how many links each VM has, in its LINKS column.

devvm link –json

devvm link --json prints the same list as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. Each of the links has its name, its port, the target VM, the target’s folder as target_folder and its status as target_status, both "" when devvm doesn’t know them, applies, which is true or false, and reason, which is why the link doesn’t apply, as APPLIES shows it, or "" when it does.

{
 "version": 1,
 "links": [
 {
 "name": "db",
 "port": 5432,
 "target": "devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c",
 "target_folder": "/Users/you/code/db",
 "target_status": "Running",
 "applies": true,
 "reason": ""
 }
 ]
}

devvm link publish –json

devvm link publish --json prints what the VM publishes as one JSON object, and it only shows, so devvm refuses a list of ports with it. ports is none or a list of ports and ranges, written as devvm link publish takes it.

{
 "version": 1,
 "ports": "5432,8000-8010"
}

Removing a link

devvm link rm TARGET PORT removes one of this folder’s VM’s links, where TARGET is the link’s name or anything that devvm link add takes:

devvm link rm db 5432 # stop reaching db:5432
devvm link rm pg 5432 # by the name given with --as

The link’s next connection is refused, while connections that are open stay until they close.

When links change

A change of links reaches a running client at once and a stopped one when it next starts, and devvm says which. On a running client, the names resolve at once, because devvm rewrites the client’s /etc/hosts, and a link’s port answers within a few seconds. The VM’s proxy reaches a new link as soon as its port answers, so the programs that use the VM’s proxy settings also reach it, including those that were already running. Nothing in the VM restarts, and the VM’s environment doesn’t change, whatever its tier.

When a target stops or goes

devvm never starts a VM for a link. A connection to a stopped target fails, and each launch of the client warns about each stopped target, until you start it with devvm in its folder. The client’s links then work again without any change to the client. When the target stops, the connections that were open through it end. A link also needs both VMs’ backends to carry links, which every backend of devvm’s does, and when one can’t, each launch of the client says so.

devvm rm of a target removes every link to it from your other VMs and names the clients that lost one. A VM that you make again in that folder isn’t linked, so publish its ports and add the links again. devvm rm of a client removes its links, and devvm stop of a client ends its links’ connections.

A link can’t listen when a program in the client already holds its port in a way that covers the link’s address, such as a server of the client’s own on all its addresses with the same port. That link alone doesn’t work, devvm says so, and the client’s other links work. Stop that program, then run devvm restart.

Groups

A group is a set of your VMs that reach each other’s published ports by name, without a devvm link add for each pair. You join each VM in its own folder, and devvm makes the links between them, so every VM in the group gets a link to each port that every other VM in it publishes. A VM is in one group at a time.

For a database in ~/code/db, an API in ~/code/api and an app in ~/code/app, each with a VM:

cd ~/code/db && devvm link publish 5432 && devvm group join web
cd ~/code/api && devvm link publish 8080 && devvm group join web
cd ~/code/app && devvm group join web

Programs in the app’s VM then reach db:5432 and api:8080, programs in the API’s VM reach db:5432, and programs in the database’s VM reach api:8080. The links a group makes are links like any other, so what this page says about names, ports, network tiers, the link log and stopped targets holds for them too, and devvm link lists them.

Joining a group

devvm group join NAME puts this folder’s VM in the group NAME. The first VM to join makes the group, and devvm says so. A group’s name is made of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starts and ends with a letter or a digit, and isn’t all digits.

devvm group join web # join the group web
devvm group join web --as api2 # join it as api2 instead of this folder's name
devvm group # the group, its VMs and the ports each one publishes
devvm group leave # leave it

When the VM joins, devvm makes the group’s links in it and in each of the group’s other VMs, and it names the links that each VM gains. The links reach a running VM at once and a stopped one when it next starts, as When links change describes. devvm refuses a VM that’s in another group already, so run devvm group leave first, and it refuses a VM whose backend can’t carry links. A VM made again in a folder isn’t in the group that the folder’s old VM was in.

devvm group shows the group this folder’s VM is in, with one row for each of its VMs:

NAME VM FOLDER PUBLISHED
api devvm-api-0f3c2a91b7d4e6 /Users/you/code/api 8080
app devvm-app-5e1d7c08a2b9f4 /Users/you/code/app none
db devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c /Users/you/code/db 5432

NAME is what the group’s other VMs reach that VM by, and PUBLISHED is the ports it publishes, or none. When this folder’s VM isn’t in a group, devvm says so.

Ports in a group

The group’s links reach every port that a VM in it publishes, so you publish and unpublish ports in each VM’s folder, as Publishing a port describes. A port that you publish reaches the links of every other VM in the group, and a port that you take out goes from them, at once on a running VM and at its next start on a stopped one. devvm names the links that each VM gains or loses. A range that you publish gives a link for each port in it.

Names in a group

The group’s other VMs reach a VM by its folder name, as VM names have it, unless it joined with --as NAME. The name follows the rules for link names, and devvm refuses localhost.

  • Two VMs in a group can’t have the same name, so when another VM in the group has the name this VM would join as, devvm refuses the join until you give this VM another with --as NAME. devvm also refuses a name that’s another VM’s folder name, because that’s the other VM’s own hostname. To change a VM’s name in its group, leave the group, then join it again with --as NAME.
  • A VM’s folder name is its own hostname, so devvm refuses to put a VM in a group where another VM’s name is this VM’s folder name, whatever --as NAME you give, because the name would reach the joining VM itself. For two folders with the same name, such as ~/work/api and ~/old/api, have the VM that’s in the group leave it and join again with another name, such as devvm group join web --as api1, then join the other with --as api2. A VM whose folder has a name of its own needs neither.
  • The links that you make with devvm link add take precedence over the group’s. When you link to a VM in the group yourself, the group’s links to that VM take the name your link gives it, and a port that you linked gets no link from the group. When one of your links has the name of another VM in the group, the group’s links to that VM go, and devvm warns you of it, until you remove your link with devvm link rm.

A group joins the trust of all its VMs

A group joins the trust of every VM in it, as a link joins the two VMs’ trust, because code in any of them can often run code in the others through the ports they publish. A VM that joins later gets the same reach into every VM in the group, and they get the same reach into it, so devvm says so on every join. Put VMs in a group only when you’d trust each of them with the others’ reach.

Groups and network tiers

A group’s VMs are all on one tier. devvm refuses to put a VM in a group whose VMs are on another tier, and it names both tiers. It checks joins one at a time, so when two VMs join a group at once, the second is checked against the first, and a devvm that waits for another says so. While a VM is in a group, devvm refuses to change its tier with devvm network, so run devvm group leave first.

Because every VM in a group is on one tier, the group’s links keep the rule that a client links only to a target on its tier or a stricter one. Each of their connections is still refused while the target’s tier isn’t in force as it runs, and devvm warns you of such a target when the group makes a link to it.

Leaving a group

devvm group leave takes this folder’s VM out of its group. It removes the links that the group made, in this VM and in the group’s other VMs, and names the links that each VM loses. The links that you made with devvm link add stay. devvm link rm doesn’t remove a link that the group made, so leave the group, or unpublish the port in its target’s folder.

devvm rm of a VM takes it out of its group, and when the group’s last VM leaves, the group is gone.

devvm group –json

devvm group --json prints the group as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. group is the group’s name, or "" when the VM is in none, and members is [] then. Each of the members has its name in the group, its vm, its folder, and the ports it publishes as published, written as devvm link publish lists them, or none.

{
 "version": 1,
 "group": "web",
 "members": [
 {
 "name": "db",
 "vm": "devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c",
 "folder": "/Users/you/code/db",
 "published": "5432"
 }
 ]
}

Containers in the VM

A container that the docker layer runs in the client has a network of its own, so it neither resolves a link’s names nor reaches its address. Run it with --network host, as in docker run --network host IMAGE, so it shares the VM’s network and reaches the links as the VM does.

The link log

devvm network log in the client’s folder shows its links’ connections, whatever its tier. A line has the time, link for a connection devvm carried or REFUSED for one it refused, the link’s name and port, and the target VM, with why devvm refused it:

2026-11-01T10:00:00Z link db:5432 to devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c
2026-11-01T10:05:00Z REFUSED db:5432 to devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c: it isn't running

When the client is on a confined tier and the target’s isn’t in force yet, the line says unenforced, as Links and network tiers describes.

A client has at most 256 of its links’ connections carried at once, and devvm refuses and logs the next one. devvm network log –json describes the events in JSON.

item.title: A VM's desktop
item.description:
A VM has no screen of its own, but with the desktop layer it gets an Xfce desktop, which devvm desktop opens in a window on this machine. This page covers adding the desktop, opening it, its password and the clipboard, and what it costs. The desktop explains how devvm keeps it to this machine.

Adding the desktop

The desktop is one of devvm’s built-in layers, so only the VMs you choose it for get it, and base and the other VMs stay without it. To add it to a new VM, check desktop under Layers in the list devvm shows when you customize a new VM, or name it with --layers:

devvm --layers desktop # a VM of base with the desktop
devvm --layers docker,desktop # the desktop on top of the docker layer

devvm builds the desktop image the first time a VM needs it, and VMs that choose it share that image. --layers is the exact list of the VM’s layers, so name every layer you want the VM to have.

To give every new VM the desktop, choose it with devvm setup --layers desktop, or add it to the layers you already chose, such as devvm setup --layers docker,desktop. New VMs then get it unless you leave it out when you customize them or give --layers without it (layers for new VMs). VMs that exist keep the layers they were made with.

A VM made without the desktop has none, and devvm desktop says so. To give it one, run devvm layer add desktop, which makes the VM again from an image with the desktop on top of its own layers, such as docker+desktop. The VM keeps its home folder, the project folder and its settings, and loses the rest of its disk, such as the packages you installed, so devvm asks first (adding layers to a VM). devvm layer rm desktop takes the desktop out again in the same way (taking layers out of a VM).

devvm layer add desktop # make this folder's VM again with the desktop, after asking
devvm layer rm desktop # make it again without the desktop

The desktop works on base, and on a base made --from a Debian, Ubuntu or Alpine image.

Opening it 

devvm desktop # serves this folder's VM's desktop and opens it in Screen Sharing
devvm desktop --no-open # only shows its address and password
devvm desktop --clipboard # shares the clipboard both ways, for this run

devvm desktop gets the VM ready as devvm host does, and starts it if it’s stopped. Then it starts the VM’s desktop, unless it’s running already, and shows its address and password:

devvm-website-0123456789abcd's desktop is at
vnc://127.0.0.1:41234
Password: k3mxq7tw
It stays there until you press Ctrl+C.

On macOS, devvm opens the address in Screen Sharing, which comes with macOS and asks for the password. Screen Sharing can keep the password in your keychain, and the address stays the same each time. On Linux, open the address in a VNC viewer of your own, such as TigerVNC’s vncviewer or Remmina.

The desktop stays at that address until you press Ctrl+C, or until the VM stops, and then devvm desktop ends. The desktop goes on running in the VM, so the windows you left open are there the next time you run devvm desktop. It’s 1600 by 1000 pixels.

The desktop is only ever on this machine, and only while devvm desktop runs:

  • devvm serves it on this machine’s 127.0.0.1 alone, so nothing else on your network reaches it. Each VM keeps its port, which no other VM and no program on this machine has. When a program has taken it, devvm chooses another one and keeps that.
  • In the VM, the desktop listens on no port at all, so a VM that forwards every port never forwards it.
  • On a confined network tier, the VM still reaches only its proxy while you use its desktop.

Browsers

The desktop has no browser of its own, so install the one you want in the VM, such as Google Chrome, Chromium or Firefox. Browsers reach the web through the VM’s proxy without asking you for a password, and so do the desktop’s other programs. Browsers ask for a proxy’s password rather than read it from the VM’s proxy settings, so the desktop’s programs use the VM’s local proxy instead. The local proxy is a small proxy in the VM, at http://127.0.77.1:3128, which adds the VM’s password to each request and sends it on to the VM’s proxy. A browser follows the desktop’s proxy settings unless you’ve given it one of its own.

The local proxy changes nothing about what the VM may reach. A host that the VM’s network tier doesn’t allow is still blocked, and a plain http:// page shows the proxy’s reason and the devvm network allow command that allows it. An https:// page shows the browser’s own error instead, such as Chrome’s ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED, so run devvm-why in the desktop’s terminal to see what was blocked.

The local proxy listens on the VM’s loopback alone, and devvm never forwards it to this machine, even on a VM that forwards every port. It starts with the desktop and runs until the VM stops.

The password

Each VM has its own password of eight lowercase letters and digits. devvm makes it the first time you run devvm desktop and keeps it with the VM’s state on this machine, so devvm rm deletes it. The password never goes into the VM, and it isn’t in devvm’s run log. devvm checks it on this machine before a viewer reaches the VM, whatever the VM’s own desktop asks for.

Other users and programs on this machine can also connect to 127.0.0.1, so the password is what keeps them out. VNC passwords are eight characters at most, and devvm lets a viewer try one password a second, so guessing it would take thousands of years.

The clipboard

The clipboard isn’t shared unless you add --clipboard. With sharing on, what you copy on this machine goes into the VM, where a coding agent can read it, and what the VM copies lands on this machine’s clipboard. Without --clipboard, devvm keeps this machine’s clipboard out of the VM, even when something in the VM has changed its desktop’s settings, and the VM’s desktop doesn’t send its clipboard.

--clipboard turns sharing on in both directions for that run, and the next run without it turns sharing off again. devvm can’t stop a VM whose desktop was changed from sending its clipboard to Screen Sharing, so when you don’t want the VM’s clipboard on this machine, also turn off Use Shared Clipboard in Screen Sharing’s Edit menu.

What it costs

  • About 370 MB of disk for the desktop image, which every VM with the layer shares, while base and the VMs without the layer stay that much smaller.
  • About 500 MB of the VM’s memory while its desktop runs, which it does from your first devvm desktop until the VM stops. A VM whose desktop you never open uses none.

When the desktop doesn’t open

  • The VM has no desktop: it was made without the desktop layer. Run devvm layer add desktop to make it again with the layer, as adding the desktop explains.
  • The desktop didn’t start: devvm shows the end of its run log. The desktop’s own log is ~/.cache/devvm-desktop.log in the VM.
  • Screen Sharing didn’t open: open the address devvm shows in Screen Sharing yourself, by typing it into Finder’s Go > Connect to Server, or in another VNC viewer.
  • Screen Sharing says the password is wrong: use the password devvm desktop shows for this VM. Each VM has its own.

item.title: Starting from a container image
item.description:
By default base starts from Ubuntu 26.04’s cloud image. --from IMAGE starts it from a Debian-, Ubuntu- or Alpine-based container image instead, such as node:24, python:3.13, debian:13, alpine:3 or an image you built yourself. Use it when your project needs a distribution or a system package set that Ubuntu doesn’t give you.

devvm --from node:24 # a new VM whose base is node:24
devvm build --from alpine:3 base # just the image
DEVVM_FROM=node:24 devvm # a default for every new VM and build

Everything above base builds and runs as usual, including base’s own setup and the layers (docker and yours). The VM gets its shared tools as any VM does, and shared tools and glibc describes where devvm builds them. devvm keeps the images from each container image apart, so each base and the images on it sit side by side with the others, and each image’s record keeps the container image its base came from and that image’s digest.

--from applies to new VMs and to devvm build and devvm rebuild, and devvm images rm takes it to delete an image on a base from that container image. An existing VM keeps what it was made from, and devvm tools add and devvm tools update build its shared tools for that base. devvm ignores another --from for an existing VM, with a warning.

Images and caching explains how devvm turns a container image into a VM’s disk and how it treats the image’s code as untrusted.

Tags and digests

devvm builds base from the exact image that a tag names when it builds, which is the image’s digest, and it records that digest:

  • When the tag moves to a new image, such as a new node:24, the next build makes a new base. That build happens for a new VM with --from, devvm build, devvm rebuild, devvm layer add or devvm update. The old base is then stale, and the VMs made from it are outdated, which devvm update changes (outdated VMs).
  • Offline, or when the registry doesn’t have the image any more, devvm uses the digest it recorded last, with a warning. With none recorded, it fails.
  • Opening an existing VM never looks anything up, because only builds do.
  • --from node:24@sha256:<digest> pins an exact image, and devvm never looks it up.

devvm reads a reference the way Docker does, so node:24 is Docker Hub’s library/node with the tag 24. A first part with a dot or a port, or localhost, names the registry, as in ghcr.io/org/image:tag or localhost:5000/app. A reference without a tag means latest. Digests explains how devvm asks a registry for them.

Images only Docker has

Public images work from any registry, such as Docker Hub, ghcr.io or quay.io. When a registry doesn’t give devvm the image, devvm takes it from Docker, as long as Docker runs and has it. That covers an image you built and never pushed, and a private one, which you get with docker login and then docker pull. devvm itself never logs in to a registry, and it never pulls, builds or deletes Docker’s images.

If the image’s tag moves to another image while devvm builds, for example because you rebuilt it, devvm stops and asks you to run it again.

Supported images

  • Debian, Ubuntu and Alpine and the distributions based on them. devvm refuses any other, and an image without a shell or /etc/os-release.
  • This machine’s architecture. devvm refuses an image without an arm64 build (or amd64), and names the ones it has.
  • Alpine uses OpenRC and musl, so its VMs get musl builds of the shared tools, built on that image and kept apart for it. Its base also gets GNU tar from Alpine’s packages in place of busybox’s, because devvm sends the VM’s setup and imports agents’ history with it.
  • Unpinned packages. While base builds, its packages come from the container image’s own sources as they are then, apt’s or Alpine’s, and so do the desktop layer’s, the docker layer’s on Alpine and the nix layer’s. devvm keeps no copy of them, unlike base from Ubuntu’s image, so building the same base again installs the sources’ packages of that day, and it needs the network for them.
  • A glibc new enough for your shared tools. A Debian or Ubuntu image’s glibc must be at least as new as each shared tool needs, which shared tools and glibc covers.
  • Tested. The end-to-end tests make VMs from node:24 (Debian 12, with node, python, claude and the docker and nix layers) and alpine:3 (with node, dotnet and the docker, nix and desktop layers), and build base from ubuntu:26.04.

Shared tools and glibc

A shared tool’s build is mounted by every VM that gets the same version of the tool, so devvm never builds one where a container image’s code could change it for other VMs:

  • Debian and Ubuntu images: their VMs get the same builds of the shared tools as VMs on Ubuntu’s own image, which devvm builds in its own base from Ubuntu’s cloud image, never in the container image. When that base isn’t built yet, devvm says so and builds it first, as it does for a VM on Ubuntu’s image.
  • Alpine images: musl builds need Alpine, so devvm builds them in the VM’s own base and keeps them for the VMs on that exact image, by its digest. When the image’s tag moves to a new image, devvm builds the tools it gives those VMs next again, on the new image.

The shared tools are their projects’ own prebuilt releases, and each one is built against a glibc version that it needs at least. devvm reads that version from each tool’s files when it builds the tool’s image, and it reads the container image’s glibc version when it converts the image. When a Debian- or Ubuntu-based image has an older glibc than a tool needs, devvm refuses to give that tool to the VM. The error names the tool, the glibc version it needs and the one the image has, and devvm doesn’t make the VM. The same happens when devvm tools add, devvm tools update or devvm update would give an existing VM such a tool.

To fix it, start from a newer container image with --from, or leave that tool out. Today no shared tool needs a glibc newer than 2.28, so Debian 10 and Ubuntu 20.04 and newer images run all of them, and toolchains lists what each one needs. devvm measures it again for every new version it builds. Alpine-based images get musl builds of the tools, which need no glibc. pi is the one shared tool without a musl build, because its project releases it for glibc alone, so devvm refuses to give pi to a VM on an Alpine-based image, before it builds anything, and the error names pi. Leave pi out of that VM, or start from a Debian- or Ubuntu-based image. devvm doesn’t check base from Ubuntu’s own image, whose glibc is newer than any shared tool needs.

Backends

Lima starts base from a container image by converting the image into a disk (backends).

item.title: What devvm keeps on this machine
item.description:
devvm, the tools it runs and Lima keep files on this machine outside your project folders. This page lists each of them: what it is, who makes it, where it is, whether devvm can make it again, and how it’s cleaned up. Most of it is in devvm’s data folder, ~/.local/share/devvm, and devvm can make all of that again except your exports and what your commands saved, such as your agents’ logins and your secrets. Lima’s own caches hold more, and they can also hold your own downloads.

devvm space

devvm space shows what devvm keeps on this machine and how much disk each kind of thing takes. It changes nothing and starts no VM, and it gives Lima 30 seconds to answer. devvm space --json prints the same as JSON, for scripts (devvm space –json). The first table has a row for each kind of thing devvm has, followed by a total:

Column
WHAT VMs, images, tools gnu or tools musl for the shared tools’ builds for each C library, history for the exports of agents’ history, network logs for the VMs’ logs and the daily tools check’s log, run logs, mise, packages for the copies of base’s packages, Nix cache for the shared Nix cache, leftover state for the whole folder of each VM that devvm gc --orphans would forget, and state for the rest of devvm’s data folder, which includes the rest of the VMs’ folders
COUNT, SIZE how many there are and the disk they take, in powers of 1024 (2.1G)
KEPT remade when devvm makes it again when it’s needed, only copy for VMs and exports, which nothing else has, log for logs, state for what devvm knows of its VMs and images, and leftover
GC what devvm gc frees of it now, which for the Nix cache is what it takes beyond its cap
FREED BY what frees the rest, such as devvm rm, images rm, which deletes images that are current, or gc --nix-cache
RETAIN the retention setting that applies to the row when it’s on, such as 30d, with what it would delete now in brackets, and - when none is on

Sizes count each file’s blocks once, as du does. On macOS a Lima VM’s disk shares its image’s blocks until the VM writes them, so those blocks count for both the VM and its image, and the total can be more than the disk they take. When Lima doesn’t answer while one of your VMs uses it, devvm says so, and its VMs and images aren’t counted.

Lima’s caches

The second table lists the caches that belong to Lima, with what each cache holds, how many entries it has, its size and where it is. That’s Lima’s download cache. devvm’s builds fill it, but it can also hold your own downloads, so it isn’t in the total. The Lima section below says what it holds.

devvm never prunes these caches on its own. devvm gc --caches frees devvm’s share of them, which is what devvm’s builds put there and nothing of devvm’s needs. It lists the entries it would delete with their sizes and asks. Without a terminal it refuses unless you give --force, which frees them without asking.

devvm space –json

devvm space --json prints both tables as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes, and devvm still says on stderr what it says without --json. devvm has a row of the first table each, with sizes in bytes:

Field
what, count, size the row’s WHAT, COUNT and SIZE
backend the backend that has them, lima, for VMs, images and shared tools, left out for the other rows and for a shared tool’s build when devvm can’t tell which backend it’s for
sized whether devvm knows the size, which SIZE shows as - when it doesn’t
kept the row’s KEPT
gc what devvm gc frees of it now
rest the row’s FREED BY
retain, retain_frees the retention setting that applies to the row and what it would delete now, both left out when none is on

total and gc are the totals row’s SIZE and GC. backends has the second table’s rows, each with its backend, name, path, count, size and sized. unknown names the backends that one of your VMs uses that didn’t answer, and strays has the VMs devvm has no state for, each with its backend, name and the data folder its label names. folder_gone has the VMs whose folder is gone, each with its backend, name and folder, and folder_not_connected has those whose folder is on a disk that isn’t connected, with the same fields. devvm leaves these out when they’re empty.

{
 "version": 1,
 "devvm": [
 {
 "what": "VMs",
 "backend": "lima",
 "count": 2,
 "size": 5368709120,
 "sized": true,
 "kept": "only copy",
 "gc": 0,
 "rest": "devvm rm"
 },
 {
 "what": "history",
 "count": 3,
 "size": 3145728,
 "sized": true,
 "kept": "only copy",
 "gc": 0,
 "rest": "gc --history",
 "retain": "30d",
 "retain_frees": 1048576
 }
 ],
 "total": 5371854848,
 "gc": 0,
 "backends": [
 {
 "backend": "lima",
 "name": "download cache",
 "path": "/Users/you/Library/Caches/lima",
 "count": 1,
 "size": 629145600,
 "sized": true
 }
 ]
}

devvm’s data folder

devvm keeps its state in ~/.local/share/devvm, or in $XDG_DATA_HOME/devvm when XDG_DATA_HOME is set. Only you can read it, because each time devvm runs, it makes this folder and the settings folder, ~/.config/devvm, yours alone (mode 700), whatever mode they had, so nothing inside either one is open to others. If devvm can’t, for example because someone else owns a folder, it warns and goes on. Whenever devvm writes into the folders that hold history, logs, keys and secrets, which are exports/, logs/, logs/runs/, run/, secrets/, and the run/, run/ca/ and logs/ folders in each VM’s folder, it makes them only yours again as well, whatever mode they had. Everything in it is devvm’s own, and devvm makes most of it again when it’s needed. The exceptions are the exports, which are the only copy of a deleted VM’s agent history, and the defaults, agents’ logins, keys and secrets that your commands saved.

Path What it is How it’s cleaned up
version, version.lock the folder’s layout version, and an empty file that each devvm checking it locks they stay, and take no space
settings.json the defaults that devvm setup, devvm size -g, devvm ports -g, devvm network -g and devvm retention save, below config.toml’s it stays, and takes almost no space
ssh_config the ssh config for running VMs devvm takes a VM out when it stops or deletes the VM
agent-keys.json the keys in devvm’s own SSH agent and their options devvm ssh-agent rm takes a key out
logins/ your agents’ logins in devvm’s agent store, one folder for each agent, which devvm agent import and devvm agent login save and only you can read they stay until you delete them
secrets/ on hosts without a Keychain, such as Linux hosts, your secrets, one file each devvm secret rm deletes one
custom-secrets.json, custom-secrets.lock the secrets of your own, each with its hosts, header, variable and prefix but never its value, and an empty file that each devvm changing them locks devvm secret rm takes a secret out, and both stay, taking almost no space
vms/<hash>/ one folder for each VM, which holds everything devvm keeps for it in its data folder. <hash> is the hash of the project folder’s path that the VM’s name ends with. The folder holds the VM’s state in vm.json, which records the VM’s name, its ssh alias, its image, folder, backend and settings and the version of the devvm that made it, and the VM’s own network rules in policy. The files of its proxy, port forwarder, link session and sandbox are in run/, with the VM’s host keys for its current start in run/known_hosts, which devvm reads again each time the VM starts, and its logs are in logs/ devvm rm deletes the whole folder with the VM
images/ a folder for each image, named by its key, which holds the image’s record, record.json; the rebuild counters in rebuilds.json, one for each backend, each image that base starts from and each image; the Ubuntu cloud image that base starts from on this machine, in ubuntu.json; and in locks/ an empty file for each image that the devvm building it locks, one, rebuilds, that a devvm changing a rebuild counter locks, one, ubuntu, that a devvm pinning the cloud image locks, and one, packages, that a devvm changing packages/ locks devvm gc and devvm images rm delete an image’s folder and its lock file with the image
packages/ a copy of each package that a first build of base installed, named by its SHA-256, and in sets/ the list of packages each base recorded, named by its key, which building the same base again installs from these copies (base) devvm gc deletes the lists of bases that are neither current nor built, then the copies that no list names. devvm rebuild base records a new list
tools/ the shared tools, one read-only image per tool version, each with a record beside it, <image>.json, which holds its checksum, the backend that built it, the C library it’s built for, when it was built and, once retention finds that no VM has it, since when devvm gc deletes the versions that no VM has and that aren’t the current ones, and devvm gc --tool-images also the current ones that no VM has, except while a VM is being made, each with its record
mise.lock, mise.lock.toml, mise.lock.checked the tools lock, which holds the tools’ versions and their checksums, the config it was resolved from, and when devvm last checked upstream for newer versions devvm replaces them when it checks again
cache/ what devvm makes again whenever it needs it: its own mise, the shared Nix cache, and in from-digests.json the digest that each container image a --from base starts from had when devvm last looked it up you can delete it at any time, and devvm makes each part again when it’s needed. An image built from a container image keeps that digest in its own record, so it stays current without the cache
cache/mise/<version> the mise that devvm runs on this machine to resolve the tools lock, one folder per mise version devvm gc deletes the folders of older versions, which an upgrade of devvm leaves
exports/ the agents’ history that devvm history export and devvm rm save, one .tar.gz per export, each with a .folder file beside it that names its VM’s project folder devvm gc --history deletes them, or with --older-than 30d those that old, and nothing else does
logs/runs/ the run logs, one per devvm run that runs a command devvm keeps the newest 20
logs/tools-check.log the output of the daily check for newer shared tools each check replaces it
vms/<hash>/logs/ a VM’s network log, network.jsonl, which holds its proxy’s decisions, its proxy’s own output, proxy.log, and its link session’s output, links.log. Before the network log or the proxy’s log would grow past 10 MiB, the proxy moves it to the same name with .1 added, replacing the older one, so each of them takes at most about 20 MiB, and devvm network log reads both of the network log’s files devvm rm deletes them with the VM’s folder, .1 files included
vms/<hash>/run/ca/ the certificate authorities that the VM trusts for its proxy, its current one and the next, with their keys, which never leave this machine devvm makes a new one when the current one has less than a week of its 30 days left, the VM’s first start after devvm network open deletes them, and devvm rm deletes them with the VM’s folder
cache/nix-cache/ the shared Nix cache: the packages that VMs with the nix layer downloaded from Nix’s binary cache, once for all of them the VMs’ proxies and devvm gc delete its least recently used files while it takes more than its cap, nix-cache.size, which is 10 GiB when it’s off, and devvm gc --nix-cache deletes all of it
run/ what running VMs need that isn’t one VM’s or whose path must be short, such as the QEMU wrapper on Linux hosts, the claims lock, claims.lock, which devvm holds while it chooses a new VM’s ssh alias or a VM’s host ports, the sockets of port forwarders and link sessions, which are named by hashes, in build-ports/ the ssh port of each build VM that’s starting, and in builds/ a folder for each build VM, laid out as a VM’s folder is devvm deletes a VM’s sockets when it deletes the VM, a build VM’s port once the VM has started or failed to, or, if the devvm that started the VM was killed, the first time it chooses a port 15 minutes later, and a build VM’s folder once its image is built, or else when it deletes the build VM
agent.sock the socket of devvm’s own SSH agent it takes no space
oci-build.lock an empty file that the devvm building a base from a container image on Lima locks, so that one such build runs at a time it stays, and takes no space
tools.lock an empty file that the devvm building shared tools or updating the tools lock locks, so that one at a time writes to tools/ it stays, and takes no space
groups.lock an empty file that each devvm joining or leaving a group, or changing a group’s links, locks, so that they take turns it stays, and takes no space
making.lock an empty file that each devvm making a VM locks, so that devvm gc --tool-images can tell a VM is being made it stays, and takes no space
retention.lock an empty file that the devvm applying the retention settings locks, so that one at a time applies them it stays, and takes no space
lima/ devvm’s own Lima home, with its VMs and images, unless DEVVM_LIMA_HOME moves it see Lima

Which ports each VM forwards is in its state, and its port forwarder’s files are in its own folder too, its log in vms/<hash>/logs/ and the rest in vms/<hash>/run/. devvm rm deletes them with the VM.

The retention settings, which are all off until you set them, make devvm delete some of these on its own: logs.runs keeps that many run logs instead of 20, history.age and history.count delete old exports of agents’ history, tools.unused-age deletes current shared tools that no VM has had for that long, and orphans.age forgets VMs that their backend no longer has. nix-cache.size sets the shared Nix cache’s cap, and each time retention runs, it deletes the cache’s least recently used files while it takes more than that. Retention also writes retention.run in the data folder, when it last ran, and records in each current shared tool’s record since when no VM has had it. It never deletes anything in cache/ but the shared Nix cache’s files.

A build also makes a temporary folder in the data folder, tools-build.<random> for the shared tools, and devvm deletes it when the build ends, even after a failure or Ctrl+C.

Shared tools

Each tool version is built once for each kind of VM that uses it, so tools/ can hold more than one build of the same version. A base on Alpine needs its tools built for its C library, musl, rather than glibc, so a node 24 that both an Ubuntu VM and an Alpine VM use is two builds, and devvm images lists both. Each Alpine container image gets builds of its own, so VMs on two different Alpine images have two musl builds of it. Cleaning up says which ones devvm gc deletes.

Exports

devvm rm saves the history of a VM whose image has an agent before it deletes the VM, so each export in exports/ can be the only copy of that VM’s transcripts and sessions. devvm deletes an export only when you ask it to. devvm history lists the exports, which are named <vm>-<date>-<time>.tar.gz, with their VM, its folder, their date and their size. devvm gc --history lists them by their VM and date, then deletes them, each with the .folder file beside it, after asking in a terminal, and devvm gc --history --older-than 30d deletes only those written 30 days ago or more. gc leaves anything else in the folder alone, such as an export that devvm history export is still writing.

Leftovers of a VM deleted outside devvm

When you delete a VM with its backend’s own command instead of devvm rm, such as limactl delete, devvm still keeps the VM’s folder, with its state, its logs and its backend’s files, the VM’s sockets in run/, its ssh config entry and its host keys. devvm gc also keeps the shared tools that the VM’s state names. devvm rm deletes these only together with the VM, so once the VM is gone it says the folder has no VM.

devvm gc --orphans deletes what devvm keeps for such a VM, as devvm rm does after it deletes a VM. That includes, for a --clone VM, the devvm remote in your repo. gc first asks each VM’s backend whether it still has the VM, lists the VMs it would forget with their project folders, and in a terminal asks. It never deletes a VM, and it leaves a VM’s state alone in these cases, saying why:

  • The backend doesn’t answer, for example because it isn’t installed. When a backend that one of your VMs uses can’t list its images, gc warns and leaves all of that backend’s VMs’ state alone, as it does the rest of that backend’s (cleaning up).
  • The VM was made elsewhere. devvm records where each new VM’s backend keeps it: the Lima home, which DEVVM_LIMA_HOME moves. When this run looks somewhere else, the VM may still exist there. A VM whose state doesn’t record it counts as made in the backend’s default place, so while DEVVM_LIMA_HOME is set, gc leaves such a VM alone.
  • Its state changed in the last hour, because the VM may still be being made.

When another devvm starts to make the VM again in its folder after gc listed it, gc refuses to forget it and stops there, and so does retention’s orphans.age.

Forgetting a VM also removes your other VMs’ links to it, as devvm rm does. devvm gc --orphans also removes links to VMs whose state is already gone, naming each one, and deletes the sockets that a link session leaves on your machine when it’s killed, which are the ones nothing listens on.

Once a VM’s state is gone, devvm gc treats its shared tools like any others. devvm space counts the whole folder of each VM that devvm gc --orphans would forget as leftover state, and each socket a link session left counts there too. A VM that gc leaves alone for one of the reasons above isn’t leftover state, so its folder counts as state and its logs as network logs.

VMs devvm has no state for

A VM can also be the other way around: the backend has it, with devvm’s label, but devvm has no state for it. Usually it belongs to another devvm, such as one run with another XDG_DATA_HOME for a test or a sandbox. devvm space names each one, with the data folder its label names, and devvm never deletes it, because the other devvm may still use it. To delete one yourself, run devvm limactl delete NAME.

VMs whose folder is gone

A VM whose project folder you deleted or moved still takes its disk, and it isn’t leftover state, because its backend still has it and it may hold that project’s work. devvm space names each VM whose backend has it and whose folder is gone, with that folder, and counts it among the VMs. Neither devvm gc nor retention ever deletes one. devvm rm VM deletes it after asking, exporting its agents’ history first (a VM whose folder is gone).

devvm space also names each VM whose folder is on a disk that isn’t connected, with that folder, and counts it among the VMs too. Connect the disk to use the VM again. devvm rm VM deletes one only after you confirm in a terminal, and --force never answers that question (a folder on a disk that isn’t connected).

What devvm doctor finds in vms/

vms/ should hold only VMs’ folders, each named by a hash of 14 hexadecimal digits and holding the VM’s vm.json. devvm doctor warns about anything else it finds there, says what to do, and changes nothing:

  • An entry that isn’t a VM’s folder, such as a file or a folder with another name, which devvm never uses. Move it out of vms/ or delete it.
  • A VM’s folder without vm.json, which a devvm that stopped while making or deleting a VM leaves, for example one holding only the VM’s lock. No VM uses the folder, so delete it.
  • A folder doctor can’t read, vms/ itself or a VM’s folder, so it can’t check what’s in it. Check that you own it and can read it, for example with ls -ld.

These warnings never make doctor fail, and devvm doctor --json lists them in warnings.

Your settings

~/.config/devvm holds what you edit: config.toml, your network rules, your agents’ settings, your own layers, and your company’s CA certificates. devvm also writes the folder’s layout version into version there when the file is missing or older. Your settings lists each file. devvm never deletes any of them.

Lima

The Lima backend’s VMs and images are in devvm’s Lima home, ~/.local/share/devvm/lima. Each image is a stopped VM named devvm-img-<key>, and each project VM is a clone of one. On macOS a clone’s disk shares its image’s blocks until the VM writes them, so du counts those blocks twice. On Linux hosts a VM’s disk is an overlay of its image’s. devvm rm deletes a VM, devvm gc deletes stale and unfinished images, and devvm images rm deletes any image you name.

Lima keeps a download cache of its own, ~/Library/Caches/lima on macOS and ~/.cache/lima on Linux, or $XDG_CACHE_HOME/lima when XDG_CACHE_HOME is set. When devvm builds base, Lima downloads Ubuntu’s cloud image into that cache, which is 600 to 900 MB for each release, and on macOS it also keeps a copy converted to a raw disk, which takes about 2.4 GB more. The cache is Lima’s and it isn’t in devvm’s Lima home, so your own Lima VMs’ downloads share it. devvm deletes something in it only when you run devvm gc --caches. Lima keeps each download in a folder named by the SHA-256 of its address, and gc frees only the folders of Ubuntu’s cloud images at the address devvm downloads base from, for its Ubuntu release, that no image record of devvm’s names and that haven’t changed in the last hour. A cloud image that one of your own Lima VMs downloaded from that same address can be among them, and Lima downloads it again the next time it needs it. No VM needs its entry once it’s made, because Lima copies the disk out of the cache. limactl prune deletes the whole cache, your own downloads included, so devvm never runs it.

Outside devvm’s folders

devvm also changes a few things outside its own folders:

  • The Keychain: on macOS, the secrets you save are Keychain items under the service devvm. devvm secret rm deletes one.
  • ~/.ssh/config: when you let it, devvm adds the line Include ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config so that ssh reaches VMs by name (SSH and editors).
  • Time Machine: on macOS, devvm keeps each VM’s run/ca/ out of Time Machine’s backups, because a copy of a key elsewhere could impersonate any site to that VM.
  • devvm itself: the install script puts each version in ~/.local/lib/devvm/<version> and links ~/.local/bin/devvm to it. A newer install removes older versions that nothing runs (upgrading). Homebrew keeps devvm in its own folders.

Uninstalling removes all of it.

item.title: The command line
item.description:
This page covers what works the same way in every command: the help, flags and their values, the questions devvm asks and what answers them beforehand, --json for scripts, and shell completion. Everyday commands lists the commands, and the CLI reference has every command with all its flags.

Help

devvm help COMMAND, devvm COMMAND --help and devvm COMMAND -h print a command’s help. It starts with a few sentences on what the command does, then its usage line and its examples, the most common first, each with a comment. Then come its commands, if it has any, and its flags, and the help ends with the address of the docs page that covers the command. devvm --help lists the commands in the groups that Everyday commands has, which are Your VM, Change your VM, Images, Disk space and This machine, with help under Additional Commands, and it ends with devvm’s issue tracker after its docs page.

devvm itself takes no word after it but a command’s name, so every word there is a command, and a layer may have any name a command has. When the word after devvm isn’t a command, devvm refuses it as a usage error. If the word names a toolchain, an agent or a layer, your own layers included, devvm points you to the flag that chooses it for a new VM, such as devvm --tools node for devvm node, and a word that joins several with + or a comma gets one line with each flag, such as devvm --tools node --agents claude for devvm node+claude. Any other word gets the closest command, such as devvm stop for devvm stpo. devvm stpo --help and devvm help stpo are refused the same way.

Flags and values

Each flag belongs to the commands that list it in their help, and only -h or --help, -v or --verbose and --no-input work with every command. -v shows the output of the commands devvm runs as they run (details), and --no-input makes devvm ask nothing (questions devvm asks). A flag can come before or after the command’s arguments, and options that take a value also work with an equals sign, such as --cpus=N.

The options for a new VM, such as --tools and --cpus, are taken only by devvm. Another command given one of them, such as devvm ls --cpus 4, fails as it does for any flag it doesn’t know (what a new VM gets).

When a flag or a setting can mean none or off, you write that as a word: devvm setup --features none, devvm --agents none, devvm ports none, devvm retention history.age=off and devvm ssh-agent add KEY_FILE --lifetime forever. devvm refuses an empty value, such as --features '', and an empty argument, so a blank never stands for none or for a default.

Every duration is a whole number followed by a unit, which is m for minutes, h for hours, d for days or w for weeks, as in 30m, 12h, 30d or 2w. That covers devvm gc --older-than, the retention settings’ ages and devvm ssh-agent add --lifetime, and only --lifetime also takes forever, for a key that devvm’s agent keeps until it ends.

Questions devvm asks

devvm asks a question only in a terminal, and each question has a flag or a command that answers it beforehand, so a script never needs to answer one. Without a terminal, with --no-input, or when the input ends before an answer, devvm can’t ask, and every question is handled the same way in all three cases. A question that only adds something, such as an agent’s folders or the Include line, gets its usual answer or a warning that says what to do, and a command that deletes something refuses unless you give it --force.

Question Answered by
the CPUs and memory new VMs get, on the first run --cpus and --memory, or devvm size -g, or nothing: where devvm can’t ask, new VMs get the size they would anyway
the coding agents new VMs get, on the first run and in devvm setup devvm setup --agents LIST or devvm setup --agents none
base’s features, on the first run before the new VM’s summary, or on the first build devvm setup --features LIST or devvm setup --features none
whether to customize a new VM, after its summary --tools, --agents, --layers, --network, --ports, --cpus, --memory and --disk, or nothing: where devvm can’t ask, the VM gets what the summary shows
a new VM’s toolchains, coding agents and layers, when you customize it --tools, --agents and --layers
a new VM’s network tier, chosen from a list when you customize it --network TIER, or devvm network -g with a tier for every new VM, or nothing: where devvm can’t show the list, the VM gets the tier the summary shows
the ports a new VM forwards, chosen from a list when you customize it: every port, none, or the ports you type --ports, or devvm ports -g with the ports every new VM forwards, or nothing: where devvm can’t ask, the VM forwards the ports the summary shows
a new VM’s CPUs, memory and disk, when you customize it --cpus, --memory and --disk, or nothing: where devvm can’t ask, the VM gets the size the summary shows
the layers new VMs get, in devvm setup devvm setup --layers LIST or devvm setup --layers none
a VM’s toolchains and agents, in devvm tools devvm tools add and devvm tools rm, or --json to show them
new VMs’ network tier, in devvm setup devvm network -g
whether to load an SSH key into your agent devvm ssh-agent add KEY_FILE beforehand
whether to restart a running VM to apply a change from devvm size, devvm network, devvm ssh-agent or devvm git-protect, or, as devvm opens it, the changes that wait for its next start, such as an agent’s new folders devvm restart afterwards, or nothing: without a terminal or with --no-input, the change waits for the VM’s next start
whether to add the Include line to ~/.ssh/config --ssh-config on devvm, devvm host and devvm code
a Claude Code token or a GitHub token devvm secret set NAME --stdin
an agent’s API key, in devvm agent login --api-key --stdin
whether to delete, in devvm rm, devvm gc, devvm gc --caches, devvm images rm and devvm secret rm --force
whether to replace the images built on one, in devvm rebuild --force
whether to replace what devvm’s agent store has, in devvm agent import --force
whether to install a release, in devvm upgrade --force
whether to use the VM made for an earlier folder here, in devvm adopt, or to move a VM to this folder, in devvm adopt VM --force
whether to move the VM made for this folder at the path it had before, in any command on this folder’s VM devvm adopt --force

--force only skips a confirmation, and it never deletes more than the command does without it. A command that would delete something asks first in a terminal, and where devvm can’t ask, it refuses unless you give --force.

A few questions protect work that only you can judge, so no flag answers them, and devvm asks them only in a terminal. They are devvm rm deleting the VM of a folder this one is inside or the VM made for an earlier folder at this path, a --clone VM’s commits that this repo hasn’t fetched and its uncommitted changes, a command giving the VM of a folder this one is inside more access, and devvm agent save saving a VM’s settings for every VM. Where devvm can’t ask, each of them refuses and says what to run instead.

With --no-input, devvm asks nothing even in a terminal, and it never reads an answer from a pipe or a file either. A question that has no usual answer fails instead, after devvm shows the question, and the error names the flag or command that answers it. A question fails the same way when the input ends before an answer, as it does when you press Ctrl+D at the prompt.

Output for scripts

Every command that shows or lists something takes --json, which prints what the command shows as one JSON object instead of a table or lines, so a script can read it. The object’s first field is "version": 1, and the page for each command lists its other fields with an example. A shape only ever gains fields. devvm adds new fields to version 1, and any other change to a shape, such as a field renamed, removed or given another type, comes with a new version.

With --json, standard output gets only the JSON. devvm’s messages, such as warnings and notes, still go to standard error, as they do without it, and the JSON is never colored. A list with nothing in it is [], never null. Sizes are in bytes, unless a field’s name gives the unit, such as memory_gib. A field that doesn’t apply, such as a VM’s from when its base is Ubuntu’s cloud image, is left out.

A command that shows a setting when you run it bare and changes the setting when you give it a value, such as devvm network or devvm size, only shows with --json. devvm refuses a value given with --json, such as devvm network open with --json, and changes nothing.

Command Its JSON
devvm ls --json the project VMs
devvm images --json the images and the shared tool images
devvm tools --json this folder’s VM’s shared tools
devvm size --json, devvm ports --json this folder’s VM’s size and ports, or with -g, new VMs'
devvm network --json this folder’s VM’s network tier and allowlist, or with -g, new VMs’ choice
devvm network log --json this folder’s VM’s network log, or with --blocked its blocks
devvm secret --json the secrets, whether each is saved and the VMs using it
devvm ssh-agent --json this folder’s VM’s SSH agent forwarding and devvm’s own agent’s keys
devvm link --json this folder’s VM’s links
devvm link publish --json the ports this folder’s VM publishes to links
devvm git-protect --json this folder’s VM’s .git protection
devvm history --json the saved exports of agents’ history
devvm space --json what devvm keeps on this machine
devvm retention --json the retention settings
devvm doctor --json what devvm needs on this machine and what’s missing, and it prints nothing else
devvm upgrade --json the newest release and how this devvm was installed, and it installs nothing

Shell completion

devvm completion SHELL prints the shell completion script for bash, zsh or fish. The script completes commands, flags and the image names that devvm build and devvm rebuild take, including layers joined with + after the ones you’ve already typed. It also completes shared tools for devvm tools add and devvm tools rm, the lists that --tools, --agents and --layers take, after the names you’ve already typed and their commas, and all and none for --ports and devvm ports. Load it from your shell’s startup file:

Shell Line In
bash source <(devvm completion bash) ~/.bashrc, with the bash-completion package installed
zsh source <(devvm completion zsh) ~/.zshrc, after compinit
fish devvm completion fish | source ~/.config/fish/config.fish

item.title: Upgrading and uninstalling
item.description:
This page covers upgrading devvm, switching between Homebrew and the install script, and removing devvm with everything it keeps. Each depends on how you installed devvm, and your images, VMs and settings stay through an upgrade or a switch, because they don’t live with devvm. Installing and updating explains what the install script and devvm upgrade check.

Upgrading

To upgrade devvm, run devvm upgrade, which installs the newest release the way you installed devvm:

devvm upgrade # install the newest release, asking first
devvm upgrade --check # say whether a newer release is out, and install nothing
devvm upgrade --force # install it without asking, as a script must
devvm upgrade --to 0.1.0 # install that release, even one older than the devvm you have
devvm upgrade --to 0.2.0-rc.1 # install a prerelease, which only --to installs

It says which release it will install in place of the devvm you have, and asks first, so without a terminal or with --no-input it needs --force.

You don’t have to remember to check. When you run devvm in a terminal, it checks at most once a day for a newer release without making you wait, and when one is out it says so in one line that names devvm upgrade. It never upgrades on its own, and release-check = false in config.toml or DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK=1 turns the check off (the release check).

You can also upgrade devvm without devvm upgrade, with the command for the way you installed it:

brew upgrade devvm

If you installed devvm-rc, Homebrew’s formula for prereleases, run brew upgrade devvm-rc instead (trying a prerelease). If you installed devvm with the install script, run the script again, as on Linux.

curl -fsSL https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash

Running the install script again installs the newest release.

Your images and VMs stay, because they live in ~/.local/share/devvm, and your settings and layers stay in ~/.config/devvm, apart from devvm itself.

Images whose inputs changed are built again the next time you use them. Existing VMs keep working, and devvm tools update moves a VM to the new shared tools. devvm gc deletes the copies of devvm’s files that older versions wrote out, except those that a VM’s proxy was started with.

How devvm upgrade upgrades

devvm upgrade tells how devvm was installed from where the devvm you ran is, and it never runs anything to find out:

  • With the install script, devvm is ~/.local/lib/devvm/<version>/devvm, and ~/.local/bin/devvm links to it, or the same folders under DEVVM_PREFIX. devvm upgrade downloads the new release and checks it, as What devvm upgrade checks describes. It unpacks the release into a folder of its own beside the devvm you have, runs the new devvm to see that it works, and then switches ~/.local/bin/devvm to it. When anything fails before the new devvm runs through ~/.local/bin/devvm, the link goes back, so the devvm you had stays the one that runs. The version you upgraded from stays in ~/.local/lib/devvm, and so does any older version that a running VM still uses, until a later upgrade finds nothing using it.
  • With Homebrew, devvm is in Homebrew’s Cellar, and devvm upgrade runs brew upgrade devvm after asking, or brew upgrade devvm-rc when you installed the formula for prereleases. Homebrew may upgrade Lima at the same time, because the formula needs it. Homebrew installs the release its formula names, which can come out a little after the release itself, so until then brew upgrade devvm finds nothing to upgrade.
  • Any other way, such as go install, a build from devvm’s source, or a copy of devvm somewhere else, devvm upgrade can’t upgrade. It says how that devvm was installed and how to upgrade it, such as with go install github.com/devvmhq/devvm/cmd/devvm@latest, and fails.

A devvm built without devvm’s release key can’t check a release’s signature, so devvm upgrade refuses to install a release with it and says to run the install script again.

What devvm upgrade checks

devvm upgrade downloads over HTTPS only, and checks each file before it uses the next:

  1. It downloads the release’s SHA256SUMS and its signature, SHA256SUMS.minisig, and checks that devvm’s release key signed it for that release’s version. The key is built into the devvm you have, so a replaced release can’t bring its own.
  2. It downloads the archive for this machine and checks it against its checksum in SHA256SUMS.
  3. It unpacks the archive, which must hold only devvm’s files in one folder.
  4. It runs the new devvm with --version, which must say the release’s version.

When a check fails, devvm upgrade installs nothing, and the devvm you have stays the one that runs. It checks the signature itself, so it doesn’t need minisign on this machine, as the install script does. It never runs a script that it downloaded, only the new devvm’s --version.

An older release

When the newest release is older than the devvm you have, devvm upgrade refuses to install it, even with --force. A server that offers an old release in place of the newest could bring back problems that a newer release fixed, so devvm upgrade never goes back a version unless you name it. devvm upgrade --to VERSION installs the release you name, newer or older, and it asks first, saying when the release is older than the devvm you have. When the devvm you have is a prerelease of a release that isn’t out yet, the newest release is older too, and devvm upgrade says so and installs nothing, without failing (trying a prerelease).

Homebrew installs only its formula’s release, so with Homebrew devvm upgrade doesn’t take --to.

Trying a prerelease

A prerelease is a version of devvm that you can try before its release is out, such as a release candidate, 0.2.0-rc.1, or a beta, 0.2.0-beta.1. devvm upgrade and the install script never pick a prerelease as the newest release, and the daily release check never announces one, so you get a prerelease only when you name it or when you install devvm-rc, Homebrew’s formula for prereleases.

The docs at devvm.dev are for the newest release. The docs for the next release, which a prerelease comes before, are at next.devvm.dev, and they change as that release is written, so they can describe more than a prerelease has.

Versions go in this order: a prerelease comes before its release, a beta before a release candidate, and the numbers in order, so 0.2.0-beta.3 comes before 0.2.0-rc.1, then 0.2.0-rc.2, then 0.2.0.

With Homebrew

Homebrew’s devvm formula always names the newest release, and the devvm-rc formula names the newest prerelease, or the newest release when that’s newer. Both install the same devvm command, so Homebrew installs only one of them at a time. To switch from devvm to devvm-rc, uninstall devvm first, then trust and install devvm-rc:

brew uninstall devvm
brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm-rc
brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm-rc

To install devvm-rc when Homebrew hasn’t installed devvm before, run only the last two lines. Your images, VMs and settings stay, because they don’t live with devvm.

brew upgrade devvm-rc moves to the next prerelease once it’s out, and to the release once that’s out, so devvm-rc never leaves you on an old prerelease. devvm upgrade runs it for you, after asking, and the daily release check announces each newer prerelease and release. Homebrew installs only its formula’s version, so devvm upgrade doesn’t take --to here either.

To go back to releases only, uninstall devvm-rc and install devvm again, after trusting it if you never installed it before:

brew uninstall devvm-rc
brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm
brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm

devvm installs the newest release, even when that’s older than the prerelease you had.

With the install script

To install a prerelease with the install script, run the copy of the script that comes with the prerelease, which installs that prerelease, or give its version to the newest release’s script with --version:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/download/v0.2.0-rc.1/install.sh | bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash -s -- --version 0.2.0-rc.1

When the install script installed the devvm you have, devvm upgrade --to 0.2.0-rc.1 installs the prerelease too. Both check a prerelease’s signature and checksum as they check a release’s.

While you run a prerelease that the install script installed, devvm upgrade offers the release it comes before once that release is out, and the daily check says so. It never offers a newer prerelease, such as 0.2.0-rc.2, so install one with devvm upgrade --to 0.2.0-rc.2.

To go back to the newest release before the prerelease’s own release is out, name the newest release’s version, such as devvm upgrade --to 0.1.0. devvm upgrade asks first, because that release is older than the prerelease you have.

devvm upgrade –json

devvm upgrade --json prints what devvm upgrade --check says as one JSON object, for scripts, as output for scripts describes, and installs nothing:

  • current is the version of the devvm you ran.
  • latest is the newest release’s version, which is never a prerelease’s, except with Homebrew’s devvm-rc, where it’s the newest prerelease’s or release’s, whichever is newer.
  • newer says whether that’s newer than current.
  • install is how devvm was installed, install.sh, homebrew or other.
  • path is where the devvm you ran is, its links followed.
{
 "version": 1,
 "current": "0.1.0",
 "latest": "0.2.0",
 "newer": true,
 "install": "install.sh",
 "path": "/Users/you/.local/lib/devvm/0.1.0/devvm"
}

One devvm

Install devvm one way, with Homebrew or with the install script, but not both. With two copies, the one that comes first on your PATH is the one that runs, and brew upgrade devvm may update the one you don’t run. So when Homebrew installed devvm, the install script stops before it downloads anything and says to run brew upgrade devvm instead, or brew uninstall devvm first if you want to use the script, and it names devvm-rc in both commands when that’s the formula you installed. It stops whether or not it runs in a terminal, and its --force installs a second copy anyway.

To switch from one way to the other, remove devvm with the command for the way you installed it, as step 5 of Uninstalling shows, and then install it the other way. Your images, VMs and settings stay, because they don’t live with devvm.

After it installs devvm, the script warns when another devvm comes before ~/.local/bin on your PATH. The warning names that copy’s path and says to remove it, or to put ~/.local/bin before its folder in PATH. devvm doctor warns the same way when the devvm first on your PATH isn’t the one you ran, naming both, and the warning doesn’t make it fail.

Uninstalling

  1. Delete your VMs: devvm ls, then devvm rm in each folder. For a --clone VM, this also removes the devvm git remote from the repo.

  2. Delete the images: devvm gc, then devvm images rm with every name devvm images lists. Images built --from a container image need the same --from: devvm images rm --from node:24 base.

  3. Free Lima’s cache. In a terminal, devvm gc --caches frees devvm’s share of it, after asking. If you don’t use Lima yourself, you can also empty its cache: Lima keeps Ubuntu’s cloud images in ~/Library/Caches/lima on macOS and ~/.cache/lima on Linux, and limactl prune deletes that whole cache.

  4. Delete your saved secrets: devvm secret rm NAME for each one devvm secret lists. On macOS they’re in the Keychain under the service devvm, and on Linux in ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/.

  5. Remove devvm itself, with the command for the way you installed it:

    brew uninstall devvm

    If you installed devvm-rc, run brew uninstall devvm-rc instead. If you installed devvm with the install script, remove it as on Linux.

    rm -rf ~/.local/lib/devvm ~/.local/bin/devvm

  6. Remove its state: rm -rf ~/.local/share/devvm ~/.config/devvm. That includes your layers, in ~/.config/devvm/layers, so copy them somewhere first to keep them. It also includes your exports, the agents’ history that devvm rm saved, and devvm’s agent store, the agents’ settings in ~/.config/devvm/agents and their logins in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins. On macOS, the Time Machine exclusions that devvm set on its CA folders and logins folders go with the folders.

  7. If you let devvm add it, remove the Include ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config line from ~/.ssh/config.

item.title: Troubleshooting
item.description:
Each section below starts with what you see, then says what to do, with a link to the details.

A command fails

devvm prints its own steps, and it sends the output of the commands it runs to a log instead of the terminal. When a step fails, devvm prints the end of the log.

To see the commands’ output as they run, add -v or --verbose to any command, as in devvm -v build base or devvm -v. devvm then shows each line on standard error as the log gets it, without the status line, and it still writes the log. The lines are the log’s own, so a VM’s proxy key is hidden in them as it is in the log, and devvm drops the control characters a command prints, so its output can’t move the cursor or change your terminal. When a step fails with -v, devvm names the log instead of printing its end again.

Each run that runs a command has one log, ~/.local/share/devvm/logs/runs/<date>-<time>-<pid>.log, which only you can read, and devvm keeps the newest 20. In the log, each command appears as a + line with its arguments, followed by its output, and a numbered step adds a # [2/5] <step> line first. A command that devvm runs in a VM adds at most 4 MiB of output to the log, because a VM could otherwise fill this machine’s disk with it, and a devvm: truncated line marks where devvm left out the rest. A VM’s proxy key and the build proxy’s password are written as devvm:<key>@. Any other password in a URL, in a command’s arguments or its output, is written as user:<password>@, and so is the password in a proxy’s address without a scheme, such as user:password@proxy.corp:8080, when the address has a port. So a company proxy’s password from your shell’s HTTPS_PROXY, which Lima can print as it starts a VM, stays out of the log, even when a command writes it in pieces. This covers the output of the commands devvm runs in a VM too, such as a VM’s setup or a devcontainer.json’s commands.

Lima keeps a log of its own for each VM, ha.stderr.log in the VM’s folder in devvm’s Lima home, and it writes a proxy password into that log as it starts the VM. Once Lima has started the VM, devvm replaces each password there with as many *, so the log keeps its length and Lima goes on writing to it. If devvm can’t change the file, it warns you and names it, and you can delete the file, which Lima makes again at the VM’s next start.

In a terminal and without -v, a status line shows the step, how long it has run, and the log’s latest line. A step that takes more than a few seconds leaves a line with its time.

A command is refused before it runs

devvm checks a command’s arguments and flags before it does anything else, so a mistyped one never reaches your VM. When one is wrong, such as a missing argument, one too many, a value the command doesn’t take or a flag it doesn’t have, devvm says what the command expected, then names that command’s own help on the last line:

$ devvm ports 5173 8080
devvm: The command devvm ports takes [all|none|LIST], not 5173 8080.
devvm: https://devvm.dev/docs/using/troubleshooting/#a-command-is-refused-before-it-runs
Run devvm ports --help to see how to use it.

Nothing has changed at that point, so you can fix the command and run it again.

Exit codes

devvm exits with one of four codes, so a script can tell what happened:

Code Meaning
0 The command succeeded.
1 The command failed, and devvm’s error says why.
2 devvm refused the command line, such as a bad argument or flag or an unknown command, before anything ran.
130 The command was interrupted by Ctrl+C or a closed terminal (you pressed Ctrl+C).

Two programs can take devvm’s place and exit with their own codes. Once devvm opens a shell in your VM, the shell replaces devvm, so the code is the shell’s, and devvm limactl exits with limactl’s code.

A build fails

When an image’s build fails in its script, or as the build VM starts or stops, devvm keeps the build VM, stopped and without a record, so you can look inside. devvm’s error names the VM and says how to open a shell in it. On Lima, that’s devvm limactl:

devvm limactl shell --start devvm-img-<key>

--start starts the VM first, outside the build’s confinement.

The next build of that image deletes the VM and starts over, and devvm gc also deletes it. A build whose create or clone fails deletes the image, once devvm has shown the end of the log, because there’s nothing in the image to look at.

A first build of base also fails when the packages its VM gives back aren’t exactly the packages apt downloaded, each named by its own checksum with apt’s entry for it. devvm then keeps none of them, so nothing it didn’t check reaches its package cache (base’s packages).

Either way, the images under it, which are already built, stay. devvm deletes and builds again any image it finds without its record, such as a failed build’s or one devvm couldn’t clean up after a crash or a power cut.
